- For **severe allergy/anaphylaxis**, arrange formal follow-up and specify future product modifications rather than simply listing ‘allergic to blood’ without describing the reaction.
- The post-event communication is part of definitive management.

## 9.4 Delayed reactions and longer-term immune consequences

- **Delayed haemolytic reaction** arises when an antibody has waned below detection and reappears after donor antigen exposure.
- Expect unexpectedly low post-transfusion Hb, jaundice, elevated bilirubin/LDH and a newly positive antibody screen/DAT.
- It is particularly important in multi-transfused patients and sickle cell disease; hyperhaemolysis may reduce Hb below the pretransfusion value, making repeat transfusion dangerous except when lifesaving and specialist-directed.

- **Alloimmunisation** complicates future crossmatching and pregnancy.
- **TA-GVHD** presents with fever, rash, diarrhoea, liver dysfunction and marrow aplasia after transfusion; irradiation prevents viable donor lymphocyte engraftment, whereas leukodepletion is insufficient.
- **Transfusion-related immunomodulation (TRIM)** describes potential immunological changes associated with donor exposure, historically linked to postoperative infection or cancer recurrence; contemporary leukoreduction and confounding make causal estimates difficult.
- It is not a separate acute bedside reaction with a definitive diagnostic assay.
- Prevention is principally avoiding unnecessary allogeneic exposure and using appropriately processed products rather than an acute antidote.

- Delayed non-immune effects include iron overload after chronic transfusion (serial ferritin, organ iron assessment/MRI and specialist chelation) and transfusion-transmitted infection.
- TRIM has no diagnostic test or specific treatment; infection and cancer recurrence associations are confounded by disease severity and surgical complexity.
- Do not withhold indicated transfusion on theoretical TRIM grounds.
- PTP: severe thrombocytopenia 5–12 days after exposure warrants HPA antibody testing and specialist IVIG; platelets may be ineffective except with life-threatening bleeding.

### Transfusion governance and consent are also safety interventions

- The transfusion ‘right patient, right product’ check prevents the most catastrophic avoidable acute haemolytic errors.
- Confirm patient identity using independent identifiers and the complete bedside protocol; never assume the pack is correct because the group on a handwritten label looks plausible.
- Document the clinical reason for each component, consent/discussion of expected benefits and risks when feasible, product number, start/end times and physiological response.
- For consent, distinguish donor RBCs from plasma, platelets, specific concentrates, albumin, cell salvage and autologous techniques: patient beliefs and priorities can differ for each.
- If a reaction occurs, retain traceability and communicate with the blood bank to protect **other recipients of components from the same donor**.
- After major haemorrhage, reconcile product use and conduct audit/debrief to identify delays, communication failures or unnecessary products.

items.title: 10. Haemoglobinopathies and haematological malignancy
items.body:
## 10.1 Haemoglobinopathies: why oxygen delivery is not only an Hb number

- Haemoglobin disorders alter globin production or structure, producing chronic anaemia, haemolysis, impaired deformability, organ injury or vaso-occlusion.
- The anaesthetic risk depends on **phenotype, baseline physiology, organ damage and procedure**, not simply whether the patient carries a trait.
- Establish genotype/clinical history, crises, pulmonary hypertension, renal function, transfusion antibodies and baseline Hb before planning surgery.

### Sickle cell disease and trait

- HbS polymerises under deoxygenation, dehydration, acidosis, cold stress and high blood viscosity, causing rigid cells, microvascular occlusion and haemolysis.
- **Sickle cell disease** carries risk of painful vaso-occlusive crisis, **acute chest syndrome**, stroke, AKI, infection (functional asplenia), pulmonary hypertension, cardiac/renal dysfunction and perioperative thrombosis.
- Sickle trait is usually much lower risk but extreme hypoxic/dehydrating stress can matter; do not equate trait with disease.

**Preoperative:**

- Determine HbSS/HbSC/other genotype, crisis burden, previous ACS/stroke, baseline Hb, oxygen requirements, sleep apnoea, pulmonary/cardiac function, renal status, hydroxyurea and transfusion/antibody history.
- Optimise infection and hydration, plan warming, oxygenation, analgesia, thromboprophylaxis and appropriate blood availability.
- In higher-risk procedures selected patients benefit from **preoperative transfusion** (simple or exchange), coordinated with haematology.
- Avoid uncontrolled Hb rise with simple transfusion because hyperviscosity can worsen vaso-occlusion; the goal depends on baseline Hb, genotype and procedure.
- Exchange transfusion can lower HbS fraction without excessive haematocrit.
- Trials show that an aggressive HbS <30% strategy is not universally superior to conservative Hb-based strategies; individualise.

**Intraoperative:**

- Prevent hypoxaemia, hypothermia, acidosis, dehydration, hypotension and venous stasis.
- Use normal oxygenation rather than unneeded prolonged hyperoxia, maintain appropriate euvolaemia, warm the patient and give effective analgesia.
- A tourniquet is a relative risk requiring planning rather than a categorical absolute contraindication in every case.
- **Postoperative:** early lung expansion/mobilisation, incentive spirometry where appropriate, adequate analgesia without excessive hypoventilation, hydration without overload and vigilant observation for acute chest syndrome (new pulmonary infiltrate with respiratory symptoms/fever or hypoxaemia).
- Acute chest syndrome needs oxygen, antibiotics when infection plausible, respiratory support and haematology-directed transfusion/exchange in severe cases.
- Pain crisis must be distinguished from surgical complications, infection and PE.

### Thalassaemia

- Reduced synthesis of α- or β-globin chains causes ineffective erythropoiesis, chronic haemolysis and variable anaemia.
- Trait/minor often causes microcytosis without major anaesthetic implications; **transfusion-dependent thalassaemia major** is a multisystem disease: iron overload may produce dilated/restrictive cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, hepatic dysfunction and endocrine disorders (diabetes/hypogonadism), plus splenomegaly, hypercoagulability and difficult crossmatching.
- Preoperative priorities are echo/ECG, endocrine/metabolic evaluation, transfusion and chelation history, infection status and antibody planning.
- Do not treat microcytosis with iron unless true deficiency is confirmed.
- For major disease, transfusion targets are haematology-specific and not the generic ICU threshold.

### Other haemoglobin disorders

- **HbE and HbC** cause variable microcytosis/haemolysis and may coexist with thalassaemia or HbS.
- **G6PD deficiency** is an enzymopathy rather than a haemoglobinopathy but a useful perioperative differential for drug-/infection-triggered oxidative haemolysis; avoid oxidant drugs according to validated medication lists and monitor haemolysis.
- **Methemoglobinaemia** is a haemoglobin functional disorder caused by oxidant exposure (including some local anaesthetics) or congenital enzymes; suspect cyanosis with saturation gap and confirm by co-oximetry, treating clinically significant cases with methylene blue when appropriate (caution G6PD deficiency).

## 10.2 Haematological malignancies: integrate marrow, treatment and organ effects

- **Leukaemia** may cause anaemia, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, DIC (especially APL), hyperviscosity/leukostasis, infection and direct organ infiltration.
- **Lymphoma** can cause mediastinal mass/airway or SVC obstruction, effusions, cytopenias and immunosuppression.
- **Myeloma** may produce renal impairment, hypercalcaemia, lytic bone lesions, anaemia, hyperviscosity and abnormal immunoglobulins.
- **Myeloproliferative neoplasms** can cause simultaneous thrombosis and bleeding (e.g. essential thrombocythaemia with acquired vWF syndrome at extreme counts).
- Management is driven by the specific diagnosis and active complications rather than one generic ‘cancer precautions’ rule.

### Preoperative assessment

- **Disease activity and complications:** CBC/film, clotting/fibrinogen if indicated, infection/neutropenia, renal/liver function, electrolytes and calcium, transfusion needs, bleeding/VTE history, lytic lesions, organomegaly and possible mass effect.
- **Therapy-related injury:** anthracyclines → cardiac dysfunction
  - Bleomycin → pulmonary injury (oxygen should be titrated to physiologic need, not withheld during hypoxaemia)
  - Alkylating agents → lung/marrow injury
  - Immunotherapy → myocarditis/endocrinopathy
  - Steroids → adrenal suppression
  - Stem-cell transplant → infection and transfusion modification requirements.
- **Blood product planning:** alloantibodies, required irradiation/CMV-safe components, platelet refractoriness, anticipated bleeding and avoidance of unnecessary transfusion.
  - A history of stem-cell transplant or purine-analogue therapy may create specific irradiation indications; consult transfusion service rather than assigning identical rules to all cancers.
- **Venous access:** catheter infection/thrombosis and difficult access may influence planning.

### Anaesthetic implications

- Maintain asepsis and avoid avoidable breaks in infection prevention.
- Neutropenia increases infection risk but is not automatically an indication for broad antibiotics unrelated to procedure; apply prophylaxis and infection treatment appropriately.
- Severe thrombocytopenia/coagulopathy can exclude neuraxial techniques until corrected or risk-assessed.
- Mediastinal lymphoma may produce **dynamic airway/cardiovascular collapse on induction or supine positioning:** investigate CT anatomy, positional symptoms, echo/vascular compression and plan spontaneous ventilation/rescue in high-risk cases.
- High tumour burden and cytotoxic treatment can provoke **tumour lysis** (hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hypocalcaemia, hyperuricaemia, AKI), requiring early recognition, fluid/electrolyte management and haematology involvement.

### Postoperative

- Monitor for haemorrhage, thrombosis, infection, delirium, renal injury and organ toxicity.
- Restart antithrombotic therapy when haemostasis permits, support early mobilisation, coordinate blood product thresholds with the disease team and prevent iatrogenic sampling losses.
- A patient with myeloma and renal injury needs different analgesic/fluids choices from a patient with acute leukaemia and severe coagulopathy.

**Hyperinflammation and neurological toxicity after cellular therapy**

- New fever, hypotension or hypoxaemia after CAR-T treatment can reflect cytokine release syndrome and can coexist with infection.
- Escalate to the cellular therapy team, obtain cultures and treat possible infection and organ dysfunction in parallel.
- New aphasia, inattention, handwriting change, reduced consciousness or seizures suggests immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity.
- Assess neurological change serially and follow centre-specific treatment.
- Tocilizumab used for cytokine release syndrome does not treat isolated neurotoxicity.
- Separately, persistent fever, progressive cytopenias, falling fibrinogen and very high ferritin can suggest HLH.
- Seek haematology input urgently for diagnostic assessment, trigger treatment and specialist control of hyperinflammation.

items.title: 11. Applied cases: from physiology to anaesthetic decisions
items.body:
## Case 1 — Revision hip replacement with Hb 108 g/L, MCV 76 fL, ferritin 12 μg/L

**Think:**

- Iron deficiency, not ‘mild anaemia to ignore’.
- Evaluate history of bleeding and cause, discuss GI investigation when indicated, optimise iron (oral if enough time, IV if shorter interval/poor absorption), quantify expected blood loss, consider TXA and cell salvage, have compatible blood available if indicated.
- Avoid prophylactic RBC simply to achieve Hb 130. In the event of ongoing surgical bleeding, transfusion decisions reflect oxygen delivery and haemodynamics, not baseline screening threshold.

## Case 2 — Open vascular repair, rapidly losing 2 L, cold and hypotensive

**Think:**

- Urgent source control, MHP and balanced warm components, not litres of crystalloid; measure iCa, temperature, gas/lactate, fibrinogen, platelets and VEM.
- Consider cell salvage.
- If FIBTEM indicates low fibrin contribution, give cryoprecipitate/fibrinogen concentrate guided by dose/response.
- Reassess whether bleeding is surgical or diffuse coagulopathic.
- Do not wait for a textbook haemoglobin of 70 before giving RBCs in exsanguination.

## Case 3 — Septic ICU patient, platelets 62, INR 1.6, fibrinogen 4.2, D-dimer elevated

**Think:**

- Possible early sepsis-associated coagulopathy with fibrinogen preserved as acute-phase reactant, rather than ‘DIC excluded because fibrinogen normal’.
- Trend CBC/PT/fibrinogen, search bleeding/thrombosis and organ injury, treat infection/source, assess prophylactic anticoagulation.
- Avoid FFP to normalise INR without bleeding or procedure.
- Exclude HIT/drug effects if timing fits.

## Case 4 — Difficult extubation after surgery and 2 RBC units: saturation falling, bilateral B-lines

**Think:** TACO, TRALI, cardiogenic oedema, aspiration, anaphylaxis and negative-pressure oedema. Stop transfusion, assess BP/JVP/balance, echo/CXR, gas, send reaction samples, support oxygenation/CPAP. Diurese if overload; avoid routine diuretic in pure TRALI. Inform blood bank immediately even if another diagnosis is possible.

## Case 5 — Day 7 ICU, platelets 220 to 72 after UFH, new femoral DVT

**Think:** HIT until assessed, not simply ‘heparin causes thrombocytopenia so stop thromboprophylaxis’. Calculate 4Ts, discontinue all heparin, send PF4/functional testing and start a non-heparin anticoagulant unless bleeding contraindicates. Avoid acute warfarin and prophylactic platelets. Evaluate limb and other thromboses.

## Case 6 — Anticoagulated patient for spinal decompression

**Think:**

- Urgency, indication, last dose, renal clearance, clot versus bleed risk, and exact neuraxial timing/catheter plan.
- Routine perioperative DOAC interruption is **not** identical to ASRA neuraxial guidance.
- Urgent decompression with anticoagulant activity requires senior anaesthesia, surgery and haematology planning, possible drug-specific reversal, and a documented postoperative restart decision.

## Case 7 — Blood-refusing patient for major surgery

**Think:**

- Ask what is accepted: fractions, albumin, autologous salvage, closed circuit, acute normovolaemic haemodilution, erythropoietin, iron and TXA.
- Consent is individual.
- Optimise Hb and haemostasis well ahead, use meticulous surgical control, minimise lab sampling, establish rescue ceiling, involve relevant hospital bloodless-medicine service.
- Respect documented informed decisions.

## Case 8 — Transfusion started 15 minutes ago; severe hypotension, bronchospasm and rash under GA

**Think:** stop unit, oxygenate/ventilate, give adrenaline for anaphylaxis, treat circulatory collapse and assess haemorrhage/surgical field. Notify blood bank, preserve pack, send tryptase and haemolysis/sepsis samples as appropriate. Monitor in ICU and arrange investigation/future product plan; do not treat with antihistamine alone.

### Case 9 — A normal ROTEM but the patient is cold, hypocalcaemic and still bleeding

- After prolonged complex surgery, the patient continues to ooze from multiple sites.
- ROTEM has reasonable clot initiation and firmness, platelets 120 ×10⁹/L, fibrinogen 2.3 g/L; however, core temperature is 33.8°C, ionised calcium 0.78 mmol/L and pH 7.12.
- Explain: the machine warms and recalcifies the sample, so a reassuring trace cannot exclude in-vivo enzyme dysfunction from hypothermia, hypocalcaemia and acidosis.
- First search for an uncontrolled surgical source; actively rewarm, correct calcium appropriately, restore perfusion and reassess bleeding, blood gas and serial haemostatic tests.
- Do not reflexively give more plasma merely because the field looks wet.
- This integrates viscoelastic methodology with NBA critical bleeding monitoring.

### Case 10 — Septic patient, platelets 44, creatinine rising and schistocytes

- A patient with pneumonia has platelets 44 ×10⁹/L, LDH 980 U/L, new renal failure and 2% schistocytes.
- INR 1.1, fibrinogen 4.5 g/L, D-dimer modestly elevated; no heparin exposure.
- The major immediate question is TMA versus severe inflammatory illness, not whether to transfuse platelets.
- Send a clean repeat film, haemolysis markers and ADAMTS13 activity/inhibitor before plasma if feasible, consider PLASMIC-style pretest evaluation, urgent haematology involvement, and start plasma exchange/steroids without waiting for ADAMTS13 if immune TTP is sufficiently likely.
- Do not be reassured by absence of the full TTP pentad.
- Assess STEC and complement-mediated TMA as clinically appropriate.
- Distinguish from DIC because conventional coagulation tests may be near normal in TTP.

items.title: Landmark trials at a glance
items.body:
Interpret each study in its population; a neutral finding does not establish equivalence.

| **Study** | **What was tested and the important result** | **What it changes in practice** |
|---|---|---|
| [TRICC, NEJM 1999](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9971864/) | Restrictive versus liberal RBC triggers in stable critical illness; restrictive was not worse for overall mortality | Avoid automatic Hb 100 g/L in stable ICU patients; exceptions remain |
| [TRISS, NEJM 2014](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25270275/) | Septic shock Hb 70 vs 90 g/L thresholds; comparable mortality with fewer units at 70 | Restrictive strategy usually appropriate in stable septic shock |
| [TRICS III, NEJM 2017](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1711818) | Cardiac surgery restrictive threshold ~75 g/L noninferior for composite serious outcomes | Cardiac surgery need not routinely maintain Hb 90–100 |
| [MINT, NEJM 2023](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2307983) | MI plus anaemia, restrictive versus liberal (<100 g/L) strategy; trend favouring liberal, primary result not statistically definitive | Don’t generalise Hb 70 g/L to active MI without clinical reasoning |
| [PREVENTT, Lancet 2020](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(20)31539-7) | Preop IV iron in anaemic major abdominal surgery improved Hb later but did not reduce transfusion/death primary endpoint | Treat iron deficiency, but don’t promise all IV iron reduces perioperative transfusion |
| [CRASH-2, Lancet 2010](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(10)60835-5) | Early TXA in bleeding trauma reduced death from bleeding; timing crucial | Give within 3 hours when indicated, never replace haemorrhage control |
| [WOMAN, Lancet 2017](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(17)30638-4) | TXA in postpartum haemorrhage reduced death due to bleeding, especially early | Treat PPH promptly with TXA plus definitive obstetric measures |
| [PROPPR, JAMA 2015](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2015.12) | 1:1:1 vs 1:1:2 plasma:platelets:RBC trauma; overall mortality difference not significant, improved haemostasis/exsanguination outcomes | Early balanced components; transition to results-guided treatment |
| [POISE-3, NEJM 2022](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2201171) | TXA in major noncardiac surgery reduced major bleeding, CV safety noninferiority not formally demonstrated | Benefits require balancing thrombosis/stroke uncertainty and procedure |
| [ATACAS, NEJM 2017](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1606424) | TXA in coronary surgery reduced bleeding/reoperation; seizures increased | Dose selection and renal adjustment matter in cardiac surgery |
| [HALT-IT, Lancet 2020](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(20)30848-5) | High-dose TXA in acute GI bleeding did not reduce death due to bleeding; VTE and seizures increased | Do not prescribe TXA for all GI haemorrhage |
| [Villanueva GI bleeding, NEJM 2013](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1211801) | Restrictive RBC strategy in acute upper GI bleeding improved outcomes in a selected cohort | Avoid liberal transfusion once stabilised; adjust for exsanguination/ischaemia |
| [HEMOTION, NEJM 2024](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2404360) | Severe TBI restrictive versus liberal transfusion; primary neurological benefit did not meet significance threshold | TBI transfusion remains individualised, not a universal number |
| [PREPIC2, JAMA 2015](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2015.3780) | Retrievable IVC filter plus anticoagulation did not reduce symptomatic recurrent PE | Avoid adding routine IVC filter when anticoagulation is possible |
| [PAUSE, JAMA Intern Med 2019](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2019.2431) | Standardised perioperative DOAC interruption without heparin bridging in AF, low major bleeding/thromboembolism | Routine DOAC bridging unnecessary in many elective patients; not neuraxial rule |
| [BRIDGE, NEJM 2015](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1501035) | In AF on warfarin, no bridging noninferior for thromboembolism and less bleeding | Avoid routine bridging in common AF scenarios; excluded mechanical valves |
| [RE-ALIGN, NEJM 2013](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1300615) | Dabigatran after mechanical valves led to harm versus warfarin | DOACs contraindicated for mechanical prosthetic valves |
| [RECESS, NEJM 2015](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1414217) | RBC storage duration in cardiac surgery not associated with major organ outcome difference | Standard-issue stored RBCs usually acceptable |
| [ABLE, NEJM 2015](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1500704) | Fresher versus standard stored RBCs in critical illness did not improve mortality | Avoid unproven ‘fresh RBC for everyone’ rules |
| [ANH (Monaco), NEJM 2025](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40503713/) | 2,010 cardiac surgery patients: RBC exposure 27.3% vs 29.2% (P=0.34) with ANH vs usual care. | No proven benefit from routine ANH in this setting. |
| [CRYOSTAT-2, JAMA 2023](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2023.21019) | 1,604 trauma patients; early empirical 6 g fibrinogen-equivalent cryo vs usual MHP; mortality 26.1% vs 25.3%. | Avoid indiscriminate high-dose cryo; replace documented deficits. |
| [TRAIN, JAMA 2024](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2024.20424) | 850 acute brain injury patients; Hb trigger 90 vs 70 g/L; unfavourable neurological outcome at 180 days 62.6% vs 72.6%. | Consider higher thresholds; compare HEMOTION population and design. |
| [SWiFT, NEJM 2026](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2516043) | Prehospital trauma: up to 2 whole-blood units vs RBC/plasma; no demonstrated superiority for death/massive transfusion within 24 h. | Logistical advantage does not prove clinical benefit. |
| [TOWAR, NEJM 2026](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2602167) | Air medical cluster RCT; 30-day mortality 25.9% whole blood vs 20.5% components (adjusted OR 1.24, 95% CI 0.87–1.76). | No demonstrated superiority; not an in-hospital MHP trial. |

items.title: Reading list and linked references
items.body:
## Oxford handbooks

- Core reference 1: Valentine P, Ford P. Chapter 11 — Haematology, pp. 253–290 (Oxford University Press; published November 2021). Used for anaemia classification, haemoglobinopathies, coagulation-factor disorders, interpretation of assays, thrombophilia and anticoagulant pharmacology. DOI: [https://doi.org/10.1093/med/9780198853053.003.0011](https://doi.org/10.1093/med/9780198853053.003.0011)

- Core reference 2: Eaddy N, Cardinal A. Chapter 17 — Blood products and fluid therapy, pp. 449–470 (Oxford University Press; published November 2021). Used for the blood supply chain, component biology, matching, transfusion practice, patient blood management and critical bleeding. DOI: [https://doi.org/10.1093/med/9780198853053.003.0017](https://doi.org/10.1093/med/9780198853053.003.0017)

- Supplementary Oxford cross-references: Chapter 37 (major trauma) for traumatic bleeding and damage control; Chapter 39 (anaesthetic emergencies) for intraoperative haemodynamic collapse and anaphylaxis; Chapter 40 (regional anaesthesia) for antithrombotic block-risk concepts; Chapter 42 (drug formulary) for mechanisms and historical dosing context.

## BJA Education

- **1.**  [**Carroll C, Young F. Intraoperative cell salvage. BJA Education 2021;21:95–101**](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7892352/). Essential for the circuit, washing, benefits, contamination, oncological/obstetric caveats and safety; directly supports the 2024.2 SAQ.
- **2.**  [**Point-of-care viscoelastic testing. BJA Education 2022;22:416–423**](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9596284/). Learn TEG/ROTEM initiation, kinetics, fibrin/platelet contributions, lysis, practical limitations and assay-specific interpretation. Read with its [published corrigendum](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9947957/).
- **3.**  [**Regional anaesthesia in patients at risk of bleeding. BJA Education 2021;21:84–94**](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7892354/). Mechanisms and complications of anticoagulants and the underlying reasoning for neuraxial precautions; **the article’s older timing table must be superseded by 2025 ASRA/local guidance.**
- **4.**  [**Anaesthetic management of abdominal trauma. BJA Education 2025;25:10–19**](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11897445/). Damage-control principles, trauma resuscitation and haemorrhage physiology.
- **5.**  [**Haemostatic agents in the management of obstetric haemorrhage. BJA Education 2024;24:426–432**](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2024.06.005). Fibrinogen, viscoelastic testing and the obstetric bleeding phenotype; detailed PPH is in the obstetrics sets.
- **6.**  [**Patient blood management and perioperative anaemia. BJA Education 2017;17:28–34**](https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkw061). Useful historical teaching framework; read alongside its [2024 corrigendum](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10874730/) and newer NBA/AABB guidelines.

## Australian/New Zealand and international guidance

- [**AABB/ICTMG International Platelet Transfusion Guidelines (2025)**](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40440268/). Updated restrictive platelet thresholds, including low-risk lumbar puncture, compressible-site CVC, major non-neuraxial surgery and avoidance of routine platelet transfusion in nonthrombocytopenic CPB.

- **3.**  [**Australian National Blood Authority. Patient blood management guideline for adults with critical bleeding (2023; minor revision September 2025)**](https://www.blood.gov.au/patient-blood-management-guideline-adults-critical-bleeding). Primary regional MHP source, component ratios, monitoring, fibrinogen dosing and critical bleeding systems.

- **4.**  [**Association of Anaesthetists. The use of blood components and their alternatives (2025)**](https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.16542). Current broad perioperative component and alternatives guidance.

- **5.**  [**Carson et al. AABB International RBC Transfusion Guidelines (JAMA 2023)**](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2023.12914). Stable adult, cardiac, orthopaedic and cardiovascular threshold recommendations.

- **6.**  [**Australian Red Cross Lifeblood. Management of suspected transfusion reactions (updated 2025)**](https://www.lifeblood.com.au/health-professionals/clinical-practice/adverse-events/management-of-suspected-reactions). Immediate reaction response and investigation.

- **7.**  [**ANZSBT Guidelines for Transfusion and Immunohaematology Laboratory Practice (June 2025)**](https://anzsbt.org.au/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Guidelines-for-transfusion-and-immunohaematology-laboratory-practice_June-2025-PUBLISHED-1.pdf). ABO/RhD, compatibility and product/laboratory practice.

- **8.**  [**ASH Guidelines for Prevention of VTE in Surgical Hospitalised Patients (2019)**](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6963238/). Surgical mechanical/pharmacological prophylaxis, extended courses and IVC filter cautions.

- **9.**  [**ASRA fifth edition: regional anaesthesia in patients receiving antithrombotics (2025)**](https://rapm.bmj.com/content/early/2025/01/21/rapm-2024-105766). Dose-specific neuraxial and deep-plexus timing; always check the latest version/local ANZCA protocols.

- **10.** [**ANZCA professional documents**](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/standards-of-practice/professional-documents). Use alongside PG07 pre-anaesthesia consultation, relevant regional anaesthesia and safety guidance.

- **11.** [**ANZCA-endorsed patient blood management resources**](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/standards-of-practice/endorsed-guidelines-and-joint-statements). Regional endorsement/links to NBA guidance.

- **12.** [**National Blood Authority PBM Companions**](https://www.blood.gov.au/companions-patient-blood-management-guidelines). Focused resources on iron, TXA, cell salvage, factor products and preoperative strategies; note historical companion materials are older than the 2023 critical bleeding guideline.

- **13.** [**International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis**](https://www.isth.org/). DIC/HIT/thrombosis consensus resources; verify the specific clinical practice document before quoting a score/threshold.

## Oxford Handbook of Critical Care Medicine (2025)

- Carter A, Singer M, Webb A. Oxford Handbook of Critical Care Medicine, 4th ed, Chapter 12: Laboratory & point-of-care monitoring, pp. 233–264. Oxford University Press, February 2025. DOI: [https://doi.org/10.1093/med/9780199688876.003.0012](https://doi.org/10.1093/med/9780199688876.003.0012) . Main sections used: full blood count, coagulation monitoring and assay limitations (pp. 250–255), TEG/ROTEM patterns (pp. 254–255), lactate and relevant preanalytical pitfalls.

- Carter A, Singer M, Webb A. Oxford Handbook of Critical Care Medicine, 4th ed, Chapter 28: Haematological disorders, pp. 493–510. Oxford University Press, February 2025. DOI: [https://doi.org/10.1093/med/9780199688876.003.0028](https://doi.org/10.1093/med/9780199688876.003.0028) . Main sections used: ICU bleeding and thrombocytopenia (pp. 494–498; 508–509), haemolysis (p. 504), TTP/HUS/DIC (pp. 506–507), haematological physiology and sickle-cell applications.

- [Hegde et al. Goal-directed bleeding management. Australasian Anaesthesia 2025](https://hdl.handle.net/11055/1387) — practical use and limitations of targeted viscoelastic testing.

- [ASH/ISTH/NHF/WFH 2021 Guideline on Management of von Willebrand Disease — major surgery targets.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7805326/)

- [World Federation of Hemophilia — living guidelines and third-edition treatment guidance.](https://guidelines.wfh.org/)

- [AHA/ACC multisociety 2026 guideline: evaluation and management of acute pulmonary embolism.](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2025.11.005)

- [ASH 2020 VTE treatment recommendations, maintained through ongoing evidence review.](https://www.hematology.org/Resources/Clinical-Practice-Guidelines/Venous-Thromboembolism-Guidelines/Treatment)

- [Variability of viscoelastic test thresholds in Queensland major haemorrhage protocols (2025).](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40702708/)

- [How I evaluate and treat thrombocytopenia in the ICU. Blood.](https://ashpublications.org/blood/article/128/26/3032/116533/How-I-evaluate-and-treat-thrombocytopenia-in-the)

- [NZBS Transfusion Medicine Handbook](https://www.nzblood.co.nz/healthcare-professionals/transfusion-medicine/transfusion-medicine-handbook) — Local component handling, administration, adverse reactions.

- [NZBS storage and time limits](https://www.nzblood.co.nz/healthcare-professionals/transfusion-medicine/transfusion-medicine-handbook/3-guide-to-good-transfusion-practice/3-11-removal-from-storage-and-time-limits-for-transfusion) — Theatre handling.

- [NZBS warfarin reversal](https://www.nzblood.co.nz/healthcare-professionals/anticoagulant-reversal/patients-on-warfarin-therapy-with-bleeding) — NZ four-factor PCC.

- [Australasian DOAC guidance 2025](https://doi.org/10.1111/imj.70103) — Interruption, assays, bleeding.

- [AABB AMI transfusion guideline 2025](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40825204/) — Conditional liberal strategy.

- [ISTH updated DIC scoring 2025](https://www.jthjournal.org/article/S1538-7836(25)00220-X/fulltext) — Revised overt DIC score.

- [ISTH TTP update 2025](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40533296/) — TTP management.

- [ASH HIT 2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6258919/) — Diagnosis and anticoagulation.

- [THS Australia/NZ HIT consensus](https://www.mja.com.au/journal/2019/210/11/diagnosis-and-management-heparin-induced-thrombocytopenia-consensus-statement) — Regional practice.

- [Cochrane CD007871](https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD007871_what-are-benefits-and-risks-using-thromboelastography-teg-and-thromboelastometry-rotem-analysers) — VEM evidence uncertainty.

- [ANZAAG/ANZCA anaphylaxis](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/standards-of-practice/perioperative-anaphylaxis-management-guidelines) — Adult management.

- [Association of Anaesthetists sickle cell guideline 2021](https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.15349) — Perioperative management.

- [Association of Anaesthetists cell salvage guideline 2018](https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.14331) — Indications and safety.

- [NZBS guideline for platelet refractoriness](https://www.nzblood.co.nz/assets/Transfusion-Medicine/PDFs/111G002.pdf)

- [AABB and ICTMG 2025 platelet transfusion recommendations](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2025.7529)

items.title: What is the pathogenesis of haemophilia A?
items.q: What is the pathogenesis of haemophilia A?
items.a: - Haemophilia A is deficient/dysfunctional factor VIII, usually X-linked, impairing intrinsic tenase and thrombin generation. Deep tissue bleeding and haemarthroses are typical; platelets and PT are usually normal, while APTT may be prolonged depending on severity and assay. Inhibitors can complicate replacement. Emicizumab shortens APTT and makes standard one-stage FVIII activity misleading.

items.title: How do you plan surgery in haemophilia A?
items.q: How do you plan surgery in haemophilia A?
items.a: - Coordinate with the haemophilia centre: phenotype, baseline FVIII, inhibitors, current replacement/emicizumab and prior response. Plan product, supply, assay and perioperative targets before surgery; major surgery commonly starts around 80–100 IU/dL with declining postoperative targets and duration matched to healing. Give replacement before invasive procedures, monitor reliable levels and avoid unnecessary trauma/NSAIDs. With emicizumab use appropriate bovine chromogenic assays; inhibitor treatment is specialist-led and aPCC combinations risk thrombosis/TMA.

items.title: What are the cautions with desmopressin?
items.q: What are the cautions with desmopressin?
items.a: - DDAVP releases stored VWF/FVIII and may help selected mild haemophilia A or type 1 vWD after assessing response. It is ineffective in type 3 and generally contraindicated in type 2B vWD. Restrict free water and monitor sodium because hyponatraemia/seizures can occur; repeated dosing causes tachyphylaxis. Consider cardiovascular/thrombotic risk, age and fluid status. It is not a substitute for a factor plan in major surgery.

items.title: How do you investigate an isolated prolonged APTT?
items.q: How do you investigate an isolated prolonged APTT?
items.a: - First check sample quality, heparin contamination and anticoagulant exposure. A mixing study that corrects suggests factor deficiency; persistent or time-dependent noncorrection suggests an inhibitor, but drug effects complicate interpretation. Assess actual bleeding and measure relevant factors/inhibitor assays with haematology. Lupus anticoagulant may cause thrombosis rather than bleeding; factor XII deficiency can prolong APTT without a bleeding phenotype.

items.title: What suggests acquired haemophilia A?
items.q: What suggests acquired haemophilia A?
items.a: - New spontaneous extensive skin/muscle or mucosal bleeding in a patient without lifelong/family bleeding, with isolated APTT prolongation and low FVIII, suggests an acquired inhibitor. Exclude anticoagulants and arrange incubated mixing/FVIII/inhibitor testing urgently. Control bleeding using specialist haemostatic therapy and eradicate the inhibitor with immunosuppression. Avoid unnecessary invasive procedures and do not assume ordinary FVIII replacement will work with a high inhibitor titre.

items.title: How do you assess a patient with a family history of von Willebrand disease?
items.q: How do you assess a patient with a family history of von Willebrand disease?
items.a: - Take a personal bleeding history, previous procedural/obstetric bleeding, family pedigree and drug history; a normal APTT does not exclude vWD. Check FBC, VWF antigen/activity and FVIII with haematology, repeating when appropriate because stress, pregnancy and inflammation can raise levels. Define subtype, DDAVP response and procedure risk. For major surgery maintain both VWF activity and FVIII ≥0.50 IU/mL for at least three days and longer as clinically required; DDAVP alone is inadequate for major surgery.

items.title: Why can normal APTT mislead in a haemophilia patient on new prophylaxis?
items.q: Why can normal APTT mislead in a haemophilia patient on new prophylaxis?
items.a:
- Emicizumab can normalise APTT and distort APTT-based FVIII/inhibitor tests without restoring endogenous FVIII.
- Use the haemophilia laboratory’s validated assays, including bovine-reagent chromogenic FVIII where appropriate.
- Other non-factor drugs rebalance antithrombin/TFPI pathways and need their own assessment, monitoring and rescue plan.
- Major surgery and neuraxial safety cannot be cleared by APTT alone.
> **Closing point:** Name the drug before choosing the assay or haemostatic rescue.

items.title: How do you interpret ferritin with raised CRP?
items.q: How do you interpret ferritin with raised CRP?
items.a: - Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant: inflammation can mask depleted iron stores and trap iron through hepcidin. A low TSAT supports iron restriction, even with a ferritin that looks normal. Interpret ferritin, TSAT, CRP, indices and context together; low ferritin remains strongly supportive of absolute deficiency. Do not dismiss iron deficiency simply because ferritin exceeds 30 µg/L during inflammation.

items.title: How do you manage a Jehovah's Witness for major surgery?
items.q: How do you manage a Jehovah's Witness for major surgery?
items.a: - Discuss privately and document decision-making capacity, informed refusal and precisely which components/fractions or autologous circuits are accepted. Do not infer acceptance from religion alone. Optimise anaemia, plan surgery and senior multidisciplinary support, appropriate TXA/salvage and meticulous haemostasis; minimise sampling and dilution. Agree emergency limits, postoperative care and advance directives. Competent adult refusal remains relevant during unconsciousness; children or uncertainty require jurisdiction-specific senior/legal advice.

items.title: What do the recent ANH and transfusion trials change?
items.q: What do the recent ANH and transfusion trials change?
items.a: - The 2025 multicentre CPB ANH trial did not significantly reduce the proportion receiving donor RBCs; selected use needs a realistic indication. FIBRES found fibrinogen concentrate noninferior to cryoprecipitate for component use after cardiac surgery, not the reverse. TRAIN and HEMOTION studied different acute-brain-injury populations/thresholds and had different primary results. Quote population, intervention, endpoint and uncertainty rather than applying one threshold to all patients.

items.title: How should you answer the historical aprotinin debate today?
items.q: How should you answer the historical aprotinin debate today?
items.a:
- Discuss efficacy against bleeding/transfusion alongside renal, thrombotic and allergy concerns.
- The 2007 report predates BART (2008); distinguish historical evidence from later safety data.
- Selected European use is restricted to high-bleeding-risk isolated on-pump CABG; verify local licence and alternatives.
- A restricted approval is not a mandate for all CPB procedures or proof of NZ access.
> **Closing point:** Give a dated, population-specific benefit–risk conclusion.

items.title: How do you detect and treat preoperative anaemia?
items.q: How do you detect and treat preoperative anaemia?
items.a: - Screen early with FBC/indices, reticulocytes and iron studies, adding CRP, renal function, B12/folate and further tests by cause. Hb <130 g/L in either sex is a perioperative screening definition, not an automatic transfusion or cancellation trigger. Identify iron deficiency and its bleeding/malignancy source, treat with oral or IV iron according to time/tolerance, and coordinate surgical timing. RBCs are reserved for clinical need rather than routine haematinic replacement.

items.title: What are the options for iron replacement?
items.q: What are the options for iron replacement?
items.a: - Oral iron is inexpensive but causes GI effects and may absorb poorly with inflammation. Lower elemental doses, about 40–60 mg daily or 80–100 mg on alternate days, can improve tolerance. IV iron repletes faster when surgery is near, oral treatment fails or absorption is poor; monitor hypersensitivity, extravasation staining and formulation-specific hypophosphataemia. Correct the cause and reassess Hb/iron response. PREVENTT did not show universal reduction in transfusion/death from preoperative IV iron.

items.title: How does cell salvage work?
items.q: How does cell salvage work?
items.a: - Shed blood mixes with manufacturer-specified anticoagulant, passes a reservoir filter and is centrifuged. Washing with IV-grade isotonic saline discards plasma, free Hb and most contaminants; labelled concentrated RBCs are returned through the appropriate filter. It supplies negligible platelets/factors, so major haemorrhage still needs haemostatic support. Use low suction, trained operators, traceability and the device expiry; avoid pressurising salvage bags.

items.title: What are the contraindications to cell salvage?
items.q: What are the contraindications to cell salvage?
items.a: - Avoid collecting gross faeces, urine, pus, antiseptic, topical haemostatic agents or unset cement. Sepsis and malignancy are relative, context-dependent cautions rather than universal absolute exclusions; washing/selected filters do not guarantee sterility or complete tumour-cell removal. Obstetric use requires a protocol and RhD assessment. Sickle disease/trait needs specialist evaluation. Respect the patient’s individual consent and accepted circuit configuration.

items.title: What are the advantages of cell salvage?
items.q: What are the advantages of cell salvage?
items.a: - Cell salvage reduces donor RBC exposure and conserves scarce/antibody-compatible blood, particularly in substantial blood loss. It returns the patient’s oxygen-carrying cells without donor storage, and can support some patients declining allogeneic blood. Benefits depend on usable yield and trained staffing; it does not replace platelets/factors, eliminate all transfusion risks or guarantee improved mortality.

items.title: How would you justify introducing cell salvage?
items.q: How would you justify introducing cell salvage?
items.a: - Audit case mix, blood loss, donor units, antibody/refusal cases and expected salvage yield. Compare equipment, disposables, maintenance and training/out-of-hours staffing with potential donor savings. Establish governance, selection/contamination protocols, consent, traceability and competencies. Pilot and audit donor exposure, yield, waste, costs and adverse events. Avoid promising automatic financial break-even or survival benefit.

items.title: What is the mechanism of tranexamic acid?
items.q: What is the mechanism of tranexamic acid?
items.a: - TXA is a lysine analogue that blocks plasminogen/plasmin binding to fibrin and reduces fibrinolysis. It stabilises formed clot rather than supplying factors or raising platelet count. Benefit depends on indication and timing: trauma and postpartum haemorrhage have time-critical evidence, while GI bleeding does not share the same benefit. Dose and renal adjustment follow the relevant local pathway.

items.title: What are the adverse effects of tranexamic acid?
items.q: What are the adverse effects of tranexamic acid?
items.a: - Rapid IV dosing can cause hypotension; seizures are dose-related, especially with high-dose cardiac regimens or renal accumulation. Consider thrombosis history, interactions and context; safety cannot be assumed from absence of statistical significance. POISE-3 reduced bleeding but did not establish prespecified cardiovascular noninferiority. TRACTION 2026 supports a noncardiac policy reducing RBC transfusion with VTE noninferiority on its specified margin, a different endpoint. TXA is not routine treatment for every haemorrhage.

items.title: What are the strategies to minimise blood loss in major surgery?
items.q: What are the strategies to minimise blood loss in major surgery?
items.a: - Apply PBM before, during and after surgery: diagnose/treat anaemia, plan antithrombotics, meticulous haemostasis, appropriate minimally invasive technique, avoid hypothermia, use indicated TXA and selected cell salvage. Limit dilution and phlebotomy; use physiological and evidence-based transfusion decisions. ANH is selective: a 2025 large CPB trial did not reduce the proportion receiving donor RBCs overall. Include consent, equipment/staff readiness and postoperative bleeding review.

items.title: What is the TXA clock and dose for treating postpartum haemorrhage?
items.q: What is the TXA clock and dose for treating postpartum haemorrhage?
items.a:
- WHO: 1 g IV over ten minutes as soon as possible, within three hours of birth.
- Repeat 1 g if bleeding continues after 30 minutes or restarts within 24 hours.
- It accompanies source control/uterotonics and resuscitation; do not wait for a VEM lysis signal.
- Treatment evidence does not justify routine prophylaxis for every birth; keep TXA away from neuraxial drugs.
> **Closing point:** Count from birth and prevent wrong-route administration.

items.title: What coagulation abnormalities occur early after major trauma?
items.q: What coagulation abnormalities occur early after major trauma?
items.a: - Trauma-induced coagulopathy can begin before dilution: endothelial injury, altered thrombin/fibrin formation, platelet dysfunction, fibrinogen loss and dysregulated fibrinolysis. Shock, tissue injury and inflammation interact; phenotypes include hyperfibrinolysis and shutdown. Dilution, hypothermia, acidosis and citrate-related hypocalcaemia worsen it. Do not present activated protein C as a single universal explanation or wait for dilution to diagnose it.

items.title: How is coagulation affected by massive transfusion?
items.q: How is coagulation affected by massive transfusion?
items.a: - Massive RBC replacement dilutes/consumes platelets and fibrinogen and can produce broader factor deficiency. Trauma/shock coagulopathy may already be present. Hypothermia, acidosis and low ionised calcium impair haemostasis; citrate metabolism depends on perfusion and organ function. Use serial clinical/laboratory or validated VEM-guided treatment with balanced initial packs. Avoid using INR alone or treating every prolonged tracing with PCC.

items.title: What was the CRASH-2 finding?
items.q: What was the CRASH-2 finding?
items.a: - CRASH-2 found that TXA reduced death from bleeding in adult trauma when given early; benefit was time-dependent and treatment after three hours was associated with harm in timing analyses. The established regimen is 1 g IV over 10 minutes then 1 g over eight hours. It supports prompt use for appropriate bleeding trauma, not universal TXA for all bleeding contexts or delayed administration.

items.title: What causes bleeding in uraemia?
items.q: What causes bleeding in uraemia?
items.a: - Uraemia causes qualitative platelet dysfunction despite a sometimes normal count and conventional coagulation tests. Anaemia, drugs and dialysis anticoagulation contribute. Treat the bleeding/source, optimise dialysis and anaemia, review antithrombotics and consider short-acting DDAVP with sodium/fluid precautions. Platelet transfusion is not routine correction of uraemia alone. Urgent specialist treatment may include other measures when bleeding persists.

items.title: Why is INR a poor guide to bleeding in cirrhosis?
items.q: Why is INR a poor guide to bleeding in cirrhosis?
items.a: - Cirrhosis reduces both procoagulant and anticoagulant proteins and changes platelets/VWF, creating fragile rebalanced haemostasis with bleeding and thrombosis risks. INR captures only part of this and was standardised for warfarin. Assess actual bleeding, portal hypertension, infection, renal dysfunction, fibrinogen and platelet context. Do not routinely give plasma to normalise INR before every procedure; its volume may worsen portal pressure. VEM is an adjunct with limits.

items.title: When is PCC inappropriate despite a prolonged VEM clotting time?
items.q: When is PCC inappropriate despite a prolonged VEM clotting time?
items.a: - First check fibrinogen, anticoagulants/heparin, sampling, temperature and the clinical bleeding context. Severe low fibrinogen can prolong clotting time and must be corrected. PCC does not replace fibrinogen or platelets and may cause thrombosis; empirical routine PCC for all trauma is unsupported. Use a validated local algorithm and reassess rather than treating one tracing in isolation.

items.title: How does FiiRST-2 differ from FARES-II and PROCOAG?
items.q: How does FiiRST-2 differ from FARES-II and PROCOAG?
items.a:
- FiiRST-2 compared an early FC-plus-PCC replacement package with frozen plasma in a trauma MHP and did not show superiority for 24-hour component use.
- FARES-II favoured PCC over plasma for haemostatic effectiveness in selected bleeding cardiac-surgery patients.
- PROCOAG did not support empirical adjunct PCC in trauma and found more thromboembolism.
- The deficit, population, comparator and endpoint matter; these trials do not support one universal PCC rule.
> **Closing point:** Do not merge distinct factor-replacement questions.

items.title: How is coagulopathy managed in multitrauma?
items.q: How is coagulopathy managed in multitrauma?
items.a: - Control bleeding and activate the local MHP early, with limited crystalloid and balanced components while results are pending. Give timely TXA for appropriate bleeding trauma within three hours of injury, without waiting for VEM. Warm, restore perfusion and correct low ionised calcium. Repeat blood gas, platelet count, PT/APTT and fibrinogen/VEM, then target deficits. Avoid indiscriminate PCC or cryoprecipitate for all trauma; reassess and stop the protocol when controlled.

items.title: What does point-of-care testing offer in major haemorrhage?
items.q: What does point-of-care testing offer in major haemorrhage?
items.a: - Blood gas/Hb and ionised calcium give rapid physiological information; VEM provides whole-blood clot initiation, strength and lysis patterns that can guide targeted products. Early amplitudes are quicker than complete tracings. Limitations include expertise, cost, device-specific triggers, assay temperature, limited endothelial/platelet-drug representation and poor exclusion of DOAC effect. Continue conventional tests and source control; a normal tracing does not rule out clinically important bleeding.

items.title: What is the definition of massive transfusion?
items.q: What is the definition of massive transfusion?
items.a: - Historical massive transfusion is ≥10 RBC units in 24 hours or replacement of a blood volume. These retrospective definitions can miss early exsanguination. Activate a major haemorrhage protocol from ongoing critical bleeding, physiological shock and predicted need, rather than waiting for a numerical threshold. Communicate cause, urgency and trajectory and reassess frequently.

items.title: What ratio of products is used in massive transfusion?
items.q: What ratio of products is used in massive transfusion?
items.a: - Use the local MHP with balanced initial components, then targeted therapy when tests and clinical response are available. Ratios must specify component equivalence: one adult platelet dose is not one donor unit or one bag of every product. Australian guidance gives minimum plasma one per two RBCs and one adult platelet dose per eight RBCs, with early delivery according to severity. PROPPR favoured haemostasis/exsanguination outcomes for 1:1:1 but did not establish an overall mortality advantage. Ensure fibrinogen and calcium are addressed.

items.title: What are the metabolic complications of massive transfusion?
items.q: What are the metabolic complications of massive transfusion?
items.a: - Watch hypothermia, citrate-related hypocalcaemia/hypomagnesaemia, hyperkalaemia, acid–base disturbance and later citrate-associated alkalosis. Coagulopathy, volume overload, pulmonary reactions, identification errors and infection also matter. Use approved warming, rapid serial blood gas/electrolytes, ECG and haemostatic tests, replace deficits and avoid excessive empiric components after control. Treat the shock producing acidosis; do not assume every disturbance comes only from stored blood.

items.title: What do ROTEM LI30, ML and TEG LY30 mean?
items.q: What do ROTEM LI30, ML and TEG LY30 mean?
items.a: - ROTEM LI30 is the percentage of clot firmness remaining 30 minutes after clotting time; a lower value indicates more lysis. ROTEM maximum lysis is percentage loss from maximum firmness; higher means more lysis. TEG LY30 is percentage amplitude loss 30 minutes after maximum amplitude. Their direction and time reference differ. Check platform/reagent/local reference limits rather than transferring one numerical trigger to another.

items.title: What are the components of the lethal triad?
items.q: What are the components of the lethal triad?
items.a: - The classical triad is hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy. Hypocalcaemia is often added as a fourth element. They form a reinforcing cycle during haemorrhagic shock. Stop bleeding and restore perfusion while warming the patient/products, replacing indicated haemostatic deficits and monitoring ionised calcium. Bicarbonate alone does not correct shock-related acidosis or restore haemostasis.

items.title: How is the fibrinogen target defined?
items.q: How is the fibrinogen target defined?
items.a: - Use clinical setting, Clauss fibrinogen or a validated functional-fibrinogen assay and serial response. During major bleeding, replace low fibrinogen, commonly targeting at least 1.5–2.0 g/L; obstetric pathways often target ≥2.0. There is no universal numerical VEM trigger across devices or settings. In NZ, high-fibrinogen apheresis cryo dosing differs from overseas pooled units. Correct documented deficiency and reassess rather than treating a number in a nonbleeding patient.

items.title: What is the difference between FFP, cryoprecipitate and PCC?
items.q: What is the difference between FFP, cryoprecipitate and PCC?
items.a: - FFP supplies a broad range of coagulation factors in a substantial volume, commonly 15–20 mL/kg when indicated. Cryo primarily supplies fibrinogen plus FVIII/VWF/FXIII; NZ high-fibrinogen apheresis units are not interchangeable with overseas pools. Four-factor PCC supplies II, VII, IX and X in low volume, principally for rapid vitamin-K antagonist reversal with vitamin K. It contains little/no useful fibrinogen and is not a universal plasma substitute. All have risks and need reassessment.

items.title: What are the features of DIC?
items.q: What are the features of DIC?
items.a: - DIC is systemic coagulation activation from an underlying disorder, causing microvascular thrombosis, consumption and sometimes bleeding. Look for falling platelets, rising D-dimer, prolonged PT and low/falling fibrinogen; early sepsis may have normal/high fibrinogen. Use trends and an appropriate score. Treat the cause and shock; give components for bleeding/high-risk procedures, not a score alone. Distinguish TTP/HUS, liver disease, HIT and massive haemorrhage. Anticoagulation is selected by phenotype and bleeding risk.

items.title: How do DIC and TTP differ?
items.q: How do DIC and TTP differ?
items.a: - DIC usually accompanies systemic illness with consumption, high D-dimer and often prolonged PT; fibrinogen may initially be high in sepsis. TTP produces thrombocytopenia and microangiopathic haemolysis, usually without marked PT/APTT prolongation; neurological/renal findings vary. Send ADAMTS13 before treatment where possible, but urgent treatment must not await the result: haematology-led plasma exchange plus corticosteroids for suspected immune TTP, with caplacizumab/rituximab considered under the specialist pathway. Routine platelet transfusion is avoided in TTP except life-threatening bleeding or an essential procedure.

items.title: How do you ensure safe administration of blood in theatre?
items.q: How do you ensure safe administration of blood in theatre?
items.a: - Confirm indication/consent and special requirements; perform bedside patient/product identity and compatibility checks according to local policy. Inspect expiry/integrity, use an approved filter/warmer and dedicated compatible line, and record baseline observations. NZBS recommends 0.9% saline for priming/flushing/co-mixing blood components. Monitor closely, especially initially, document traceability and respond promptly to reactions. Do not heat blood above 41°C.

items.title: Why is the haemoglobin trigger flexible?
items.q: Why is the haemoglobin trigger flexible?
items.a: - Hb is one part of oxygen delivery: consider bleeding trajectory, perfusion, ischaemia, cardiopulmonary reserve and physiological compensation. In stable adults, restrictive thresholds around 70 g/L often apply, with selected 75 cardiac/80 orthopaedic or CVD thresholds. Acute MI has distinct 2025 guidance favouring a conditional liberal strategy below 100 g/L with low certainty. Active haemorrhage and brain injury need separate assessment. A higher oxygen requirement may justify a higher, not lower, Hb transfusion threshold.

items.title: What did TRICC and FOCUS show?
items.q: What did TRICC and FOCUS show?
items.a: - TRICC supported a restrictive strategy in selected haemodynamically stable ICU patients; it was not an acute-haemorrhage or acute-MI rule. FOCUS found no functional/mortality advantage to a liberal 100 g/L strategy over restrictive/symptom-based transfusion in high-risk patients after hip-fracture surgery. Both require population and exclusions to be stated; neither proves that every patient should wait until 70 g/L regardless of ischaemia.

items.title: What are the risks of allogeneic transfusion?
items.q: What are the risks of allogeneic transfusion?
items.a: - Acute risks include haemolysis, febrile/allergic/anaphylactic reactions, bacterial sepsis, TRALI, TACO and metabolic complications. Delayed risks include alloimmunisation, delayed haemolysis/hyperhaemolysis, iron overload and selected TA-GVHD/infections. Leukodepletion does not replace irradiation when indicated. Explain absolute risk using current local haemovigilance rather than one universal infection number, and balance these risks against harm from untreated anaemia/haemorrhage.

items.title: When do you transfuse platelets in a nonbleeding patient?
items.q: When do you transfuse platelets in a nonbleeding patient?
items.a: - Use the cause and procedure rather than one universal threshold. AABB/ICTMG 2025 recommends <10 ×10⁹/L for nonbleeding hypoproliferative chemotherapy/allogeneic transplant; selected ICU consumptive settings are conditional. Major nonneuraxial surgery generally uses <50, lumbar puncture <20, and compressible-site CVC <10. These are not neuraxial-anaesthesia thresholds. HIT/TTP/ITP require disease-specific judgment, particularly without bleeding.

items.title: Which blood products require irradiation?
items.q: Which blood products require irradiation?
items.a: - Irradiation prevents transfusion-associated GVHD from donor lymphocytes; it does not replace leukodepletion, CMV strategies or pathogen screening. RBC indications include selected lymphoid disease/treatments, cellular transplantation and certain donor relationships; follow current blood-bank guidance. Not every malignancy or haemoglobinopathy requires irradiated RBCs. NZ platelets are routinely irradiated. Consider RBC expiry/potassium and urgency with the blood bank.

items.title: How long can red cells be out of the blood fridge?
items.q: How long can red cells be out of the blood fridge?
items.a: - Keep RBCs in validated monitored storage at 2–6°C until needed. Start promptly, ordinarily within 30 minutes of removal; if delayed, consult the blood bank about safe return rather than storing in an unvalidated theatre fridge. Complete transfusion within the applicable four-hour limit. Validated transport systems may have different controlled arrangements. These rules do not apply unchanged to platelets, plasma, cryo or salvaged RBCs.

items.title: What if emergency RBC compatibility is delayed by antibodies?
items.q: What if emergency RBC compatibility is delayed by antibodies?
items.a: - Explain urgency to a senior blood-bank clinician/scientist, send correct samples and historical antibody details and control bleeding. Group O avoids ABO incompatibility but may still carry a relevant non-ABO antigen. The blood bank selects emergency-release blood when delay would be more dangerous. Warm autoantibodies can make every crossmatch reactive; seek underlying alloantibodies and best matching without withholding lifesaving transfusion for perfect serological compatibility.

items.title: What patient factors increase the risk of perioperative VTE?
items.q: What patient factors increase the risk of perioperative VTE?
items.a: - Previous VTE, active malignancy, inherited/acquired thrombophilia, age, obesity, oestrogen exposure, pregnancy/postpartum, immobility and major lower-limb/pelvic surgery increase risk. Add acute illness, ICU admission and central venous devices. Assess bleeding risk and use a locally validated tool in its intended population; a score supports clinical judgment.

items.title: How do you reduce perioperative VTE risk?
items.q: How do you reduce perioperative VTE risk?
items.a: - Mobilise early, avoid dehydration and use appropriately fitted intermittent pneumatic compression when indicated. Add pharmacological prophylaxis once haemostasis permits, choosing agent, renal-adjusted dose and duration for the operation and patient. Check neuraxial timing and review daily. Regional anaesthesia does not replace prophylaxis; stockings need vascular/skin assessment.

items.title: What is the pharmacokinetic profile of rivaroxaban?
items.q: What is the pharmacokinetic profile of rivaroxaban?
items.a: - Rivaroxaban directly inhibits Xa, peaks after about 2–4 hours and has a half-life around 5–13 hours, prolonged with age/organ dysfunction. Clearance is partly renal and partly hepatic; strong P-gp/CYP3A interactions matter. Treatment doses 15/20 mg require food. PT/INR cannot reliably quantify or exclude an effect; use a rivaroxaban-calibrated anti-Xa assay when needed.

items.title: How long do you stop dabigatran before high-bleeding-risk surgery?
items.q: How long do you stop dabigatran before high-bleeding-risk surgery?
items.a: - Confirm the last actual dose and Cockcroft–Gault creatinine clearance. For elective high-bleeding-risk surgery, the THANZ 2025 schedule omits dabigatran for two full days before plus the surgery day if CrCl ≥50 mL/min, and four full days plus the surgery day if CrCl 30–49. Neuraxial high-dose intervals differ: ASRA ≥72 or ≥120 hours respectively. AKI, interactions and uncertain timing require reassessment and a specific assay where available.

items.title: How do you plan anticoagulation for a transplant waiting list patient?
items.q: How do you plan anticoagulation for a transplant waiting list patient?
items.a: - Agree a written transplant-centre plan before listing: indication/thrombotic risk, agent, renal function, unpredictable call-up, last dose, testing and reversal availability. A fixed short hold is unsafe in organ failure. At call-up verify actual ingestion, CrCl and calibrated drug testing; delay or reverse only when urgency and residual effect justify it. Dabigatran is dialysable; Xa inhibitors are poorly removed. Andexanet can interfere with subsequent heparinisation for CPB. Specify restart and specialist ownership.

items.title: What is the reversal of dabigatran and anti-Xa agents?
items.q: What is the reversal of dabigatran and anti-Xa agents?
items.a: - Dabigatran: idarucizumab 5 g IV for appropriate urgent/life-threatening indications; reassess for rebound, especially with renal failure. Xa inhibitors: stop drug, haemostatic resuscitation and specialist-directed four-factor PCC when indicated; andexanet depends on current local access/approval and substantial thrombotic risk. US sales ended in December 2025; this does not establish New Zealand availability. Vitamin K, protamine and plasma do not specifically neutralise DOACs. Recheck bleeding and plan restart.

items.title: What are the timings for neuraxial block after LMWH?
items.q: What are the timings for neuraxial block after LMWH?
items.a: - Before neuraxial needle placement: at least 12 hours after low-dose LMWH and 24 hours after high-dose LMWH, longer/assay assessment for impaired clearance when appropriate. For once-daily low-dose postoperative LMWH, first dose ≥12 hours after placement; remove a catheter ≥12 hours after the last dose and wait ≥4 hours before the next. Twice-daily and high-dose regimens have separate restrictions. Four hours after catheter removal is not permission to give LMWH four hours after a new spinal.

items.title: How do you detect an epidural haematoma early?
items.q: How do you detect an epidural haematoma early?
items.a: - Watch for new severe back/radicular pain, progressive leg weakness or sensory change, and bladder/bowel dysfunction; pain may be absent. Do not label unexpected persistent block as routine. Stop the neuraxial infusion, urgently examine and escalate for spinal MRI and neurosurgical assessment. Reverse anticoagulation as directed and expedite decompression where indicated. Frequent documented neurological observation is essential when anticoagulants and neuraxial techniques overlap.

items.title: What is the 4T score?
items.q: What is the 4T score?
items.a: - Score thrombocytopenia, timing, thrombosis/other sequelae, and other causes, each 0–2. Total 0–3 is low, 4–5 intermediate and 6–8 high probability. A fall >50% can be important even if the count remains normal. Typical onset is day 5–10, or rapid after recent exposure. Use the score before immunoassay testing and recalculate if information changes; ICU competing causes reduce specificity.

items.title: How do you manage aspirin and clopidogrel before surgery after a stent?
items.q: How do you manage aspirin and clopidogrel before surgery after a stent?
items.a: - Establish PCI date/type, ACS versus stable indication, complexity, DAPT plan, surgical urgency and bleeding consequences; involve cardiology and surgery. Continue aspirin where feasible. Elective surgery requiring interruption is ideally delayed ≥12 months after DES for ACS or ≥6 months for chronic coronary disease; selected time-sensitive surgery may proceed ≥3 months. Clopidogrel interruption is usually 5–7 days, with neuraxial rules checked separately. Heparin does not replace antiplatelet protection. Restart promptly once haemostasis permits.

items.title: What are the features of a massive pulmonary embolism?
items.q: What are the features of a massive pulmonary embolism?
items.a: - High-risk PE causes haemodynamic instability: sustained hypotension, shock, syncope or arrest, often with acute RV failure, hypoxaemia and a sudden fall in ETCO₂ under anaesthesia. Size alone does not define severity. Call for expert rescue, support oxygenation and systemic pressure, avoid excessive fluid and unsafe induction/ventilation, and obtain bedside echo when too unstable for CT. Anticoagulation and reperfusion decisions depend on bleeding and recent surgery; catheter/surgical options may be preferable to systemic lysis.

items.title: How do you recognise and initially manage acute limb ischaemia?
items.q: How do you recognise and initially manage acute limb ischaemia?
items.a: - Sudden pain, pallor, coolness, absent pulses, paraesthesia or weakness require urgent vascular assessment; neurological loss indicates threatened viability. Document perfusion and Doppler signals, give analgesia and systemic UFH unless contraindicated, and arrange urgent imaging/revascularisation without delaying rescue. After reperfusion monitor potassium, acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, AKI and compartment syndrome. Treat the embolic/thrombotic source and plan ongoing antithrombotics.

items.title: What makes mechanical-valve pregnancy anticoagulation different from ordinary VTE?
items.q: What makes mechanical-valve pregnancy anticoagulation different from ordinary VTE?
items.a:
- Effective valve protection is essential; DOACs are not an alternative.
- VKA gives reliable maternal protection but crosses the placenta; no fetal dose is proven safe.
- If LMWH is chosen, use a specialist therapeutic twice-daily regimen with anti-Xa monitoring, not a standard prophylaxis prescription.
- Plan gestation, delivery transition, neuraxial constraints and postpartum restart with the Pregnancy Heart Team.
> **Closing point:** The maternal and fetal risks change with stage and regimen.

items.title: What do Highlow and intermediate-dose LMWH mean for neuraxial planning?
items.q: What do Highlow and intermediate-dose LMWH mean for neuraxial planning?
items.a: - Highlow did not demonstrate better recurrent-VTE prevention with intermediate than low-dose prophylaxis in its prior-VTE pregnancy population. Higher dosing can reduce neuraxial access after unplanned labour. There is insufficient evidence for one precise intermediate-dose 12–24-hour interval; seek the actual-dose/local specialist plan. Do not extrapolate to acute-VTE or mechanical-valve under-treatment.

items.title: What is the approach to VTE prophylaxis in knee replacement?
items.q: What is the approach to VTE prophylaxis in knee replacement?
items.a: - Balance previous VTE/cancer/immobility against bleeding, renal function and neuraxial procedures. Combine early mobilisation and mechanical measures with the local arthroplasty drug pathway, commonly LMWH or an approved DOAC. Continue the recommended postoperative course, often at least 10–14 days with extension for selected patients. Aspirin is pathway- and risk-dependent: EPCAT II used it after initial rivaroxaban; CRISTAL did not establish aspirin-alone noninferiority to enoxaparin.

items.title: When do you need bridging for warfarin?
items.q: When do you need bridging for warfarin?
items.a: - Most AF patients and many VTE patients do not need therapeutic bridging. Consider only selected very high thrombotic risks, such as recent VTE or particular mechanical-valve situations, with the responsible specialist. Guidelines differ for valves. Weigh bleeding, procedure and interruption duration; document stop/restart and neuraxial plans. A high score alone is not an automatic bridging prescription.

items.title: How do you reverse warfarin urgently?
items.q: How do you reverse warfarin urgently?
items.a: - Stop warfarin, control bleeding and send INR plus full haemostatic tests. For major/life-threatening bleeding or genuinely urgent reversal, give four-factor PCC with IV vitamin K, using the current product/INR/weight protocol. Recheck INR and clinical haemostasis; watch thrombosis. Vitamin K sustains reversal as PCC wanes. Plasma is an alternative if PCC unavailable, with volume/delay limitations. Plan anticoagulation resumption.

items.title: What are the advantages and disadvantages of dabigatran over warfarin?
items.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of dabigatran over warfarin?
items.a: - Dabigatran directly inhibits thrombin, has predictable dosing and fewer dietary interactions than warfarin, usually without routine INR monitoring. Its disadvantages include substantial renal clearance, accumulation with AKI, dyspepsia/GI bleeding, P-gp interactions and rapid loss of protection when doses are missed. Idarucizumab specifically reverses it. It is unsuitable for mechanical valves; dose, indication and renal function still require monitoring.

items.title: How do you reverse heparin?
items.q: How do you reverse heparin?
items.a: - Protamine neutralises UFH, approximately 1 mg per 100 units of recent heparin, adjusted for elapsed time and local limits; give slowly with monitoring. Excess protamine itself impairs coagulation and can cause hypotension, anaphylactoid reactions and pulmonary hypertension. LMWH reversal is partial and product/time-dependent. Check the actual heparin preparation, dose, timing and response; do not apply a UFH formula indiscriminately.

items.title: How do you treat heparin-induced thrombocytopenia?
items.q: How do you treat heparin-induced thrombocytopenia?
items.a: - With intermediate/high suspicion, stop all heparin including flushes, assess bleeding and initiate a suitable non-heparin anticoagulant while arranging immunoassay and, when indicated, functional testing. Argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux or a DOAC are selected by stability, organ function and procedure needs. Avoid starting warfarin before platelet recovery; reverse newly started warfarin with vitamin K. Do not routinely transfuse platelets, except appropriate bleeding/procedural indications. Document HIT and plan duration.

items.title: How does regional citrate anticoagulation differ from systemic heparin?
items.q: How does regional citrate anticoagulation differ from systemic heparin?
items.a: - Citrate chelates circuit calcium and usually needs separate calcium replacement and protocolised circuit/systemic ionised calcium, total calcium and acid–base monitoring. It does not provide systemic VTE treatment. Impaired citrate metabolism can cause falling systemic calcium, rising calcium needs, an increased total-to-ionised calcium ratio and acidosis. Heparin anticoagulates the patient and circuit, with bleeding/HIT risks. Select the strategy to the patient and local expertise.

items.title: What causes apparent heparin resistance?
items.q: What causes apparent heparin resistance?
items.a: - Check dose delivery, sampling and the assay before escalation. High FVIII/fibrinogen can shorten APTT despite therapeutic heparin activity, whereas low antithrombin can reduce heparin effect; ACT is also affected by temperature, platelets and haemodilution. Compare a suitable anti-Xa assay and clinical circuit/thrombotic findings. Clarify assay antithrombin supplementation with the laboratory and seek specialist treatment rather than chasing one number.

items.title: How does VITT differ from ITP or ordinary HIT?
items.q: How does VITT differ from ITP or ordinary HIT?
items.a: - VITT is an exposure-linked anti-PF4 syndrome with thrombocytopenia and thrombosis, often at unusual sites, high D-dimer and sometimes low fibrinogen. Send PF4 ELISA and symptom-directed imaging; rapid HIT tests may miss it. With strong suspicion, involve haematology for prompt IVIg and non-heparin anticoagulation while results are pending. Avoid routine platelets; catastrophic bleeding is an individual exception.

items.title: How do you interpret a low platelet count before surgery?
items.q: How do you interpret a low platelet count before surgery?
items.a: - Confirm the count, trend and blood film; exclude EDTA clumping and review drugs, sepsis/DIC, liver/splenic disease, marrow disease and HIT/TMA. Assess bleeding phenotype, platelet function and procedure consequence. A count of 45 ×10⁹/L does not automatically mandate platelets for every procedure: major nonneuraxial surgery generally uses a 50 threshold, while compressible CVC and LP thresholds differ. Neuraxial decisions need separate cause- and context-specific assessment.

items.title: What IVIg safety points matter in haematology?
items.q: What IVIg safety points matter in haematology?
items.a: - Confirm indication, product, total grams and dosing weight; follow the product-specific infusion chart and distinguish g/kg dose from mL/kg/hour rate. Watch for infusion reactions/anaphylaxis, thrombosis, AKI, aseptic meningitis and haemolysis/positive DAT. Assess fluid, renal and thrombotic risk. An IgG product is not risk-free or interchangeable with platelets.

items.title: What are the compensatory responses to anaemia?
items.q: What are the compensatory responses to anaemia?
items.a: - Lower viscosity and reduced oxygen content trigger increased cardiac output, sympathetic activation and redistribution of flow, with greater tissue oxygen extraction. Chronic anaemia increases 2,3-DPG and shifts the dissociation curve right; these responses are not instantaneous in acute bleeding. Compensation is limited by coronary/valvular disease, beta blockade, age or hypovolaemia. Oxygen delivery remains CO × arterial oxygen content, dominated by Hb-bound oxygen.

items.title: What is your first approach to unexplained ICU anaemia?
items.q: What is your first approach to unexplained ICU anaemia?
items.a: - Confirm the trend and sampling, assess physiology and exclude occult surgical/GI/retroperitoneal bleeding. Consider phlebotomy, haemodilution, haemolysis, inflammation/low erythropoietin, renal failure, deficiencies and marrow suppression. Use reticulocytes, film and directed tests. Treat the cause, conserve sampling and use population-appropriate transfusion decisions; do not give iron or RBCs reflexively.

items.title: How do you manage ITP before splenectomy?
items.q: How do you manage ITP before splenectomy?
items.a: - Confirm ITP and exclude other causes; coordinate a target count and haemostasis plan with haematology/surgery. Steroids and/or IVIG can raise platelets; TPO agonists may be useful when time permits. Platelet transfusion is short-lived but appropriate for major bleeding or urgent surgical support, timed with therapy/procedure rather than categorically withheld. Plan postsplenectomy infection prevention, immunisation and thromboprophylaxis, and monitor for postoperative thrombocytosis/thrombosis.

items.title: How do you recognise platelet transfusion refractoriness?
items.q: How do you recognise platelet transfusion refractoriness?
items.a:
- Confirm the platelet dose and check the count before and 10–60 minutes after each of two adequate transfusions.
- Use the local blood service definition. NZBS describes a poor response as an increment below 10 × 10⁹/L or a corrected count increment below 5,000/µL.
- Investigate consumption, bleeding, sepsis, splenic sequestration and drugs. With suspected alloimmune refractoriness, ask the blood service about HLA/HPA investigation and compatible platelets.
- Agree an urgent plan for active bleeding instead of waiting for specialist testing.

items.title: How do you diagnose a transfusion reaction under anaesthesia?
items.q: How do you diagnose a transfusion reaction under anaesthesia?
