items.a: - Suspect a reaction with otherwise unexplained hypotension, bronchospasm, rash, fever, rising airway pressure/hypoxaemia, haemoglobinuria or diffuse bleeding; anaesthesia can hide symptoms. Stop the unit, call for help and blood-bank advice, support ABC and check identity. Keep IV access using fresh tubing/normal saline; save bag/tubing and send directed samples. Assess haemolysis, sepsis, anaphylaxis, TRALI/TACO and other causes concurrently.

items.title: What do you do for a suspected acute haemolytic reaction?
items.q: What do you do for a suspected acute haemolytic reaction?
items.a: - Stop transfusion immediately; check patient/unit identity and alert the blood bank. Support oxygenation, circulation and renal perfusion with monitored resuscitation, treating shock and DIC. Send repeat compatibility/DAT, haemolysis and coagulation samples and urine, returning the unit/tubing. Monitor potassium, renal function and urine output. Do not routinely force diuresis with furosemide/mannitol in a shocked patient; treat physiology and obtain specialist advice.

items.title: How do you distinguish TRALI from TACO?
items.q: How do you distinguish TRALI from TACO?
items.a: - Both cause acute hypoxaemia and pulmonary oedema and can overlap. TRALI is permeability oedema beginning during/within six hours, without hydrostatic oedema as the main explanation; fever/hypotension may occur. TACO is circulatory overload during/within twelve hours, supported by fluid balance, cardiac findings and response to diuresis. BNP, hypertension or echo alone are not definitive. Stop transfusion, support ventilation; diurese TACO as appropriate, but avoid routine diuresis for hypovolaemic TRALI.

items.title: What suggests delayed haemolysis or hyperhaemolysis after transfusion?
items.q: What suggests delayed haemolysis or hyperhaemolysis after transfusion?
items.a: - Days to weeks after transfusion, falling Hb, jaundice, dark urine and rising haemolysis markers suggest delayed immune haemolysis; antibodies may have been historically undetectable. In SCD, hyperhaemolysis can lower Hb below the pretransfusion value and may occur without a positive DAT. Involve haematology/blood bank urgently: further transfusion can worsen it and needs specialist justification/matching and treatment.

items.title: What suggests post-transfusion purpura?
items.q: What suggests post-transfusion purpura?
items.a: - Profound thrombocytopenia with bleeding about 5–12 days after cellular transfusion, often in someone previously sensitised by pregnancy/transfusion. Recipient anti-HPA responses cause donor and bystander platelet destruction. Notify blood bank/haematology, test HPA antibodies and use specialist IVIg. Avoid routine random-donor platelets; life-threatening bleeding needs selected support and future product planning.

items.title: What are the anaesthetic issues in haematological malignancy?
items.q: What are the anaesthetic issues in haematological malignancy?
items.a: - Assess anaemia, thrombocytopenia/qualitative dysfunction, neutropenic infection and both bleeding and thrombosis. Consider tumour lysis with K/phosphate/uric-acid changes, hyperviscosity/leukostasis, DIC in APL, mediastinal masses and bone disease. Review chemotherapy-related cardiac/pulmonary/renal injury, steroids and interactions. Coordinate counts/products and infection management with haematology; irradiated RBC requirements depend on diagnosis/treatment, not every malignancy. NZ platelets are routinely irradiated.

items.title: When should you suspect HLH in ICU?
items.q: When should you suspect HLH in ICU?
items.a: - Persistent fever, falling counts and a markedly high/rising ferritin with organ dysfunction should trigger an HLH assessment, especially when expected improvement with sepsis treatment does not occur. Check fibrinogen, triglycerides, liver tests and HScore with specialist input. Ferritin alone is not diagnostic; marrow haemophagocytosis is neither required nor specific. Infection and HLH can coexist.

items.title: What are the immediate treatment priorities in probable HLH?
items.q: What are the immediate treatment priorities in probable HLH?
items.a: - Support failing organs, continue indicated antimicrobials and call the specialist team. Treat hyperinflammation and investigate/treat triggers in parallel. Glucocorticoids, anakinra and/or IVIg are context-dependent initial options; selected cases need etoposide or other directed therapy. Avoid delaying treatment for every diagnostic result. Follow counts, ferritin, fibrinogen and organ response.

items.title: What are the perioperative problems of sickle cell disease?
items.q: What are the perioperative problems of sickle cell disease?
items.a: - SCD causes haemolytic anaemia, vaso-occlusive pain, acute chest syndrome and multiorgan injury; consider renal/cardiopulmonary disease, stroke, transfusion antibodies and chronic therapy. Avoid hypoxaemia, hypothermia, dehydration, acidosis, pain and prolonged stasis without causing fluid overload. Coordinate analgesia, respiratory care, VTE prophylaxis and a haematology transfusion plan. HbSC and sickle β-thalassaemia may have important disease despite a higher baseline Hb.

items.title: What is the role of exchange transfusion in sickle cell disease?
items.q: What is the role of exchange transfusion in sickle cell disease?
items.a: - Exchange lowers HbS without an excessive rise in viscosity and is considered for severe disease, high-risk surgery or a baseline Hb too high for simple transfusion. ASH suggests individualised preoperative transfusion for operations under GA lasting over one hour, rather than universal exchange. A typical postoperative Hb range is 90–110 g/L; HbS <30% is reserved for selected high-risk settings, not every case. Consider alloimmunisation, compatible matching and delayed hyperhaemolysis.

items.title: What is the key airway feature of thalassaemia major?
items.q: What is the key airway feature of thalassaemia major?
items.a: - Marrow expansion can cause maxillary prominence and facial changes, potentially complicating mask fit/intubation, but airway assessment must be individual. Other major issues are chronic anaemia, transfusional iron overload with cardiac/endocrine/liver disease, antibodies, splenectomy-related sepsis/thrombosis and chelation effects. Thalassaemia trait differs greatly from transfusion-dependent disease; do not reduce the condition to one airway sign.

items.title: How do HbC, HbE and sickle variants change the haemoglobinopathy overview?
items.q: How do HbC, HbE and sickle variants change the haemoglobinopathy overview?
items.a: - Sickle variants include HbSS, HbSC and sickle β-thalassaemia, with different anaemia and vaso-occlusive phenotypes. HbC disease can cause haemolysis, while HbSC carries sickling risk. HbE trait is usually mild but HbE/β-thalassaemia can be severe. α/β-thalassaemia range from trait to transfusion-dependent disease. Identify the genotype, phenotype and organ/transfusion history. G6PD deficiency is an enzymopathy rather than a structural haemoglobinopathy.

items.title: Why is acute promyelocytic leukaemia a haemostatic emergency?
items.q: Why is acute promyelocytic leukaemia a haemostatic emergency?
items.a: - APL can cause severe DIC and hyperfibrinolysis with catastrophic bleeding and thrombosis. Urgently involve haematology, obtain film/coagulation/fibrinogen trends and support platelets/fibrinogen according to the specialist pathway. Start disease-specific treatment promptly when suspected under haematology direction. Avoid nonessential invasive procedures and do not treat this as uncomplicated isolated thrombocytopenia.

items.title: How do you distinguish CAR-T CRS from ICANS?
items.q: How do you distinguish CAR-T CRS from ICANS?
items.a: - CRS typically causes fever with hypoxia/hypotension; treat possible infection concurrently, support organs and use the CAR-T centre grading/treatment pathway, including tocilizumab when indicated. ICANS causes language, attention, handwriting or consciousness change and seizures. Assess ICE score, exclude mimics and obtain neurological/ICU help. Steroids are central for significant ICANS; tocilizumab alone is not treatment of isolated ICANS.

items.title: 1. A 55-year-old Jehovah's Witness with a haemoglobin of 105 g/L is scheduled for…
items.q: A 55-year-old Jehovah's Witness with a haemoglobin of 105 g/L is scheduled for an elective major abdominal operation. Discuss your perioperative management.
items.a:
### Consent and a feasible treatment plan

- Discuss privately with the patient, check capacity/voluntariness and document **each accepted or declined intervention:** donor RBC/plasma/platelets, cryoprecipitate, fractions/concentrates, albumin, cell salvage, continuous circuit, swab washing and ANH.
- Do not infer choices from religion or ask relatives to overrule a capable adult.
- Explain expected blood loss, residual risk including death, alternatives, advance decisions and emergency limits.
- Involve senior surgery/anaesthesia, haematology/PBM and a liaison service if the patient wants.
- If an elective operation cannot be offered within those limits, arrange an alternative team/approach with continuity of care; do not abandon care.

### Optimise before elective major surgery

- Hb 105 g/L warrants cause-based investigation: FBC/indices, reticulocytes, ferritin/TSAT with CRP, renal function, B12/folate when indicated and investigation of losses.
- Correct genuine deficiencies, use IV iron if the interval/absorption favours it, and consider ESA only with specialist advice, thrombosis assessment and acceptability of the preparation.
- Recheck response and discuss deferral/less invasive surgery; do not aim “as high as possible” with an ESA.
- Review antithrombotics and bleeding disorders, minimise sampling and agree the surgical rescue plan.

### Theatre and postoperative conservation

- Experienced surgery, meticulous haemostasis, appropriate TXA, accepted salvage/selected ANH, normothermia, physiological calcium/pH and targeted haemostatic agents if accepted.
- Deliberate hypotension is not safe simply because donor blood is refused—maintain coronary/cerebral/renal perfusion.
- Maximise oxygenation and flow and reduce avoidable demand (pain, fever, shivering)
- **do not deliberately cool the patient**, which worsens coagulopathy. rFVIIa and haemoglobin-based oxygen carriers are not routine substitutes
- Exceptional rescue needs specialist/regulatory access and individual consent.

- Include senior theatre briefing, ready access to the documented choices and a plan for deterioration.
- Explicitly discuss acceptability of RRT, plasma exchange or ECMO if relevant; acceptance of salvage does not imply acceptance of every circuit.
- If wishes are unclear during incapacity, urgently involve senior clinical/medicolegal support under the local jurisdiction.
- A conscious patient may change a decision, but reassess capacity, pain/distress and possible coercion rather than pressuring them mid-crisis.
- Arrange staff support after a serious adverse outcome.

Plan monitored recovery/ICU according to risk, detect ongoing loss early, minimise phlebotomy, treat deficiency and continue a documented anaemia/thrombosis strategy. Record the accepted emergency ceiling clearly for every team.

## Self-marking checklist

- Individual capacity/consent and exact product choices
- Documents emergency limits and coordinates an appropriate team
- Investigates Hb 105 and treats the cause before elective surgery
- Uses selective iron/ESA with reassessment
- Appropriate TXA/salvage/ANH only if accepted
- Maintains perfusion and normothermia, avoids unproven routine rescue
- Postoperative monitoring, sampling conservation and handover

items.title: 2. Discuss the principles of patient blood management in the perioperative period…
items.q: Discuss the principles of patient blood management in the perioperative period and the evidence for restrictive versus liberal transfusion thresholds.
items.a:
### Three PBM pillars across the pathway

**Optimise red-cell mass/haemostasis:**

- Early Hb and cause-based anaemia investigation, iron/B12/folate treatment where indicated, selective ESA, bleeding-history/drug review, appropriate surgery timing and blood-bank planning.
- **Reduce loss:** expert surgical control, appropriate TXA, selected salvage/ANH, normothermia/physiological iCa, targeted components and reduced phlebotomy.
- **Optimise tolerance of anaemia:** oxygenation, cardiac output/perfusion, reduce unnecessary demand and use an individualised transfusion decision.
- Hb130 is an optimisation/screening aim, not an RBC transfusion target.

### Evidence: populations and outcomes matter

- TRICC supports a restrictive approach in many stable ICU adults; TRISS found no mortality advantage from a 90 versus 70 g/L trigger in septic shock, with fewer RBCs at 70. FOCUS did not improve its main functional/mortality outcome with routine Hb100 versus Hb80/symptoms after hip fracture.
- TRICS III supports a restrictive ~75 trigger in its cardiac-surgery population; TITRe2's secondary mortality signal reminds us not to equate every trial/outcome.
- **MINT** in MI did not meet statistical superiority for the primary liberal-versus-restrictive comparison, but possible harm from restriction remained; **2025 AABB conditionally suggests a liberal strategy at Hb <100 g/L in AMI**, low-certainty evidence.

- Acute brain injury is another exception to blanket generalisation: **TRAIN** found better neurological outcome with a 90 versus 70 trigger in its mixed brain-injury population; **HEMOTION** did not show statistically definitive primary neurological benefit of 100 versus 70 in moderate/severe TBI.
- **SAHARA** (2025 issue) did not establish primary neurological benefit of mandatory Hb≤100 versus optional Hb≤80 transfusion after aneurysmal SAH.
- Different populations, thresholds and endpoints mean these trials do not establish one universal neurocritical threshold.
- See R36 for the full comparison.
- Detailed neuroapplication remains in Set 6.

### Practical decision and implementation

- For haemodynamically stable adults, **consider** RBCs below 70 g/L; ~75 in cardiac surgery and 80 in orthopaedic/pre-existing cardiovascular disease are supported options.
- These are thresholds for consideration, not mandatory targets.
- Active haemorrhage, acute ischaemia, severe hypoxaemia, haemoglobinopathy and clinical intolerance need separate reasoning.
- In stable nonbleeding patients give one unit and reassess; do not wait for Hb70 during exsanguination or repeatedly transfuse to correct a number without investigating its cause.

- Match plasma/platelets/fibrinogen to actual haemostatic need.
- Organise preadmission pathways, electronic support, bedside identification, transfusion consent, supply/traceability, TACO prevention and audit of patient outcomes and exposure/wastage.
- PREVENTT, neutral routine ANH and new TXA trials illustrate why physiological/Hb benefit is not automatically proven mortality benefit.

### PBM includes diagnostic blood loss and implementation

- A 2026 BJA systematic comparison of international PBM guidance found particularly variable advice on reducing diagnostic blood loss and gaps in national coordination.
- That supports including minimum necessary sampling, appropriate small-volume tubes/closed sampling systems and a multidisciplinary implementation plan, rather than treating PBM as a transfusion-trigger number.
- Audit unnecessary samples, anaemia-treatment completion, transfusion appropriateness and patient outcomes.
- The review searched in March 2024: its 2026 publication date does not make it a synthesis of every 2025–2026 trial. [Primary abstract](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42115060/) reviewed; no full-review claim.

### Anaemia definitions are not interchangeable with optimisation goals

The 2024 BJAEd corrigendum specifies the conventional adult WHO cut-offs of Hb <130 g/L for men and <120 g/L for nonpregnant women. Many perioperative PBM pathways use <130 g/L in either sex to trigger investigation/optimisation before major blood-loss surgery. Name the definition and population; neither number is an automatic transfusion target.

## Self-marking checklist

- All three PBM pillars with pre/intra/post application
- Cause-based anaemia treatment without prophylactic Hb130 transfusion
- Accurate TRICC/TRISS/FOCUS/cardiac-trial scope
- MINT uncertainty plus current AMI guideline
- TRAIN versus HEMOTION without universal neuro threshold
- Stable thresholds versus active haemorrhage/physiological exceptions
- Single-unit reassessment, component selection and systems audit
- Includes diagnostic blood-loss reduction, implementation ownership and a publication-date/search-date distinction
- Separates conventional sex-specific anaemia definitions from perioperative Hb130 screening/optimisation

items.title: 3. Discuss the role of acute normovolaemic haemodilution (ANH), preoperative…
items.q: Discuss the role of acute normovolaemic haemodilution (ANH), preoperative autologous donation and cell salvage in reducing allogeneic transfusion.
items.a:
### Compare the interventions by what they return

| Technique | Method and useful setting | Benefit and limitations |
|---|---|---|
| ANH | Collect a **patient-specific volume** of autologous whole blood after induction, maintain normovolaemia, label/store and return under protocol | Fewer RBCs lost per mL shed; returns platelets/factors as well as RBCs. Requires adequate baseline Hb/reserve and predictable loss; avoid arbitrary 1–2-L removal or a universal Hb80 nadir |
| Predeposit donation | Store the patient's donated units before a planned operation | May help rare antibodies/limited matched supply, but causes preoperative anaemia, wastage, logistics/clerical and bacterial risks; rarely routine under modern PBM |
| Washed intraoperative salvage | Collect, centrifuge, wash and return RBCs | Reduces donor exposure with sufficient recoverable loss; trained staff, cost, contamination and haemolysis risks; essentially no haemostatic-factor/platelet replacement |
| Postoperative drain systems | Device-specific recovery with or without washing | Unwashed products can contain free Hb/cytokines/activated debris; evidence and local approval differ; not interchangeable with washed intraoperative salvage |

### Evaluate contemporary evidence

- Cell salvage can reduce donor exposure in selected operations; volume and case mix determine cost-effectiveness, and donor-exposure reduction is not automatically survival benefit.
- Older small ANH trials/meta-analyses suggested benefit in some settings, but the **2025 multinational RCT (2010 CPB patients)** did not reduce the proportion receiving donor RBCs (27.3% vs 29.2%; RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.81–1.07).
- This argues against claiming routine ANH benefit in all cardiac surgery while not resolving every selected noncardiac scenario.
- Predeposit can reduce allogeneic exposure yet increase total transfusion/anaemia and waste; assess the net outcome.

### Implement within PBM

- Treat anaemia and review drugs first; use surgical haemostasis, appropriate TXA, normothermia, physiological calcium/pH and rational component decisions.
- Define staff competence, exact collection/storage/return limits, labels, contamination handling, emergency fallback and audit.
- Patient acceptance is individual: continuous circuit, disconnected storage and swab washing may have different consent decisions.
- Do not promise these techniques avoid all need for donor products during catastrophic bleeding.

### Other proposed conservation techniques

- Hypervolaemic haemodilution lacks robust evidence for safety/clinical benefit and risks dilution/overload; it is not a routine replacement for ANH.
- Local haemostatic agents and tourniquets can improve the field in suitable operations, but reduced visible loss or faster local haemostasis is not automatically reduced total blood loss, transfusion or better outcomes.
- Evaluate patient-specific vascular, thrombotic and organ risks.
- The 2026 blood-refusal review's older ANH meta-analytic benefit estimates do not override the newer large neutral CPB trial.

## Self-marking checklist

- Explains ANH physiology and patient-specific volume/reserve
- Returns whole blood versus washed RBC distinction
- Predeposit anaemia/waste and limited indications
- Salvage and unwashed drain-product differences
- Includes neutral 2025 ANH trial without overgeneralising
- Combines with PBM and appropriate selection
- Consent, traceability, storage and fallback/audit

items.title: 4. A patient reports excessive bleeding after dental extraction and previous…
items.q: A patient reports excessive bleeding after dental extraction and previous surgery. Platelet count, PT and APTT are normal. Describe your assessment, further investigations and perioperative plan.
items.a:
### Establish whether there is a clinically important bleeding phenotype

- Clarify severity, timing and treatment of previous dental/surgical/obstetric bleeding, spontaneous bruising, epistaxis, heavy menstrual bleeding and deep haematomas/haemarthroses.
- Obtain old records and family history, including affected women/carriers.
- A structured bleeding-assessment tool can organise the history but does not replace judgment.
- Review aspirin/P2Y12 inhibitors, anticoagulants, NSAIDs, supplements, alcohol, renal/liver disease and connective-tissue features.
- Decide urgency and consequence of bleeding; refer to haematology before elective high-risk surgery.

### Explain what normal screening tests miss

Primary haemostasis involves platelet adhesion through VWF/GPIb, activation and GPIIb/IIIa-mediated aggregation. Secondary haemostasis generates thrombin and cross-linked fibrin. Mucocutaneous/immediate bleeding suggests platelet/VWF problems; deep or delayed bleeding suggests factor/clot-stability problems, but patterns overlap.

| Test/pattern | Interpretation and useful follow-up |
|---|---|
| Normal platelet count | Does not establish platelet function. Consider drug/uraemic dysfunction and inherited disorders; specialist aggregation/flow-cytometry testing may identify Glanzmann or other inherited phenotypes; Bernard–Soulier typically has large platelets with thrombocytopenia |
| Normal PT/APTT | Does not exclude vWD, mild VIII/IX/XI deficiency, factor XIII deficiency, platelet dysfunction or selected fibrinolytic disorders |
| Isolated prolonged PT | Consider warfarin/vitamin K, factor VII and early liver disease; assess medication and clinical context |
| Isolated prolonged APTT | Exclude contamination/drug effect, then VIII/IX/XI deficiency or inhibitor; contact-factor deficiency/lupus anticoagulant may not predict bleeding |
| Both prolonged | Assess DIC/dilution, liver disease, common-pathway defects or substantial anticoagulant effect |

- Repeat appropriate samples and obtain blood film, fibrinogen, renal/liver tests, VWF antigen/activity and FVIII, with further factor, platelet or fibrinolysis testing directed by the phenotype.
- Mixing studies distinguish correction from persistent/time-dependent inhibition, with drug and laboratory caveats.
- Delayed bleeding with normal routine tests warrants consideration of FXIII/clot stability.
- FXI activity and APTT do not reliably predict procedural bleeding in isolation.
- Acquired VWF deficiency can accompany high-shear cardiac/mechanical-support or haematological disease.
- A normal VEM trace cannot clear these diagnoses.

### Translate less common diagnoses into treatment

- Haemophilia B requires **FIX**, not FVIII, replacement under a factor-centre plan; DDAVP does not correct FIX deficiency.
- Inhibitors and prior allergic reactions change replacement/bypassing choices.
- For FXI deficiency, procedure and personal bleeding history matter as well as activity; selected mucosal procedures may use TXA, while major procedures may need plasma or a locally available specialist factor strategy, with thrombotic risk considered.
- Factor XIII deficiency needs a specific clot-stability diagnosis and appropriate replacement despite normal PT/APTT.
- Congenital fibrinogen deficiency/dysfunction needs quantitative and functional assessment and targeted replacement when indicated; some phenotypes also thrombose.
- Do not prescribe one generic factor concentrate for all rare disorders.

### Make a specific plan

- Delay elective surgery when needed to define risk, with a written specialist treatment and rescue plan: adequate factor/VWF replacement, a tested appropriate DDAVP response, TXA where suitable, or platelet support for defined indications.
- Do not use DDAVP or plasma indiscriminately for every positive history.
- Some patients retain a bleeding disorder of unknown cause despite normal testing; their history still informs haemostatic planning.
- Specify products, monitoring, invasive/neuraxial precautions and delayed postoperative surveillance.
- Detailed haemophilia A and vWD worked plans remain in the SAQ bank.

## Self-marking checklist

- Documents personal, procedural, family and medication history
- Explains primary versus secondary haemostasis and phenotype
- Recognises normal count/PT/APTT limitations
- Uses VWF/factor/platelet and clot-stability testing selectively
- Interprets mixing studies with drug/inhibitor caveats
- Does not equate normal VEM with safe haemostasis
- Coordinates a diagnosis-specific plan and delayed surveillance

items.title: 5. Discuss the pharmacology, evidence and risks of tranexamic acid in the…
items.q: Discuss the pharmacology, evidence and risks of tranexamic acid in the perioperative period.
items.a:
### Pharmacology and indication-specific dosing

- TXA is a synthetic lysine analogue that reduces plasminogen binding to fibrin and inhibits fibrinolysis.
- It does not replace factors or stop an unsecured vessel.
- Predominantly renally cleared (half-life roughly 2–3 h): use indication/product-specific dose adjustment.
- Trauma commonly **1 g IV over 10 min then 1 g over 8 h within 3 h of injury**; PPH **1 g over 10 min within 3 h of birth**, repeat once after 30 min if continuing or within 24 h if recurrent.
- Elective orthopaedic regimens vary (IV/oral/topical); do not transfer one infusion schedule to all surgery.

### Evaluate the evidence

- CRASH-2: early bleeding-trauma benefit; late administration after 3 h can increase bleeding death. Do not wait for VEM-confirmed lysis.
- WOMAN: reduced death from bleeding in PPH, particularly early; not proof that prophylactic TXA benefits every delivery.
- ATACAS: less bleeding/transfusion in cardiac surgery, with a seizure concern; dose and renal function matter.
- Orthopaedic evidence supports reduced blood loss/transfusion. **POISE-3** reduced its composite bleeding endpoint in major noncardiac surgery, but **cardiovascular noninferiority was not established**. Similar point estimates are not proof of safety equivalence.
- **TRACTION (2026):** a hospital-policy cluster-crossover trial reduced RBC transfusion (7.4% vs 9.8%) and met its specified **VTE** noninferiority margin.
  - This strengthens evidence in its mainly oncological major-surgery population; it does not retroactively change POISE-3's different composite safety result or prove zero thrombosis risk.
- HALT-IT: no bleeding-death benefit in GI bleeding and increased VTE/seizures; not routine treatment. CRASH-3's early TBI signal must be described by severity, not as universal neurological benefit.

### Harms and safe use

- Dose-related seizures (cardiac/high-dose/renal accumulation), hypotension with rapid injection, selected thrombotic risk, visual adverse effects and urinary-tract clot obstruction are important.
- Avoid indiscriminate treatment of active thrombosis/thrombotic DIC; consider specialist phenotype-specific exceptions.
- Never give intrathecally: separate TXA from spinal local-anaesthetic storage, label syringes, verify route.
- Use renal-adjusted protocols and continue appropriate postoperative thromboprophylaxis.
- Balance trial-specific benefit against patient bleeding/thrombotic risk; TXA complements haemostasis.

- Evaluate the benefit in terms of outcomes the patient can notice.
- Reduction in measured drainage or calculated blood loss is a surrogate and may not translate into shorter admission or fewer major complications.
- Compare the baseline transfusion risk, the transfusion policy and the co-interventions in the studies.
- A similar relative effect will prevent fewer transfusions in a unit where the baseline rate is already low.
- Check whether the trial populations excluded patients at higher thrombotic risk and whether the number of events was sufficient to assess safety.
- Absence of a statistically significant increase in uncommon harms leaves uncertainty in underrepresented groups.
- Explain the local route and timing policy and verify renal function before deciding whether dose adjustment or a different strategy is appropriate.
- Combine the drug with correction of preoperative anaemia, surgical haemostasis and a consistent transfusion plan.
- Monitor the actual blood loss, haemoglobin, perfusion and postoperative course, rather than giving extra doses solely on the assumption that more treatment will produce more benefit.

## Self-marking checklist

- Mechanism, renal clearance and dosing by indication
- Trauma/PPH early time windows
- Distinguishes efficacy from safety/noninferiority
- Correct POISE-3 and 2026 TRACTION interpretation
- GI/TBI evidence kept population-specific
- Seizures, renal/urinary/thrombotic risks
- Wrong-route prevention and haemostasis/prophylaxis

items.title: 6. Your department is revising its major-haemorrhage protocol. Explain how you…
items.q: Your department is revising its major-haemorrhage protocol. Explain how you would move from empiric component delivery to targeted treatment and prevent complications.
items.a:
### Activate for critical bleeding, not a retrospective unit count

- Historical definitions (>10 RBC units/24 h or one blood volume) describe exposure but are poor activation triggers.
- Use rapid ongoing loss, shock/perfusion, likely need for escalating blood and the local **major haemorrhage protocol (MHP)**.
- Call a leader, senior surgeon/anaesthetist, blood bank, runner and laboratory support; achieve surgical/IR haemostasis concurrently.
- Protect oxygen delivery, obtain large-bore access, warm the patient and use a validated rapid infuser.
- Blood refusal/special antibodies require immediate communication.

### Initial component support and monitoring

- Use the local balanced pack while results are pending, then target deficits.
- State ratio order and adult platelet-dose equivalence: **1:1:1 is not one adult apheresis platelet bag for every RBC unit**.
- NBA guidance suggests at least 1 FFP per 2 RBC and 1 adult platelet dose per 8 RBC in ratio-based support; local trauma packs can target higher ratios.
- These are minimum delivery recommendations, not reasons to wait until the eighth unit.
- PROPPR did not show significant overall 24-h/30-day mortality superiority, but 1:1:1 improved haemostasis/early exsanguination outcomes.

- Measure serial gas/Hb, iCa/K/Mg, lactate/pH, core temperature, platelets, PT/APTT, fibrinogen and VEM, with repeat intervals set by bleeding speed and intervention (often 15–30 min during unstable loss).
- Maintain physiological iCa and normothermia.
- Use platelets commonly >50 ×10⁹/L (>100 for selected intracranial/critical-site bleeding), fibrinogen generally >1.5–2 g/L (obstetrics ≥2), and assay/local thresholds.
- Give TXA for the indicated population/time window; do not give routine empirical PCC or rFVIIa.
- Use appropriate emergency-release group O RBCs (O RhD-negative prioritised when needed), transition to group-specific/compatible stock under blood-bank policy; do not prescribe O-negative for every adult indefinitely.

### Prevent and respond to complications

- Citrate-related hypocalcaemia/hypomagnesaemia, early hyperkalaemia/later shifts, hypothermia, dilution/consumption, acidosis then possible citrate-related alkalosis, TACO/TRALI, haemolysis, contamination and errors need active surveillance.
- Source control and restored perfusion treat shock acidosis; routine bicarbonate does not replace these.
- Avoid treating a normal initial Hb as reassuring.
- Special populations use weight-based volumes and dedicated protocols.

### Build, stand down and audit

- Define activation/escalation, logistics, lab access, rapid infuser/salvage staffing, emergency stock, packs, communication, special populations and stop rules.
- Stand down clearly once bleeding is controlled, reconcile unused products and transition to individual replacement/prophylaxis.
- Audit timeliness, ratios/targets, wastage, complications and outcome; rehearse with simulation.

### Transfer principles without treating obstetric and trauma bleeding as identical

- A 2026 BJA narrative review distinguishes loss/dilution of factors from pathological fibrinogen destruction in acute obstetric coagulopathy.
- Pregnancy baseline haemostasis, the cause of bleeding and the coagulopathy phenotype differ from nonpregnant trauma.
- Consequently a trauma-derived pack ratio is not proof of optimal treatment for every PPH.
- Start urgent resuscitation/source control, then use the obstetric pathway, serial fibrinogen/VEM and clinical response to individualise haemostatic replacement.
- This is a transferable Set 2 haemostasis point; detailed obstetric emergency management remains in its primary set. [Primary author-repository abstract](https://orca.cardiff.ac.uk/id/eprint/187688/) reviewed; not a full-text review.

## Self-marking checklist

- Uses clinical early MHP activation
- Roles, communication and source control
- Explains ratios and adult platelet equivalence
- Transitions to monitored deficit-guided therapy
- TXA indication plus temperature/calcium/fibrinogen
- Recognises metabolic, immune and volume complications
- Emergency blood selection and special populations
- Stand-down, logistics, audit and simulation
- Explains why obstetric coagulopathy and trauma evidence cannot be treated as identical

items.title: 7. A patient continues to bleed after initial empiric resuscitation. The first…
items.q: A patient continues to bleed after initial empiric resuscitation. The first viscoelastic trace shows delayed initiation and low firmness. Explain how to interpret the trace, select follow-up channels and use serial results.
items.a:
### Interpret in the context of active bleeding

- First confirm patient/sample, platform/cartridge, time after activation, temperature, drug exposure and the surgical source.
- Standard ROTEM/TEG are low-shear whole-blood assays, not complete endothelial/platelet-function tests.
- Classical cup/pin devices and newer TEG resonance platforms differ.
- EXTEM is tissue-factor activated; INTEM contact activated; HEPTEM adds heparinase; FIBTEM inhibits platelet contribution; APTEM uses an antifibrinolytic reagent (check the local cartridge).
- TEG R/K/angle/MA and ROTEM CT/CFT/A5/MCF are analogous but not numerically interchangeable.

| Pattern | Interpretation and next step |
|---|---|
| Long CT/R | Drug/heparin, factor or severe fibrinogen deficit. Compare paired heparinase tests and labs; reverse a demonstrated drug effect or replace indicated factors, not automatic PCC |
| Low whole-clot strength plus low FIBTEM/functional fibrin | Low fibrinogen/function → cryo or concentrate in a validated algorithm |
| Low whole-clot strength with adequate fibrin contribution | Low platelet count/contribution → count/function assessment and indicated platelets; standard VEM cannot identify every antiplatelet defect |
| Progressive narrowing | Lysis: **TEG LY30 and ROTEM ML increase; ROTEM LI30 (remaining firmness) decreases**. Confirm assay/timing; consider APTEM comparison and appropriate antifibrinolysis |
| Apparently normal trace with continued bleeding | Search surgical source AND defects not measured (vWD, platelet dysfunction, some DOACs/FXIII defects), temperature and sampling errors |

### Act and reassess

- Use the validated local assay/setting-specific thresholds, not a universal FIBTEM/LY30 cutoff across cardiac, obstetric and trauma care.
- Correct temperature/iCa/perfusion and give the treatment for the identified deficit.
- Repeat a clinically useful early trace after treatment and track actual bleeding.
- **Normal VEM does not exclude DOAC activity or rule out mild/moderate fibrinolysis**, and should not withhold indicated early TXA in major trauma.

### Evaluate limitations and implementation

- Most instruments measure at 37°C, potentially masking hypothermic dysfunction.
- Endothelium, vWF/platelet-drug effects and protein-C pathways are incompletely represented; reagent, haematocrit, timing, handling and operator/QC matter.
- VEM-guided algorithms can reduce components, particularly in cardiac/liver settings; mortality estimates vary and the large ITACTIC primary trauma result was neutral.
- The Blue Book 2025 emphasises contextual algorithms, fibrinogen-first correction **when deficient**, training, result access and audit; it does not make every published threshold a universal prescription.

## Self-marking checklist

- Defines correct platform, assays and context
- Interprets initiation, fibrin and platelet contribution separately
- Correct LY30/ML versus LI30 direction
- Drug/heparin comparison without automatic PCC
- Normal trace does not exclude every bleeding disorder
- Local validated thresholds and repeat assessment
- Does not delay clinically indicated trauma TXA
- Limitations, evidence and implementation

items.title: 8. Critically evaluate whole blood compared with component therapy for early…
items.q: Critically evaluate whole blood compared with component therapy for early major-trauma resuscitation, including the 2026 SWiFT and TOWAR trials.
items.a:
### Explain the proposed role

- Whole blood can deliver oxygen-carrying cells and plasma together, with platelet contribution dependent on the actual collection, processing and storage product.
- It can simplify emergency delivery compared with multiple separately supplied components.
- Low-titre group O whole blood requires a specific blood-service policy: group O RBC compatibility does not make donor plasma universally harmless, and RhD/anti-A/anti-B exposure, cold chain, traceability, stock and wastage matter.
- Do not assume every product called whole blood has identical platelet content or equals a fixed adult component pack.

### Use the new randomised evidence

| Trial | Setting/comparison | Primary interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| SWiFT, 2026 | English air-ambulance services; up to two units of prehospital whole blood versus early RBC/plasma component care | Whole blood was not superior for the composite of death or massive transfusion within 24 hours |
| TOWAR, 2026 | North American air-medical cluster-randomised strategy; early low-titre group O whole blood versus components | No demonstrated reduction in 30-day mortality; account for cluster allocation and baseline imbalance |

- These trials weaken a claim of proven superiority for **the tested limited prehospital strategies**.
- They do not prove equivalence, universal harm, or that all in-hospital, paediatric, obstetric and larger-dose whole-blood strategies have been settled.
- The comparator was early blood components, not a licence to delay blood while giving large crystalloid volumes.
- Trial product, dose, transport system and endpoints affect generalisability.

### Decide what to implement locally

- Prioritise prompt haemorrhage control and timely blood within the local trauma/MHP system.
- Either selected whole-blood or component pathways need reliable supply, trained teams, patient identification, warming, ionised calcium monitoring and serial haemostatic assessment.
- Whole blood does not remove later needs for targeted platelets/fibrinogen or drug reversal.
- Assess operational benefits, donor constraints, emergency compatibility and monitoring, as well as trial outcomes, before changing stock policy.

The NZ SWiFT Aotearoa feasibility work compares locally relevant products and must not be confused with the completed English SWiFT effectiveness trial. Detailed prehospital trauma systems belong in the trauma set; the blood-product comparison and recent evidence belong here.

- Repeat coagulation and perfusion measurements after major treatment steps.
- A result obtained before several units of blood or a major change in shock may no longer represent the patient.
- Look for ongoing anatomical bleeding while correcting fibrinogen, clotting factors and platelets as indicated.
- Restore temperature and ionised calcium, and address hypoperfusion to reverse acidosis.
- Relay results and actions aloud during the resuscitation so empiric treatment is reviewed once reliable results and bleeding control are available.

## Self-marking checklist

- Defines whole-blood rationale and product variation
- Explains emergency ABO/RhD and logistical considerations
- Correct SWiFT comparison and composite outcome
- Correct TOWAR setting and mortality interpretation
- Distinguishes no demonstrated superiority from equivalence/harm
- No extrapolation to every population or unlimited dose
- Links local implementation to source control and targeted ongoing care

items.title: 9. Compare fresh frozen plasma, cryoprecipitate, fibrinogen concentrate and…
items.q: Compare fresh frozen plasma, cryoprecipitate, fibrinogen concentrate and prothrombin complex concentrate in the management of perioperative bleeding.
items.a:
### Treat the specific deficit

| Component | Contents / purpose | Typical approach | Limitations |
|---|---|---|---|
| FFP | Multiple soluble clotting factors, including V/VIII, some fibrinogen | Often 10–15 mL/kg for significant factor deficit with bleeding/procedure, then assess | Volume, thawing, TACO/TRALI; not routine volume expansion or correction of mild INR alone |
| Cryoprecipitate | Concentrated fibrinogen with VIII, XIII, vWF/fibronectin | **NZ high-fibrinogen apheresis cryo: ~1 unit/30 kg** is a local starting guide; NZBS estimates ~1 g/L increment, with measured reassessment | Unit content differs markedly between countries; do not prescribe a universal “10-unit pool” |
| Fibrinogen concentrate | Standardised fibrinogen, small volume | Common adult initial 3–4 g under a critical-bleeding algorithm, adjusted to weight/deficit and response | Cost, thrombosis, reconstitution; acquired use subject to local approval, no platelet/other-factor replacement |
| 4F-PCC | II, VII, IX, X and proteins C/S; product-specific heparin | Rapid VKA reversal with vitamin K; selected off-label Xa bleeding protocols | No fibrinogen/V/VIII replacement; thrombosis, HIT caution if heparin-containing; not routine trauma/DIC replacement |

NZ uses **Beriplex 4F-PCC** following the 2025 transition; historical Prothrombinex-VF dosing/composition should not be assumed interchangeable. Consult the current protocol and maximum/rate limits.

### Bedside selection and evidence

- In ongoing major bleeding, source control and the MHP run concurrently with serial labs/VEM, temperature, iCa/pH and perfusion.
- Replace low fibrinogen early (commonly >1.5–2 g/L; obstetric ≥2), but do not give it before every other component regardless of the actual deficit.
- Low whole-clot strength with adequate fibrin contribution suggests a platelet problem; prolonged CT may reflect drug, fibrinogen or factor deficiency, not an automatic indication for PCC.

**FARES-II (2025)** supports PCC rather than plasma for selected post-CPB factor-replacement bleeding, with greater haemostatic effectiveness in its trial setting; it does not support empirical PCC for every trauma patient. See R32 for the worked evidence comparison.

- **FIBRES** established **fibrinogen concentrate noninferior to cryoprecipitate** for 24-h component use in bleeding, hypofibrinogenaemic post-CPB adults—not the reverse trial claim, universal superiority, or guaranteed mortality benefit.
- PROCOAG discourages empirical 4F-PCC in all trauma bleeding.
- Repeat the clinical and measured response; a good laboratory number does not control a surgical vessel.

### Obstetric haemostatic replacement is targeted therapy

- Pregnancy has a higher baseline fibrinogen; a low-normal nonpregnant result can be important during PPH.
- In ongoing obstetric bleeding, use the local pathway, serial fibrinogen and validated VEM thresholds to identify a deficit; commonly aim at least 2 g/L.
- FIB-PPH, OBS2 and FIDEL did not justify routine empirical fibrinogen concentrate in women whose fibrinogen was already adequate.
- This does not show that correction of a true severe deficit is futile.
- Plasma is not a concentrated fibrinogen replacement, and a trauma ratio is not automatically optimal for every atonic PPH.
- Do not turn this into withholding emergency components during life-threatening uncontrolled bleeding while waiting for tests.
- Routine PCC is not established treatment of PPH; specialist rescue rFVIIa does not replace source control and carries thrombotic risk.
- Foreign cryoprecipitate unit content, costs and licensing must not be copied into NZ prescriptions.

## Self-marking checklist

- Correct contents and missing factors
- FFP indication, dose and volume burden
- NZ-specific cryo unit equivalence and measured response
- Fibrinogen concentrate indication/local approval
- 4F-PCC plus vitamin K, product and thrombosis/HIT caveats
- Correct FIBRES direction and trial population
- Uses deficit-directed selection alongside haemostasis
- Distinguishes targeted obstetric fibrinogen replacement from empirical concentrate use and universal trauma-pack extrapolation

items.title: 10. During life-threatening haemorrhage the blood bank reports that fully…
items.q: During life-threatening haemorrhage the blood bank reports that fully compatible red cells will be delayed because of antibodies. Describe your response and the distinction between alloantibodies and autoimmune crossmatch reactivity.
items.a:
### Coordinate lifesaving transfusion and haemostasis

- Control the bleeding, activate/escalate the MHP and notify a **senior transfusion scientist/haematologist** of urgency, physiology and expected ongoing loss.
- Send correctly labelled pretransfusion samples and establish past antibodies, transfusions, pregnancy and special requirements.
- Consider salvage if appropriate/accepted.
- Do not wait for perfect serological compatibility while the patient exsanguinates; the blood bank selects emergency-release RBCs balancing immediate death against immunohaemolytic risk, with explicit clinician communication/documentation.

### Why compatibility is delayed

- An **alloantibody** targets a nonself RBC antigen (e.g. K/E/Jk): clinically significant historical antibodies matter even if currently undetectable.
- Antigen-negative matched RBCs may take time to identify or obtain.
- Emergency group O prevents many ABO issues but **does not guarantee absence of the implicated non-ABO antigen**.
- RhD-negative/Kell considerations and childbearing potential matter, but critical stock/urgency requires specialist prioritisation.

- A warm **autoantibody** can react broadly with patient/donor RBCs, making a completely nonreactive crossmatch impossible.
- The laboratory seeks underlying clinically significant alloantibodies using specialist methods and selects the best-matched product; do not withhold necessary blood until every auto-reactivity disappears or imply that the label “least incompatible” guarantees safety.
- Determine whether there is active haemolysis and treat its cause with haematology.

### Treatment-related test interference

- Ask about **daratumumab/anti-CD38 therapy:** it can cause panreactivity in indirect antiglobulin testing and mask relevant alloantibodies.
- Notify the laboratory early and retrieve pretreatment phenotype/genotype where available; DTT-based methods can affect Kell antigen detection and influence component selection.
- Do not assume this pattern proves autoimmune haemolysis.
- See R35.

### Continue monitoring and transition

- Check identity meticulously despite urgency, assess transfusion response, haemolysis, K/iCa/coagulation and organ perfusion, and communicate product/volume needs.
- Switch to group-specific and antigen-negative/compatible RBCs as soon as the blood bank advises.
- Record emergency authorisation, units and unresolved antibodies, explain the event to the patient when appropriate and preserve permanent antibody history for future care.
- Avoid ordering unnecessary plasma/platelets as a substitute for oxygen-carrying RBCs.

- Ask the transfusion laboratory what is available immediately and what will become available after antibody identification.
- Communicate urgency clearly and keep reassessing the balance between active exsanguination and incompatibility risk.
- Send a correctly labelled pretransfusion sample early if feasible, without delaying emergency issue.
- Document and review the transition to the safest compatible units as soon as they are ready.

## Self-marking checklist

- Immediate source control and senior blood-bank communication
- Correct samples/history and emergency authorisation
- No unsafe delay for complete compatibility in exsanguination
- Alloantibody antigen-negative selection and group O limitations
- Warm auto-reactivity versus masked alloantibody
- Monitors haemolysis/physiology and changes to ideal blood when feasible
- Documentation, disclosure and future antibody record

items.title: 11. Evaluate red-cell transfusion thresholds in stable general ICU patients, acute…
items.q: Evaluate red-cell transfusion thresholds in stable general ICU patients, acute myocardial infarction and acute brain injury. Explain why a single restrictive threshold is insufficient.
items.a:
### Start with oxygen delivery and the clinical setting

- Hb-bound oxygen dominates arterial oxygen content, but delivery also depends on saturation and cardiac output.
- Blood loss, low flow and hypoxaemia require correction alongside Hb.
- Establish whether the patient is actively bleeding, stable but anaemic, ischaemic or unable to compensate; identify transfusion harms including TACO.
- An initially normal Hb can conceal acute whole-blood loss.
- Threshold trials in stable patients do not justify waiting during exsanguination.

| Population | Evidence-informed interpretation |
|---|---|
| Stable general ICU/sepsis | TRICC/TRISS support restrictive strategies in their populations; a consideration threshold around 70 g/L is commonly appropriate, with symptoms and physiology considered |
| Cardiac/orthopaedic or stable cardiovascular disease | AABB-supported options include about 75 g/L for cardiac surgery and 80 g/L for orthopaedic/pre-existing cardiovascular disease; these are not universal postoperative targets |
| Acute MI | MINT did not demonstrate statistically definitive superiority for its primary comparison, but harm from restriction could not be excluded. The 2025 AABB AMI guideline conditionally favours a liberal strategy below 100 g/L, with low-certainty evidence |
| Mixed acute brain injury | TRAIN compared approximately 90 versus 70 g/L and favoured the liberal strategy for its neurological outcome; do not assume all brain injuries share its effect |
| Moderate/severe TBI | HEMOTION compared approximately 100 versus 70 g/L and did not establish a statistically definitive primary neurological benefit; this is not proof of equivalence |
| Aneurysmal SAH | SAHARA, published in issue in 2025, compared mandatory transfusion at ≤100 with optional transfusion at ≤80 g/L. Its primary 12-month neurological result did not show significant benefit of the liberal strategy |

### Critically compare rather than vote-counting trials

- Different injury types, transfusion protocols, comparator thresholds, outcome definitions, follow-up and uncertainty explain why “liberal neurotransfusion works/does not work” is too crude.
- No significant difference is not equivalent to demonstrated equivalence.
- Evaluate the patient's ongoing ischaemia, cardiac reserve, oxygenation, cerebral context, bleeding and overload risk with the responsible ICU/neuro/cardiac team.
- Do not extrapolate an acute-MI recommendation to every patient with old coronary disease.

### Prescribe and reassess

- For stable nonbleeding adults, consider one RBC unit then reassess symptoms, Hb and physiology rather than automatically ordering two units.
- Treat the underlying anaemia, reduce phlebotomy and document the indication/target.
- Major haemorrhage uses a separate resuscitation strategy; haemoglobinopathies and chronic transfusion programmes also need disease-specific plans.
- Detailed cerebral perfusion management belongs in Set 6, while the comparison of transfusion evidence is covered here.

## Self-marking checklist

- Uses delivery, bleeding and symptoms rather than Hb alone
- States stable ICU and selected surgical thresholds with scope
- Accurate MINT uncertainty and conditional 2025 AMI guidance
- Differentiates TRAIN, HEMOTION and SAHARA populations/protocols
- Distinguishes nonsignificance from equivalence
- Individualises ischaemia/organ reserve versus TACO risk
- Single-unit reassessment and cause-based anaemia care

items.title: 12. Discuss the risks of allogeneic blood transfusion and how they can be minimised.
items.q: Discuss the risks of allogeneic blood transfusion and how they can be minimised.
items.a:
### Immediate and delayed risks

- Immediate: incompatible/wrong-patient haemolysis, bacterial contamination (particularly platelets), anaphylaxis/allergy, FNHTR, TRALI, **TACO**, hypotensive reactions and metabolic complications during rapid large-volume exposure.
- Delayed: alloimmunisation/delayed haemolysis, post-transfusion purpura, TA-GVHD, infection and chronic iron loading.
- Immunomodulation and associations with infection/cancer outcomes require causal caution: sicker, bleeding patients are more likely to receive blood.
- Do not teach that transfusion has proven to cause every observational adverse outcome.

- Wrong-blood errors are catastrophic and preventable, but **TACO is a major cause of transfusion morbidity/death**; no single statement that clerical error is always the “biggest risk” is accurate across denominators.
- Modern donor selection/testing make viral transmission very rare; use current NZ haemovigilance estimates if quoting numbers.
- “HIV, HBV and HCV all <1 per million” is not a verified universal/local figure.
- Residual bacterial/emerging-pathogen risks vary by product and place.

### Reduce exposure and choose the right component

PBM: investigate/treat anaemia, minimise surgical/phlebotomy loss, use appropriate TXA/salvage, and rational thresholds. In a stable nonbleeding adult give one RBC unit then reassess; active haemorrhage needs a different approach. Obtain informed consent about indication, alternatives and material risks.

- ABO/Rh-compatible blood, historical antibody identification, antigen-negative products where needed and a validated bedside independent identification process prevent major errors.
- Leukodepletion reduces some febrile/CMV risks; **irradiation prevents TA-GVHD in specific at-risk recipients and is not equivalent to leukodepletion**.
- NZ platelets are irradiated routinely; RBC indications depend on diagnosis/treatment, transplant, HLA/family donation and blood-service advice.
- Selected washed/IgA-deficient products are used for appropriate severe allergy, not for every incidental IgA deficiency.

- Assess TACO risk (age, low weight, heart/renal disease, severe anaemia), prescribe the rate/volume, monitor baseline and early observations and consider divided units/diuretic in selected patients.
- Maintain the cold chain, approved filter/warmer rules and traceability.
- Recognise reactions, stop the implicated unit promptly, investigate/report and arrange future-product precautions.

Document the indication and the endpoint for treatment before ordering a component. During active bleeding, interpret measurements in relation to sampling time, recent resuscitation and the anatomical source. Once haemostasis is achieved, reassess ongoing need to avoid additional exposure, circulatory overload and unnecessary depletion of stock.

## Self-marking checklist

- Immediate immune, septic, volume and metabolic risks
- Delayed alloimmune/TA-GVHD/iron/infection risks
- Qualifies causal immunomodulation and infection estimates
- PBM and stable single-unit practice
- Bedside identification and compatible/antigen-matched components
- Distinguishes leukodepletion, irradiation and washing
- TACO risk/rate/monitoring and reaction/reporting plan

items.title: 13. Discuss the options for reversal of warfarin, direct oral anticoagulants and…
items.q: Discuss the options for reversal of warfarin, direct oral anticoagulants and heparin in a patient requiring urgent surgery.
items.a:
### Decide whether reversal is needed

- Assess urgency, site/severity of bleeding, procedure, thrombotic indication, exact dose/time, CrCl, interactions and available drug-specific tests.
- Pause the drug and control the source.
- If a procedure can safely wait, clearance may be safer than reversal.
- Do not delay resuscitation of critical bleeding for a laboratory result.
- Normal PT/APTT does not exclude DOAC activity; calibrated anti-Xa for Xa drugs and dilute thrombin time/ecarin testing for dabigatran are more useful when available.

### Match reversal to the agent

| Drug | Urgent strategy | Important limits |
|---|---|---|
| Warfarin | **4F-PCC plus IV vitamin K** for life-threatening bleeding/urgent reversal; common protocol ranges PCC 25–50 IU/kg by INR/weight and vitamin K 5–10 mg IV slowly | Use current NZ Beriplex protocol, maximum doses and rate; recheck INR promptly and later. Vitamin K takes hours but sustains correction. FFP is a fallback if PCC unavailable, not required routinely with 4F-PCC |
| Dabigatran | **Idarucizumab 5 g IV**, two 2.5-g doses, for qualifying uncontrolled bleeding/urgent surgery | Renal failure can cause rebound; repeat appropriate assays/clinical review. Dialysis removes dabigatran but is slower/logistically difficult |
| Apixaban/rivaroxaban/edoxaban | For selected critical bleeding, specialist-directed **4F-PCC**, commonly 25–50 IU/kg under protocol | Off-label haemostatic support, not drug removal; thrombosis risk. Andexanet has restricted indications/availability, is not routine urgent-surgery reversal, and does not cover every Xa drug |
| UFH | Stop; **protamine ~1 mg per 100 U recently administered**, reduce for elapsed time and use local maximum/rate | Slow administration; hypotension, anaphylaxis and pulmonary hypertension; excess protamine can impair haemostasis |
| Enoxaparin/LMWH | Protamine partly reverses; common example **1 mg per 1 mg enoxaparin if within 8 h**, lower dose later, further dose only with specialist review | Anti-Xa activity is incompletely reversed; renal dysfunction prolongs effect |
| Fondaparinux | Stop; supportive/source-directed care and specialist rescue decision | No specific antidote; do not routinely prescribe rFVIIa/PCC for every exposure |

**Andexanet update:**

- The FDA concluded serious thrombotic risks outweighed benefits; US commercial sales ended December 2025. This is not a statement about NZ stock.
- Check current local approval/availability.
- It can cause heparin unresponsiveness, an important problem before CPB.
- It should not be taught as universally preferred first-line reversal.
- Activated charcoal is an early-ingestion option with airway protection (usually around 2 h; later only drug-specific advice), not a blanket 8-hour rule.

### Support and restart

- Maintain temperature, physiological iCa and perfusion; use RBCs/components for the actual deficit, and TXA for an appropriate indication.
- Plasma/platelets do not specifically neutralise a DOAC; normal VEM does not prove clearance.
- Avoid unsafe neuraxial techniques.
- Document repeat INR/drug assessment, source control, thrombotic surveillance and a plan to restart prophylactic or therapeutic anticoagulation when haemostasis permits; therapeutic restart is often later than prophylaxis after major surgery.

### Related initiation decision: new postoperative AF

- Starting anticoagulation for new postoperative AF is a separate question from reversing a pre-existing drug.
- Establish onset/duration, recurrence, stroke risk, the operation's bleeding consequences and achieved haemostasis.
- Treat acute physiological triggers with the cardiac/ICU team.
- Persistent or recurrent AF needs a documented decision on anticoagulation and follow-up; a brief apparently transient episode should not simply be forgotten.
- A duration such as 48 hours is not a universal command to anticoagulate a freshly bleeding patient, and a bleeding score alone is not an automatic veto.
- Agent, start time and duration need shared assessment, renal review and reassessment after recovery.
- Haemodynamic instability may require urgent cardioversion without waiting for a prolonged pre-anticoagulation schedule.
- Full arrhythmia management belongs to the cardiac set.

## Self-marking checklist

- Defines critical bleeding/urgency and balances thrombosis
- Checks last dose, CrCl and appropriate assays
- Warfarin: 4F-PCC plus sustained vitamin K correction
- Dabigatran: idarucizumab 5 g and rebound assessment
- Xa drugs: qualified PCC/andexanet discussion, not universal first-line antidote
- UFH/LMWH protamine dosing and incomplete reversal
- Source control, supportive treatment and restart plan
- Separates postoperative-AF anticoagulation initiation from reversal, with haemostasis and follow-up

items.title: 14. A patient on day 7 of heparin after cardiac surgery has a platelet count that…
items.q: A patient on day 7 of heparin after cardiac surgery has a platelet count that has fallen from 250 to 90 x 10^9/L and a new arterial thrombosis. Discuss the diagnosis and management, including implications for anaesthesia.
items.a:
### Probability and confirmation

- The platelet fall is **64%**, with onset day 7 and new arterial thrombosis: a high-probability HIT pattern unless a strong competing explanation changes the score.
- **4Ts: 0–3 low, 4–5 intermediate, 6–8 high**.
- Distinguish the expected early post-CPB fall/recovery from a second day-5–10 fall; PF4 antibodies are common after CPB and a positive immunoassay alone does not diagnose HIT.
- Send an IgG PF4 immunoassay and functional assay as appropriate, but do not wait to treat a high-probability case.
- Review sepsis, DIC, drugs and TMA.

### Immediate treatment

- Stop **all heparin**, including flushes, LMWH and heparin-containing products/devices where relevant.
- Begin a **nonheparin anticoagulant** at treatment intensity for thrombosis unless bleeding dictates an individual plan: argatroban, bivalirudin, danaparoid, fondaparinux or a DOAC according to stability, organ function and availability.
- Argatroban needs major dose reduction with hepatic dysfunction/critical illness; bivalirudin needs renal adjustment.
- Use the agent-specific monitoring protocol; CPB doses differ markedly from routine ICU infusion doses.

- Urgent vascular review for limb-threatening arterial occlusion; assess/screen for additional thrombosis.
- Avoid routine prophylactic platelets, but serious bleeding or an urgent intervention can justify them.
- Do not start warfarin until platelet recovery (usually ≥150 ×10⁹/L); reverse early warfarin with vitamin K if appropriate and plan specialist overlap/INR interpretation.
- Duration depends on isolated HIT versus HIT with thrombosis, often 3–6 months for HITT.

### Anaesthetic and future bypass implications

- Document a clear HIT alert and timing/laboratory status.
- Defer nonurgent CPB during acute/subacute-A HIT until an appropriate phase if possible; urgent CPB often uses **bivalirudin in an experienced centre**, or specialist plasma-exchange/heparin strategies.
- Brief intraoperative heparin may be appropriate in subacute-B or remote HIT, with avoidance before/after and postoperative platelet surveillance; “wait until every antibody is negative” is too absolute.
- Avoid neuraxial techniques during active parenteral direct-thrombin inhibition; an assumed washout alone is not sufficient permission.

The absolute count can still be within the normal range at presentation. A fall of more than half from the postoperative peak with the right timing and new thrombosis is much more informative. Establish the timing of every heparin exposure, including line flushes. Discuss renal or hepatic impairment with haematology before selecting and monitoring an alternative anticoagulant.

## Self-marking checklist

- Calculates fall and applies correct 4Ts categories
- Distinguishes post-CPB antibodies from clinical HIT
- Stops all heparin and treats before delayed tests when indicated
- Selects nonheparin treatment by organ function and setting
- Treats limb thrombosis and looks for other events
- Avoids routine platelets/early warfarin with justified exceptions
- Explains acute versus remote HIT and CPB/regional implications

items.title: 15. Explain how anticoagulation differs between CRRT and ECMO, and how you would…
items.q: Explain how anticoagulation differs between CRRT and ECMO, and how you would investigate apparent heparin resistance in an ICU patient.
items.a:
### Separate circuit patency from systemic thrombosis treatment

- CRRT may use **regional citrate:** chelate calcium in the extracorporeal circuit, replace systemic calcium and monitor circuit/systemic iCa, acid-base, electrolytes and calcium requirements.
- It reduces systemic anticoagulant exposure; it does **not treat a concurrent DVT/arterial thrombosis**.
- Citrate accumulation is suggested by rising total:iCa **molar** ratio (often >2.5), increasing calcium requirements and metabolic disturbance; alkalosis may instead reflect metabolised citrate load.
- Severe shock/liver dysfunction requires careful protocol assessment, not a universal “always safe” or “absolutely prohibited” statement.
- UFH/no anticoagulation are selected alternatives when appropriate.

- ECMO commonly uses **systemic UFH**, but flow, oxygenator/circuit clot, acquired vWF/platelet dysfunction, haemolysis and bleeding require an ECMO-specific protocol.
- Anti-Xa/APTT/ACT each have limitations; a single normal APTT is not proof of effective anticoagulation or safe haemostasis.
- HIT requires a nonheparin strategy, usually a specialist direct-thrombin inhibitor protocol with organ-function adjustment.

### Apparent heparin resistance

- Check infusion delivery, line/sample problems, actual dose/weight and assay.
- High FVIII/fibrinogen in inflammation can shorten APTT, giving **pseudo-resistance despite therapeutic/high anti-Xa**; blindly escalating UFH may cause bleeding.
- Genuine low response can reflect antithrombin deficiency or increased binding/clearance.
- Compare APTT with appropriately interpreted anti-Xa, antithrombin if indicated, clinical/circuit thrombosis and laboratory limitations (haemolysis, bilirubin, residual Xa drugs).
- Antithrombin supplementation or changing agent is selected specialist management, not an automatic reaction to a low APTT.

### Ongoing assessment

- Document the indication, systemic versus regional effect, target/assay and response.
- Review bleeding, platelet fall/HIT, renal/hepatic function, procedures and restarts daily.
- Recurrent circuit clot may be mechanical/flow-related and does not automatically mean insufficient systemic heparin.
- Detailed circuit prescriptions remain in the RRT/ECMO sets; this question tests the Set 2 anticoagulant decisions.

- Establish the indication, last dose, measured INR, recent thrombosis or stroke and surgical timing in parallel with resuscitation.
- Recheck INR after reversal and follow its trajectory after the short-lived replacement factors.
- The decision to restart depends on durable haemostasis and the independent risk of interruption.
- Distinguish prophylactic anticoagulation from returning to full-dose therapy and document a named review time.

When laboratory assays disagree, check sample quality, timing and the clinical circuit findings before escalating anticoagulation.

## Self-marking checklist

- Separates regional citrate from systemic treatment
- Citrate/calcium/acid-base monitoring and accumulation clues
- ECMO systemic strategy and acquired haemostatic defects
- Checks delivery/sample/assay before escalating UFH
- Pseudo-resistance versus antithrombin-related resistance
- Uses multiple assays and clinical circuit/bleeding assessment
- Organ function, HIT and procedure/restart planning

items.title: 16. An ICU patient develops a cold, painful, pulseless leg after femoral arterial…
items.q: An ICU patient develops a cold, painful, pulseless leg after femoral arterial instrumentation. Outline your assessment and management, including the anticoagulation and reperfusion issues.
items.a:
### Treat as threatened acute limb ischaemia

- Call vascular surgery immediately; note onset, instrument/procedure and embolic/thrombotic history.
- Examine both limbs for pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis and temperature; motor/sensory deficit signals threatened viability.
- Use Doppler, capillary perfusion and compartment examination, and assess systemic shock/other embolic sites.
- Analgesia, oxygen if needed, resuscitation and protect the limb from trauma/direct heating.
- Check access-site bleeding, anticoagulant exposure, AF, aortic disease, dissection, low-flow vasoconstriction and HIT timing.

### Prevent propagation and restore flow

- Senior vascular/ICU decision on **IV UFH** promptly when not contraindicated; a recent intracranial/major bleed or suspected HIT changes the plan (nonheparin anticoagulant for HIT).
- Follow local dosing/assay protocol; do not choose a DOAC for an unstable patient needing imminent intervention.
- Limb duplex/CTA helps define occlusion if it will not delay reperfusion of an immediately threatened limb.
- Remove/reposition an implicated catheter only in coordination with the procedural/vascular team; avoid losing a useful route or provoking uncontrolled bleeding without a plan.

- Revascularisation may use open embolectomy/thrombectomy, repair/bypass or catheter intervention according to viability/anatomy and timing.
- Catheter thrombolysis is unsuitable with major bleeding contraindications and not a substitute for immediate surgery in a severely threatened limb.
- An irreversibly ischaemic limb may require amputation; specialist classification determines this.

### Anticipate the anaesthetic and systemic effects

- Account for full anticoagulation, blood loss, cardiac disease and neuraxial/deep-block contraindications.
- Reperfusion can produce **hyperkalaemia, acidosis, arrhythmia, vasoplegia, myoglobin-related AKI and compartment syndrome**.
- Check ECG, gas/K/iCa/renal function, prepare treatments and monitor urine/compartments; fasciotomy may be required.
- Plan ICU, ongoing anticoagulation by cause, secondary prevention and assessment of embolic source.
- Treating venous DVT pathways alone misses the urgency of arterial occlusion.

### Prevention and catheter-related harm

- The 2025 arterial-catheter review reinforces early recognition, prompt vascular input and prevention through ultrasound-guided placement, appropriate catheter size/site, minimal attempts and regular limb/site checks.
- A normal pre-insertion collateral test does not guarantee protection from subsequent ischaemia.
- Consider haematoma/compartment compression as well as intraluminal thrombosis.
- Routine addition of heparin to a flush has no established universal patency advantage and is inappropriate in suspected HIT; use the local line protocol.

## Self-marking checklist

- Recognises limb threat and urgent vascular referral
- Examines viability, timing and instrument/embolic causes
- Anticoagulation with bleeding/HIT exceptions
- Imaging without delaying threatened-limb reperfusion
- Definitive open/catheter strategy and lysis limitations
- Anaesthetic anticoagulation constraints
- Reperfusion electrolyte/renal/compartment surveillance
- Links catheter-thrombosis recognition to prevention, compression complications and a safe flush strategy

items.title: 17. Discuss the diagnosis and management of disseminated intravascular coagulation…
items.q: Discuss the diagnosis and management of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) in the perioperative period.
items.a:
### Identify the syndrome and cause

- DIC is acquired systemic coagulation activation, microvascular thrombosis, consumption and dysregulated fibrinolysis.
- Phenotype varies: septic DIC often suppresses fibrinolysis; obstetric catastrophe/APL may cause severe hyperfibrinolytic bleeding.
- Triggers include sepsis, severe tissue injury, obstetric events, malignancy/APL and acute haemolytic reactions.
- Massive transfusion can produce dilutional coagulopathy and is not synonymous with DIC.

- Look for diffuse oozing, purpura, limb/circuit thrombosis and renal/neurological/respiratory injury.
- Trend platelets, PT/APTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer/FDP, blood film and haemolysis studies.
- **Normal/high fibrinogen early in sepsis does not exclude DIC**.
- ISTH overt score uses platelets, fibrin markers, PT prolongation and fibrinogen; ≥5 supports overt DIC only with an appropriate disorder and serial assessment.
- APTT and VEM may be normal early; neither rules it out.

### Exclude time-critical mimics

TTP/HUS: MAHA/schistocytes, thrombocytopenia, organ injury and often relatively normal PT/APTT; urgent haematology, ADAMTS13 sample and treatment without waiting if TTP likely. HIT: timed platelet fall with thrombosis after heparin; stop heparin and use an alternative anticoagulant. Also assess liver disease, drugs, marrow failure, vitamin K deficiency and simple dilution.

### Treat the driver and phenotype

- Source control/antibiotics, obstetric control/delivery as appropriate, immediate specialist ATRA for suspected APL, or other cause treatment; organ support in parallel.
- For active bleeding/urgent procedures, replace the demonstrated deficit: platelets often to >50 ×10⁹/L (higher for critical sites), fibrinogen commonly >1.5–2 g/L, plasma for significant multiple-factor deficiency; RBCs for delivery/haemorrhage.
- **PCC is not complete DIC replacement** and routine use can worsen thrombosis.
- Do not give FFP just to normalise an INR in a nonbleeding patient.

- VTE prophylaxis when safe; treatment anticoagulation may be justified for a predominant thrombotic phenotype with specialist advice.
- TXA is generally avoided in thrombotic DIC, but a selected severe hyperfibrinolytic bleeding phenotype requires disease-specific specialist judgment.
- Avoid neuraxial puncture in active DIC and minimise unnecessary invasive procedures.
- Repeat clinical/laboratory assessment because treatment needs change.

- Set a time for repeat coagulation testing and interpret changes against the course of the underlying disease.
- A declining fibrinogen or platelet count can matter even before the laboratory flags it.
- Establish whether the immediate issue is bleeding, thrombosis, both, or abnormal tests alone.
- Avoid component therapy solely to improve the appearance of results when the patient is stable and has no procedure planned.

## Self-marking checklist

- Systemic coagulation plus variable fibrinolysis
- Identifies cause and serial diagnostic pattern
- Normal fibrinogen/APTT does not exclude early disease
- Uses ISTH score in the right context
- Differentiates TTP, HIT, liver disease and dilution
- Cause treatment plus deficit replacement only when indicated
- Qualifies PCC, TXA and heparin; procedure precautions

items.title: 18. Discuss the causes of abnormal bleeding in a patient with chronic renal failure…
items.q: Discuss the causes of abnormal bleeding in a patient with chronic renal failure and a patient with cirrhosis, and how you would manage each perioperatively.
items.a:
### Uraemia: primarily a qualitative platelet problem

- Uraemic toxins, impaired adhesion/aggregation, endothelial mediators, anaemia and dialysis anticoagulation contribute; count/PT/APTT can be normal.
- Assess bleeding history, antithrombotics, dialysis timing, Hb/count and intended procedure.
- Optimise dialysis with a plan for residual heparin, treat demonstrated anaemia under renal guidance and avoid NSAIDs.
- **DDAVP 0.3 micrograms/kg IV over 20–30 min** may transiently improve clinically important bleeding/procedural haemostasis: monitor sodium, restrict appropriate free water and anticipate tachyphylaxis.
- Do not transfuse to a universal Hb100 solely for platelet function.
- Platelets, cryo, oestrogen or renal-adjusted TXA are specialist-selected rescue/indication-specific options, not a routine combination for every CKD patient.

### Cirrhosis: fragile rebalanced haemostasis

- Reduced procoagulants coexist with reduced anticoagulants (protein C/S/antithrombin), increased VWF/FVIII, thrombocytopenia and sometimes dysfibrinogenaemia.
- Portal pressure/vascular lesions can drive bleeding; renal failure/infection alter the balance.
- **INR is not a global bleeding-risk test**, but neither is VEM a complete validated predictor of every procedure's bleeding.
- Assess clinical bleeding, platelets/fibrinogen, drugs, renal function and procedure; VEM can help guide active bleeding/reduce unnecessary components.

- Do not give prophylactic FFP to normalise INR.
- Treat source/portal-hypertensive bleeding by the appropriate endoscopic/medical pathway, vitamin K only if deficiency plausible, and use platelets/fibrinogen/plasma for a clinically relevant deficit in bleeding/high-risk intervention.
- Avoid unnecessary large-volume plasma, but **PCC is not a universally safer substitute**; it can provoke thrombosis and does not replace all deficits.
- TXA is **not routine for variceal/GI bleeding** (HALT-IT); a documented hyperfibrinolytic surgical phenotype is different.
- A low-CVP technique is operation-specific (e.g. selected liver resection), not a blanket prescription in shocked cirrhosis.

### Shared plan

Specialist input, source control, normothermia, physiological iCa/pH and careful fluid/perfusion management. Individualise regional anaesthesia by haemostasis/function/drugs, assess both bleeding and thrombosis, and reassess after each treatment.

- Set a time for repeat coagulation testing and interpret changes against the course of the underlying disease.
- A declining fibrinogen or platelet count can matter even before the laboratory flags it.
- Establish whether the immediate issue is bleeding, thrombosis, both, or abnormal tests alone.
- Avoid component therapy solely to improve the appearance of results when the patient is stable and has no procedure planned.

## Self-marking checklist

- Uraemic qualitative platelet mechanisms
- Dialysis, anaemia review and DDAVP safety
- Avoids a routine rescue-drug cocktail/Hb target
- Explains rebalanced cirrhotic haemostasis
- Limits of INR and VEM
- Targeted products without reflex FFP/PCC or routine GI TXA
- Source/portal treatment, perfusion and specialist/regional plan

items.title: 19. A patient with new severe soft-tissue bleeding has an isolated prolonged APTT…
items.q: A patient with new severe soft-tissue bleeding has an isolated prolonged APTT, normal PT and no previous bleeding history. Explain your diagnostic approach and immediate management.
