items.a:
### Triage while investigating

- Assess ABC/perfusion, bleeding source and Hb trend; call haematology early.
- Stop nonessential anticoagulants/traumatic procedures, obtain suitable access carefully and provide RBC/physiological support as required.
- An acquired factor VIII inhibitor is a dangerous possibility; other causes include heparin contamination/exposure, dabigatran, inherited VIII/IX/XI deficiency and lupus anticoagulant.
- Factor XII/contact deficiency can prolong APTT without clinical bleeding.

- Repeat from a clean peripheral sample; review drugs, pregnancy/postpartum state, autoimmune disease and malignancy.
- Check FBC/platelets/film, fibrinogen, TT, relevant anti-Xa/dabigatran assay and haemolysis/organ tests as indicated.
- **Mixing study:** correction suggests deficiency; persistent or time-dependent prolongation suggests inhibitor.
- A delayed inhibitor effect requires incubated assessment; laboratory interpretation is essential.
- Send FVIII/IX/XI and inhibitor titre/Bethesda testing.
- Lupus anticoagulant often confers thrombosis risk and is not itself an explanation for this degree of haemorrhage.

### Treat suspected acquired haemophilia appropriately

- For clinically significant bleeding, specialist haemostasis may require **rFVIIa, aPCC or recombinant porcine FVIII**, selected by disease/antibodies, monitoring and availability.
- FFP alone is usually inadequate against a significant inhibitor; normal VEM does not exclude it.
- Avoid assuming congenital-haemophilia replacement will work without an inhibitor assessment.
- Immunosuppression to eradicate the inhibitor is a separate specialist treatment, balancing infection risk.
- If emicizumab is involved, APTT/one-stage assays are misleading and aPCC combinations can cause TMA/thrombosis.

Monitor ongoing loss, Hb/perfusion and treatment response, minimise invasive/IM/neuraxial trauma, manage pain and plan monitored care. Do not wait for a final inhibitor titre to act on life-threatening bleeding with a strongly suggestive presentation.

- Discuss extended testing with the laboratory before giving haemostatic treatment where practical, while treating severe bleeding in parallel.
- Review the sampling site and medication history because line contamination or anticoagulants can confound the tests.
- With probable acquired haemophilia, avoid unnecessary invasive procedures until a haemostatic plan is agreed.
- Review clinical bleeding and haemoglobin serially.
- Changes in the APTT alone are an unreliable indicator of treatment response with some therapies.
- Plan treatment of the inhibitor and assessment for an associated condition with haematology.

An absence of previous bleeding in an older patient increases suspicion of an acquired disorder.

## Self-marking checklist

- Recognises acquired inhibitor and immediate bleeding risk
- Excludes drug effect/contamination with clean sample
- Interprets immediate/incubated mixing study
- Sends factor/inhibitor testing and considers nonbleeding APTT causes
- Specialist haemostatic versus eradication treatment
- Explains FFP/VEM limitations and emicizumab caveat
- Avoids unnecessary trauma and monitors response

items.title: 20. An ICU patient develops platelets 18 ×10⁹/L, anaemia with schistocytes and new…
items.q: An ICU patient develops platelets 18 ×10⁹/L, anaemia with schistocytes and new confusion. PT is near normal. Discuss the differential diagnosis and immediate management.
items.a:
### Recognise a thrombotic microangiopathy without waiting for the full pentad

- Thrombocytopenia plus microangiopathic haemolysis and organ injury suggests TMA.
- Assess ABC, neurological/cardiac/renal injury, bleeding, blood pressure, infection, pregnancy/postpartum context, medicines, cancer and transplant history.
- Obtain film, reticulocytes, LDH, bilirubin, haptoglobin, creatinine/electrolytes, urine, coagulation/fibrinogen and ECG/troponin.
- Check previous Hb/platelets and exclude sampling artefacts.
- Involve haematology and ICU immediately.

| Possibility | Distinguishing considerations |
|---|---|
| Immune TTP | Severe ADAMTS13 deficiency/inhibitor; neurological/cardiac involvement can be prominent and renal injury varies. Normalish PT/APTT supports TMA but is not diagnostic |
| Shiga-toxin-associated HUS | Diarrhoeal/infectious context and renal injury; investigate with microbiology/nephrology |
| Complement-mediated HUS/TMA | Significant renal/systemic injury; exclude alternative causes and seek urgent specialist complement-directed assessment |
| DIC | Underlying sepsis/trauma/malignancy, falling platelets, high fibrin turnover and often prolonged PT/low or falling fibrinogen; early results can overlap |
| Other TMA/mimics | Severe hypertension, pregnancy-associated disease, drugs/transplant, mechanical haemolysis and malignancy; HIT is a different prothrombotic mechanism |

### Act urgently for suspected immune TTP

- Send ADAMTS13 activity/inhibitor samples **before plasma treatment if feasible**, but do not delay treatment for results.
- A validated probability tool can help when testing is delayed.
- Arrange emergency therapeutic plasma exchange and corticosteroids through an experienced centre; rituximab and caplacizumab are specialist additions.
- Caplacizumab limits VWF-mediated platelet microthrombosis; it does not eradicate the inhibitor and carries bleeding risk.
- Plasma infusion is not an equivalent definitive substitute for promptly accessible exchange in immune TTP.

- Avoid routine prophylactic platelets in TTP; life-threatening bleeding or an indispensable procedure needs a joint decision.
- Give RBCs for clinical need and treat organ complications.
- Do not give heparin merely to “treat the microclots” or manage every TMA as DIC with repeated empirical components.
- Treat HUS/other TMA according to its cause rather than assuming every patient needs the same exchange regimen.

### Reassess diagnosis and response

Trend count, haemolysis and organ function, avoid unnecessary invasive procedures and document recovery/relapse follow-up. ISTH's 2025 update retains the acute immune-TTP treatment recommendations; its new recombinant ADAMTS13 recommendation concerns **congenital TTP**, principally replacement/prophylaxis, and must not be substituted for the immune-TTP pathway.

## Self-marking checklist

- Recognises TMA without requiring the classic pentad
- Differentiates TTP, HUS, DIC and important secondary causes
- Obtains ADAMTS13 before plasma when feasible without treatment delay
- Urgent plasma exchange plus corticosteroids for suspected immune TTP
- Explains specialist caplacizumab/rituximab roles and limits
- Avoids routine platelets and unjustified heparin
- Tracks organ injury and distinguishes congenital from immune TTP

items.title: 21. A 45-year-old woman with a platelet count of 35 x 10^9/L due to immune…
items.q: A 45-year-old woman with a platelet count of 35 x 10^9/L due to immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) requires an elective laparoscopic splenectomy. Discuss your perioperative management.
items.a:
### Assess the patient rather than the count alone

- Confirm ITP/true thrombocytopenia, trend and bleeding phenotype, medications, other cell lines/film, previous treatment response and competing DIC/TMA/HIT/liver disease.
- At **35 ×10⁹/L**, elective splenectomy needs a haematology/surgical haemostatic plan; GA is generally preferable to neuraxial techniques at this count.
- A single 70–80 threshold is not universally safe for neuraxial anaesthesia.

### Improve haemostasis before elective surgery

- Haematology may use corticosteroids, IVIG (commonly 1 g/kg with response/repeat guided by protocol), or a TPO-receptor agonist when time permits.
- Account for adverse effects, thrombosis and steroid adrenal suppression.
- Selected anti-D treatment is not routine and has haemolysis risks.
- Major surgery often uses ≥50 ×10⁹/L as a general component threshold, but **ITP-specific elective major-surgery targets may be higher**, depending on procedure and team guidance.
- Splenectomy may be feasible at lower counts in experienced centres; avoid imposing one universal target.

- Platelets have a short survival in ITP.
- Do not transfuse prophylactically simply to normalise a number, but **life-threatening bleeding or an urgent invasive operation can justify platelet transfusion alongside IVIG/steroids**.
- During splenectomy, timing near/after splenic artery control may improve survival **if the patient is stable**; never delay lifesaving platelets until clamping as an absolute rule.

### Anaesthesia and postoperative plan

Gentle airway/vascular instrumentation, avoid unnecessary nasal/IM trauma and NSAIDs, source control and appropriate haemostatic adjuncts. Assess accepted block alternatives by site/compressibility. Plan blood/platelet availability, sufficient IV access and response monitoring. Consider steroid cover by actual exposure.

Vaccination against pneumococcus, meningococcus and Hib, asplenia antibiotic/fever education and local prophylaxis plan. After splenectomy monitor count, bleeding, infection and portal/systemic thrombosis; provide appropriate mechanical/pharmacological VTE prevention when haemostasis permits. A postoperative platelet rise does not justify ignoring thrombosis risk.

### IVIg is a product with important hazards

- IVIg provides pooled IgG with immunomodulatory effects, including altered Fc-mediated immune-cell activation; it can produce a relatively rapid, often temporary platelet response in ITP.
- Confirm indication, product, total grams, dosing weight and monitoring with haematology.
- Use the current product-specific infusion chart: a concentration and a rate in mL/kg/hour must not be confused with a dose in g/kg.
- Watch for infusion reactions/anaphylaxis, thrombosis, renal injury, aseptic meningitis and haemolysis/positive DAT.
- Assess fluid tolerance and renal/thrombotic risk; select an appropriate formulation and rate.
- It is not a risk-free substitute for donor platelets and does not make every urgent procedure safe immediately.

## Self-marking checklist

- Confirms diagnosis, trend and bleeding risk
- Specialist elective target rather than generic count rule
- Steroid/IVIG/TPO options and time to response
- Platelets for severe bleeding/urgent intervention, not clamp-only rule
- Appropriate GA and instrumentation precautions
- Asplenia vaccination/infection planning
- Postoperative VTE, count and bleeding surveillance
- Explains IVIg mechanism/temporary benefit and renal, thrombotic, haemolytic and infusion risks

items.title: 22. An ICU patient has a progressive haemoglobin fall without obvious external…
items.q: An ICU patient has a progressive haemoglobin fall without obvious external bleeding. Outline your investigation and management, including when you would transfuse.
items.a:
### Confirm the fall and assess urgency

- Repeat an unexpected result and check sampling dilution, Hb trend, fluids, transfusions and vital signs/perfusion.
- Shock, ischaemia or rapidly falling Hb warrants urgent source assessment/resuscitation; do not attribute it to “ICU anaemia” prematurely.
- Review surgery/drains, GI/urinary loss, puncture sites, retroperitoneal/abdominal bleeding, CRRT/ECMO circuit loss and repeated phlebotomy; image/endoscope according to findings and stability.

### Classify loss, destruction, dilution or low production

- FBC/indices, reticulocytes and film organise the differential.
- Haemolysis: LDH/bilirubin/haptoglobin, DAT and urine; review transfusion timing, mechanical circuit/valve damage, drugs, G6PD triggers and TMA.
- Low/inappropriately normal reticulocytes: inflammation/hepcidin-mediated restriction, renal EPO deficiency, marrow suppression, nutritional deficiency or malignancy.
- Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant; interpret TSAT/CRP and B12/folate selectively rather than automatically treating every high-ferritin inflammatory patient with iron.
- Check renal/liver function, coagulation and associated cytopenias.

### Treat the cause and preserve oxygen delivery

- Control bleeding, stop causative drugs/circuit injury, treat sepsis/haemolysis and refer for unexplained pancytopenia/blasts.
- Minimise sampling, use small tubes and correct demonstrated deficiencies.
- Routine ESA for anaemia of critical illness is not supported simply to avoid a transfusion and can increase thrombosis.
- IV iron is not an immediate rescue for low oxygen delivery; weigh infection/indication and time to response.

- RBC transfusion treats inadequate oxygen-carrying capacity: for many stable nonbleeding ICU adults consider Hb <70 g/L, one unit followed by reassessment.
- Acute MI, selected neurocritical states, severe hypoxaemia, ongoing haemorrhage and clinical intolerance require a different discussion.
- Do not use tachycardia/lactate alone to assume RBC deficiency when flow, infection or pain is the cause.
- Document response, TACO precautions and a durable cause-treatment plan.

- Trend the timing of the haemoglobin fall against fluid balance, procedures and cumulative blood sampling.
- A stable patient can tolerate a staged investigation.
- Ongoing shock, rising support requirements or a rapid fall warrants active examination for bleeding, imaging when safe and early surgical or interventional review.
- Compare serial indices, reticulocytes and the blood film with previous results to distinguish impaired production from loss or destruction.
- Before transfusing, define the clinical goal and reassess symptomatic response and volume tolerance after each unit in a stable adult.

## Self-marking checklist

- Confirms trend/specimen and assesses instability
- Searches occult and iatrogenic blood loss
- Uses reticulocytes/film and haemolysis studies
- Evaluates inflammatory, renal, nutritional and marrow causes
- Treats cause and conserves diagnostic blood
- Qualifies stable threshold and key exceptions
- Single-unit reassessment and avoids automatic ESA/iron

items.title: 23. An ICU patient has platelets 45 ×10⁹/L. Discuss your diagnostic approach and…
items.q: An ICU patient has platelets 45 ×10⁹/L. Discuss your diagnostic approach and whether platelets are required for no procedure, a central venous catheter or major surgery.
items.a:
### Confirm and define the clinical problem

- Review the film/repeat a citrate sample for clumping.
- Establish baseline, trajectory, timing of sepsis/CPB/heparin/new drugs, bleeding, thrombosis, fever, organ injury and other cell lines.
- Platelet function and anticoagulants matter independently of count.
- Causes: artefact, dilution, sepsis/DIC, HIT, immune drug-induced thrombocytopenia/ITP, TTP/HUS, marrow suppression/infiltration, hypersplenism and circuits.
- A fall with MAHA/neurological/renal injury needs urgent TMA assessment, while day-5–10 fall/thrombosis suggests HIT.
- Do not equate every low ICU count with DIC.

### Decide according to context

| Situation | Decision at 45 ×10⁹/L |
|---|---|
| Stable, no bleeding/procedure | Usually no prophylactic platelets; treat cause and trend. AABB 2025 uses <10 for many nonbleeding adult consumptive/hypoproliferative contexts, with important disease-specific exceptions |
| Ultrasound-guided compressible-site CVC | Not an automatic transfusion to 50. AABB conditionally recommends transfusion below 10; operator, site, function/drugs and local policy matter |
| Major nonneuraxial surgery | General guidance recommends transfusion below 50; coordinate timing/target and cause with the surgeon/haematologist |
| Intracranial/other critical-site bleeding | Higher individual targets often around 100; separate evidence and procedure-specific assessment |
| Diagnostic lumbar puncture | AABB recommends transfusion below 20, but this is **not a neuraxial anaesthesia/epidural threshold** |

### Cause-specific treatment and follow-up

- TTP: urgent plasma exchange/specialist therapy, no routine prophylactic platelets.
- HIT: stop heparin, alternative anticoagulant; avoid routine platelets.
- ITP: immunomodulation, with platelets for serious bleeding/urgent intervention as part of the plan.
- DIC: cause control and components for bleeding/procedure, not isolated tests.
- Marrow suppression: disease-directed support and infection care.
- Recheck count/bleeding after transfusion, consider refractoriness and HLA/immune assessment if the increment is poor.
- Apply an individual VTE prevention plan as the platelet count recovers.

### Worked delayed-transfusion pattern: post-transfusion purpura

- If a patient's platelets fall profoundly with purpura/bleeding approximately 5–12 days after cellular-component transfusion, especially after previous pregnancy/transfusion, consider **post-transfusion purpura**.
- This is not the same as an immediate transfusion reaction, platelet refractoriness or red-cell hyperhaemolysis.
- An anamnestic recipient anti-HPA response causes destruction of donor and the patient's own platelets.
- Notify blood bank/haematology, investigate HPA antibodies and exclude competing causes.
- NZBS recommends IVIg **2 g/kg total in divided doses over 2–5 days**, with specialist monitoring.
- Avoid reflex repeated random-donor platelets; life-threatening bleeding can require urgently selected compatible/HPA-negative support.
- Record future component requirements.

### Thrombosis plus thrombocytopenia without the expected heparin history

- With the appropriate adenoviral-vector vaccination history, severe thrombocytopenia, very high D-dimer, low fibrinogen and unusual-site thrombosis, consider **VITT** rather than assuming ITP.
- Send a PF4 ELISA and imaging directed by symptoms; a rapid HIT assay can be falsely negative.
- Treat a strong suspicion urgently with haematology while results are pending: IVIg plus a suitable non-heparin anticoagulant, with organ-function/bleeding assessment.
- ASH describes IVIg 1 g/kg daily for two days; use the specialist protocol.
- Avoid routine platelet transfusion, but catastrophic bleeding/urgent surgery requires an individual rescue decision.
- This is a historical exposure-linked differential, not a claim that all current vaccines cause VITT.

## Self-marking checklist

- Confirms true count, timing and clinical phenotype
- Differentiates sepsis/DIC, HIT, TMA, ITP and production failure
- Applies modern no-procedure/CVC/major-surgery distinctions
- Separates LP from neuraxial anaesthesia
- Respects disease-specific platelet-transfusion cautions
- Reviews post-transfusion response and refractoriness
- Plans cause treatment and thrombosis prevention
- Recognises and treats post-transfusion purpura with appropriate HPA investigation/product planning
- Recognises exposure-linked VITT and distinguishes it from ITP, HIT and DIC

items.title: 24. A patient receiving chemotherapy remains severely thrombocytopenic after two…
items.q: A patient receiving chemotherapy remains severely thrombocytopenic after two platelet transfusions. Explain how you would investigate refractoriness and select further blood components.
items.a:
### Confirm the response and clinical urgency

- Check bleeding, impending procedures and the actual indication for more platelets.
- Verify transfusion completion, dose/product, pretransfusion count and a count **10–60 minutes after completion**, ideally on two occasions.
- Exclude clumping or sampling/dilution artefacts.
- Ask transfusion medicine to calculate the corrected count increment (CCI), accounting for body surface area and delivered platelet dose.
- NZBS uses a poor increment below 10 × 10⁹/L or CCI below 5,000/µL.
- A next-morning result alone cannot establish alloimmune failure.

### Separate consumption from alloimmunity

- Nonimmune causes are common: ongoing bleeding, sepsis/fever, DIC, splenic sequestration, medicines and circuit consumption.
- A good early increment followed by a later fall suggests consumption, but timing patterns are not definitive.
- Poor early increments raise alloimmune destruction as a possibility, particularly after pregnancy or repeated transfusion.
- HLA class I antibodies are more common than HPA antibodies.
- Refractoriness and alloimmunisation are not synonyms.

- Discuss HLA/HPA testing, platelet crossmatching and provision of selected compatible components with transfusion medicine.
- HLA-selected, antigen-compatible or crossmatch-compatible platelets are chosen by the demonstrated mechanism and availability; they are not a routine order for every low count.
- Treat nonimmune drivers.
- Continue necessary emergency haemostatic support during bleeding while optimal products are arranged; repeatedly giving unselected platelets to correct an isolated number can cause exposure without benefit.

### Specify what each product modification achieves

| Modification | Purpose and limits |
|---|---|
| Leukodepletion | Reduces donor leukocytes and some febrile/CMV/alloimmunisation risks; does not replace irradiation |
| Irradiation | Prevents donor-lymphocyte TA-GVHD for specific recipients/treatments/donations. NZ platelets are routinely irradiated; not every malignancy needs irradiated RBCs |
| Washing | Reduces residual plasma for selected severe allergic indications; not routine treatment of platelet alloimmunity |
| HLA/HPA selection | Addresses demonstrated alloimmune platelet destruction; requires advance planning and response checks |
| RBC antigen matching | Addresses RBC alloantibodies/haemoglobinopathy requirements; does not solve HLA-mediated platelet failure |

Confirm transplant/therapy-specific irradiated and CMV requirements with the blood bank. Recheck clinical haemostasis and early increments after selected products, documenting which intervention worked. Use disease-specific exceptions for TTP/HIT/ITP rather than applying chemotherapy prophylaxis thresholds to every patient.

- Interpret the platelet trend in relation to the chronology of drug exposure, procedures and transfusion.
- Repeat an unexpected result, review the blood film and assess for competing causes.
- The urgency of correction depends on the bleeding phenotype and the planned intervention.
- Check the treatment response and revisit the diagnosis if the expected increment or haemostatic improvement does not occur.

## Self-marking checklist

- Confirms true poor response on timed post-transfusion counts
- Uses correctly scaled CCI with blood-bank assistance
- Prioritises nonimmune consumption before assuming HLA antibodies
- Distinguishes HLA/HPA testing and compatible platelet options
- Treats bleeding and cause while products are arranged
- Distinguishes leukodepletion, irradiation, washing and matching
- Documents response and treatment-specific requirements

items.title: 25. Compare transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) and…
items.q: Compare transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) and transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO) in terms of pathophysiology, diagnosis and management.
items.a:
### Similar presentation, different dominant mechanism

- Both cause hypoxaemia and bilateral pulmonary opacities after transfusion; mixed cases occur.
- **TRALI is permeability oedema**, typically during/within 6 h, without hydrostatic overload as the main cause.
- Type I has no ARDS risk factor; Type II may occur with an ARDS risk factor or mild pre-existing ARDS if respiratory status was stable for the preceding 12 h.
- **TACO is hydrostatic overload**, during/within 12 h, and may follow a small volume in a susceptible patient.

| Finding | Supports TRALI | Supports TACO |
|---|---|---|
| Context | Inflammatory susceptibility; donor antibody/neutrophil/endothelial mechanisms | Cardiac/renal impairment, low body weight, rapid infusion or positive balance |
| BP/JVP | Hypotension or normal BP can occur | Hypertension/JVP rise common, but neither obligatory |
| Echo/volume assessment | Overload is not dominant; cardiac disease may coexist | Evidence of raised filling pressure/congestion supports |
| BNP/NT-proBNP | Cannot exclude/confirm alone, especially in critical illness | Elevated or increased value is supportive, not a stand-alone diagnosis |
| Response | Diuretics do not treat pure permeability injury | Diuresis/afterload/respiratory support often helps |

There is no reliable bedside “low BNP = TRALI, high BNP = TACO” rule. Do not assume normal EF excludes TACO or abnormal EF excludes TRALI. Consider aspiration, anaphylaxis, bacterial sepsis, AHTR, cardiogenic/negative-pressure oedema and evolving ARDS.

### Immediate management

Stop transfusion, assess ABC, give oxygen/ventilatory support, check identifiers and alert blood bank. Preserve the bag/set; maintain access through a fresh line/set without flushing the implicated unit. Send reaction/haemolysis/sepsis tests as indicated; obtain CXR/lung ultrasound, echo, gas and volume assessment without delaying support.

- TRALI: supportive lung-protective ventilation if needed, cautious haemodynamic treatment and specialist/ICU care; no routine steroids or diuresis unless a coexisting indication exists.
- Report so the blood service can investigate and manage co-components.
- TACO: stop unnecessary fluids, sit up if appropriate, oxygen/CPAP and diuretics, treat heart/renal failure.
- Reassess uncertainty as treatment proceeds.

### Prevention

Avoid unnecessary transfusion. TACO risk assessment, single-unit prescribing/reassessment for stable patients, slower or divided transfusions and selective diuretic use. TRALI mitigation relies on donor/plasma policies and reporting; bedside screening cannot prevent all cases.

- Keep the implicated bag and giving set for transfusion service investigation.
- Maintain emergency resuscitation through fresh tubing or alternate access.
- If the patient still needs urgent components, agree on the safest replacement with transfusion medicine.
- Once stabilised, document the sequence of products, symptoms and treatments and communicate the suspected reaction to the patient and future treating teams.

## Self-marking checklist

- Mechanism and 6 h versus 12 h windows
- TRALI I/II and coexistence with cardiac disease
- Uses BNP/echo as supportive, not definitive
- Stops transfusion, fresh access, identity/blood-bank steps
- Differential and targeted investigations
- Ventilatory support and indication-specific diuretics
- Prevention and haemovigilance

items.title: 26. A patient with sickle cell disease returns ten days after transfusion with…
items.q: A patient with sickle cell disease returns ten days after transfusion with pain, dark urine and haemoglobin below the pretransfusion value. Discuss your investigation and management.
items.a:
### Suspect delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction with hyperhaemolysis

- An apparent pain crisis after transfusion can conceal destruction of donor and patient RBCs.
- Hb below the pretransfusion baseline is particularly concerning for hyperhaemolysis.
- Assess perfusion, oxygenation, chest symptoms, neurological findings and renal function; involve haematology and transfusion medicine urgently.
- Consider bleeding, infection, acute chest syndrome, aplasia, splenic sequestration and other haemolytic causes concurrently.

- Send FBC/reticulocytes, film, bilirubin/LDH/haptoglobin, renal/electrolytes and urine.
- Obtain DAT, antibody screen and repeat compatibility testing, retrieving all historical antibodies and recent transfusion details.
- Follow HbA/HbS fractions where useful to identify rapid donor-cell disappearance.
- A negative DAT or current antibody screen does **not** exclude the reaction; antibodies may be evanescent or initially undetectable.
- Reticulocytes may be low relative to the patient's usual response.

### Avoid reflex transfusion while treating dangerous anaemia

- Provide careful respiratory/perfusion support, analgesia and cause-directed treatment, avoiding fluid overload.
- Further RBCs can intensify hyperhaemolysis: do not automatically chase the previous Hb.
- Conversely, life-threatening anaemia may make transfusion necessary; make that decision jointly with haematology/blood bank, using extended antigen matching and a documented rescue plan.
- Do not delay lifesaving treatment to obtain a perfectly negative serological result.

- ASH conditionally supports immunosuppression for ongoing hyperhaemolysis with very low-certainty evidence: specialist first-line therapy commonly involves IVIG and corticosteroids; eculizumab is a selected subsequent option.
- Rituximab may help prevent additional alloantibody formation when further transfusion is anticipated.
- These drugs have important adverse effects and need specialist protocols.
- Support erythropoiesis and correct demonstrable deficiencies; iron is not automatically appropriate in a chronically transfused patient.

### Monitor and prevent recurrence

Trend Hb, reticulocytes, haemolysis, renal function, oxygenation and treatment response. Record the reaction and all antibody history permanently, communicate future component requirements across institutions and explain warning symptoms to the patient. This is a delayed reaction, distinct from immediate ABO haemolysis and from routine postoperative anaemia.

- Ask about prior alloantibodies, delayed reactions, baseline haemoglobin, usual oxygen saturation and disease severity.
- Involve the specialist team and transfusion service early so compatible blood and a perioperative plan are available.
- Avoid dehydration as well as fluid overload.
- In recovery follow oxygenation, respiratory symptoms and pain closely, and act on unexpected changes from baseline rather than attributing them automatically to the underlying disorder.

## Self-marking checklist

- Recognises delayed haemolysis/hyperhaemolysis rather than pain alone
- Assesses competing diagnoses and organ injury
- Tests haemolysis, reticulocytes, antibodies and Hb fractions
- Understands negative DAT does not exclude the diagnosis
- Balances transfusion aggravation against life-threatening anaemia
- Specialist immunotherapy, matching and erythropoietic support
- Documents lifelong antibody/reaction history and follow-up

items.title: 27. Outline the major haemoglobinopathy groups and explain how their phenotype…
items.q: Outline the major haemoglobinopathy groups and explain how their phenotype changes perioperative assessment and transfusion planning.
items.a:
### Classify the disorder before prescribing treatment

- Haemoglobinopathies involve abnormal globin structure, reduced globin-chain production or combinations.
- Establish genotype, clinical severity, baseline Hb/reticulocytes, haemolysis, prior complications, current treatment and transfusion history.
- HPLC/electrophoresis and, where needed, molecular testing distinguish variants; recent donor transfusion can alter the measured fractions.
- Microcytosis alone is not proof of iron deficiency.

| Group | Clinical significance and anaesthetic implications |
|---|---|
| HbSS and sickle β⁰-thalassaemia | Often substantial haemolytic/vaso-occlusive disease; assess acute chest, stroke, pulmonary/cardiac/renal injury, pain and transfusion complications |
| HbSC and sickle β⁺-thalassaemia | Variable sickle disease; a higher baseline Hb does not imply negligible risk. Avoid an excessive viscosity rise from indiscriminate simple transfusion |
| Sickle trait | Usually asymptomatic; differs from SCD and does not justify routine preoperative exchange. Assess individual extreme physiological exposures and comorbidity |
| α/β-thalassaemia | Spectrum from trait to HbH/intermedia/transfusion-dependent disease. Severe forms require attention to ineffective erythropoiesis, organ effects, iron overload, antibodies and splenectomy risks |
| HbC/HbE | HbC disease can cause haemolysis; HbSC is a sickling disorder. HbE alone is often mild, but HbE/β-thalassaemia may cause severe or transfusion-dependent disease |

### Translate phenotype into a perioperative plan

- Assess oxygen delivery and organ reserve rather than using a single generic Hb target.
- Severe thalassaemia may have iron-related cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia, hepatic/endocrine disease and marrow-expansion/airway or skeletal changes.
- Investigate relevant organ effects, not every possible test in an asymptomatic carrier.
- Review chelation, chronic therapies and infection risk, including asplenia vaccination/fever precautions.

- For SCD, avoid hypoxaemia, acidosis, hypothermia, dehydration, uncontrolled pain and excessive fluid.
- Plan postoperative respiratory care and VTE prevention.
- For significant haemoglobinopathy, coordinate antigen matching and all historical antibodies early; leukodepletion and irradiation address different risks.
- Simple versus exchange transfusion is individualised to baseline Hb, operation and disease severity, with hyperviscosity and previous delayed haemolysis considered.
- Routine HbS <30% or exchange is not required for every operation.

- Treat proven coexisting deficiency, but do not routinely prescribe iron for thalassaemic microcytosis.
- G6PD deficiency is an enzymopathy, and methaemoglobinaemia a dyshemoglobinaemia; recognise them as related differentials rather than misclassifying them as a major inherited globin-chain group.
- The existing SCD/thalassaemia cases provide detailed disease-specific anaesthetic plans.

## Self-marking checklist

- Separates structural variants from reduced-chain production
- Distinguishes sickle genotypes, disease and trait
- Covers α/β-thalassaemia and HbC/HbE combinations
- Uses phenotype and organ reserve rather than Hb alone
- Plans antibody matching and individual simple/exchange transfusion
- Avoids routine iron for microcytosis and universal HbS target
- Includes organ/airway, asplenia and postoperative risks

items.title: 28. A 24-year-old man with sickle cell disease (HbSS) requires an elective…
items.q: A 24-year-old man with sickle cell disease (HbSS) requires an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Discuss his perioperative management.
items.a:
### Risk and multidisciplinary planning

- HbSS produces deoxygenation-related HbS polymerisation, haemolysis and vaso-occlusion.
- Assess crises, acute chest syndrome/stroke, baseline Hb/SpO₂, pulmonary hypertension, renal/cardiac disease, infection/asplenia, analgesic use and prior transfusion reactions/alloantibodies.
- Involve a sickle specialist and blood bank early; provide appropriately phenotype/genotype-matched RBCs if needed.

### Transfusion before this operation

- ASH conditionally favours preoperative transfusion for GA lasting >1 h, but the decision depends on genotype, baseline Hb, surgical risk, phenotype and previous transfusion harms.
- For Hb <90 g/L, simple transfusion may achieve an appropriate **90–110 g/L** range; avoid excessive viscosity, commonly not exceeding **110 g/L** with simple transfusion.
- If baseline Hb is already >90–100, exchange may be preferable when transfusion is beneficial; very high-risk surgery or severe phenotype can warrant a lower HbS target (often <30%).
- **HbS <30–40% is not mandatory for every laparoscopic cholecystectomy**, and Hb >100 is not universally prohibited.
- Do not delay emergency surgery merely to reach an elective target.

### Anaesthesia and recovery

- Avoid prolonged fasting, hypoxaemia, hypovolaemia/overload, hypothermia, acidosis, hypotension and venous stasis.
- Use approved clear-fluid policy and IV fluid if needed rather than automatic deficit replacement.
- GA/laparoscopy and regional analgesia can be appropriate; manage insufflation/ventilation and monitor perfusion.
- Provide effective multimodal analgesia without hypoventilation, warming, antibiotics for the procedure and indicated asplenia/infection care.

- Postoperative lung expansion/incentive spirometry, mobilisation, euvolaemia and suitable VTE prophylaxis are important.
- Suspect **acute chest syndrome** with a new infiltrate plus fever/respiratory features/hypoxaemia: urgent specialist review, oxygen/respiratory support, infection treatment, analgesia and simple/exchange transfusion as indicated.
- Distinguish PE, atelectasis and surgical complications from painful crisis.
- High-flow oxygen is not routine when saturation is normal.

- Ask about prior alloantibodies, delayed reactions, baseline haemoglobin, usual oxygen saturation and disease severity.
- Involve the specialist team and transfusion service early so compatible blood and a perioperative plan are available.
- Avoid dehydration as well as fluid overload.
- In recovery follow oxygenation, respiratory symptoms and pain closely, and act on unexpected changes from baseline rather than attributing them automatically to the underlying disorder.

Establish a plan for prompt review if hypoxaemia and a new infiltrate develop after surgery.

## Self-marking checklist

- Explains sickling, phenotype and organ risk
- Specialist and antigen-matched blood planning
- Individualises simple/exchange transfusion and avoids hyperviscosity
- Uses ASH targets without universal HbS or Hb100 rule
- Protects oxygenation, temperature, perfusion and hydration
- Analgesia, lung expansion, VTE prevention and mobilisation
- Recognises and treats acute chest syndrome

items.title: 29. Outline the anaesthetic considerations for a patient with beta-thalassaemia…
items.q: Outline the anaesthetic considerations for a patient with beta-thalassaemia major presenting for a splenectomy.
items.a:
### Multisystem disease and operation-specific risks

Transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia causes ineffective erythropoiesis/haemolysis, marrow expansion and iron loading. Review regular transfusions/chelation, baseline Hb, alloantibodies, reactions and infection history. Splenomegaly and hypersplenism may cause cytopenias; splenectomy adds haemorrhage, infection and portal/systemic thrombosis risk.

- Preoperatively involve haematology and assess ECG/echo, cardiac MRI T2* where available, heart failure/arrhythmia/pulmonary hypertension
- Hepatic fibrosis/function
- Diabetes, thyroid/parathyroid dysfunction/calcium
- Renal function, osteoporosis and growth/skeletal change.
- Blood-bank planning requires compatible antigen-matched blood with historical antibodies respected.
- Routine chronic targets are often around **95–105 g/L pretransfusion**, but perioperative targets depend on cardiac disease and the specialist regimen; do not apply a generic ICU 70 threshold.

### Anaesthetic plan

- Maxillary expansion, dentition and skeletal abnormalities may complicate mask/intubation; prepare a tailored airway plan rather than assuming every patient is difficult.
- Protect fragile bones and pressure areas.
- Maintain oxygenation, temperature, perfusion/rhythm and carefully judged volume in iron-overload cardiomyopathy.
- Use invasive monitoring for the actual cardiac/bleeding risk, not automatically in all cases.
- Assess platelet/coagulation status and anatomy before regional techniques.

RBCs should be leukodepleted/appropriately matched; **thalassaemia alone does not automatically require irradiated RBCs**. NZ platelet irradiation follows blood-service policy. Salvage in haemoglobinopathy is a specialist decision, not an unqualified routine option.

### Splenectomy and recovery

- Plan vaccines, local antibiotic prophylaxis and fever/asplenia education; time vaccination before elective splenectomy where feasible.
- Anticipate splenic-bed bleeding, postoperative thrombocytosis and portal-vein thrombosis.
- Provide appropriate VTE prevention, postoperative cardiac/respiratory monitoring, analgesia, glucose/electrolyte review and a coordinated transfusion/chelation plan.
- Trait/minor disease has very different risk from transfusion-dependent major disease; do not prescribe iron for microcytosis unless deficiency is demonstrated.

- Ask about prior alloantibodies, delayed reactions, baseline haemoglobin, usual oxygen saturation and disease severity.
- Involve the specialist team and transfusion service early so compatible blood and a perioperative plan are available.
- Avoid dehydration as well as fluid overload.
- In recovery follow oxygenation, respiratory symptoms and pain closely, and act on unexpected changes from baseline rather than attributing them automatically to the underlying disorder.

Explain which organ complications would change postoperative destination, especially cardiac dysfunction, pulmonary hypertension or active infection.

## Self-marking checklist

- Explains major disease and splenectomy risks
- Cardiac iron, hepatic/endocrine/renal and skeletal assessment
- Airway, bone/positioning and monitoring plan
- Antibody-compatible blood and specialist Hb target
- Does not mandate irradiation/salvage for every case
- Vaccination, antibiotics and asplenia education
- Bleeding, VTE/portal thrombosis and chronic-care follow-up

items.title: 30. A 30-year-old woman with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia on chemotherapy requires…
items.q: A 30-year-old woman with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia on chemotherapy requires a central line and an emergency laparotomy. Discuss the perioperative issues.
items.a:
### Parallel urgent assessment and source-directed treatment

- Discuss the cause/urgency of laparotomy with surgery, haematology and ICU.
- Assess ABC/perfusion, fever/neutropenic sepsis, bleeding, mucositis, bowel obstruction/ileus and recent chemotherapy/steroids.
- Obtain CBC/differential/film, coagulation/fibrinogen, renal/liver function, electrolytes/urate/LDH, gas/lactate and cultures where appropriate without delaying treatment.
- Review cardiac symptoms/anthracycline exposure, renal injury, tumour lysis and airway/vascular mass effects if suggested by diagnosis/symptoms; not every ALL patient has bleomycin exposure or a mediastinal mass.

### Infection, cytopenias and products

- Prompt broad-spectrum IV antibiotics for **suspected neutropenic sepsis/intra-abdominal infection**, plus procedure prophylaxis as indicated; neutropenia alone does not create an identical antibiotic regimen for every operation.
- Treat volume/perfusion carefully with cardiomyopathy risk.
- Prepare antigen-compatible leukodepleted RBCs and platelets for the actual indication.
- Confirm **irradiated RBC/CMV requirements by specific treatment/transplant history**, not the generic label of malignancy; NZ platelets are irradiated routinely.
- Consider platelet refractoriness/alloimmunisation.

- A count below 50 ×10⁹/L commonly prompts platelets for major nonneuraxial surgery; **compressible-site ultrasound-guided CVC thresholds differ** (2025 AABB conditionally recommends transfusion below 10 in adults).
- Use site, operator, function, trend and urgency; do not apply a universal platelet100 neuraxial permission rule.
- Active coagulopathy/sepsis/thrombocytopenia often makes neuraxial techniques unsuitable.

### Anaesthesia and recovery

- Experienced airway management with care of mucosa; aspiration strategy appropriate to bowel pathology.
- A symptomatic mediastinal mass requires a dedicated positioning/airway/cardiovascular rescue plan before induction.
- Ultrasound-guided access with aseptic technique; invasive monitoring by instability/organ risk.
- Avoid fluid overload in cardiomyopathy, maintain warmth/calcium and source haemostasis; TXA only if indicated.
- If bleomycin was actually used, titrate oxygen to need—never withhold necessary oxygen.
- Steroid cover by exposure/risk.

ICU/HDU as indicated; monitor bleeding, infection, TLS/electrolytes/AKI, respiratory/cardiac dysfunction, pain and resumption of prophylaxis/oncological care. Explain that urgent surgery and resuscitation proceed together rather than waiting to normalise every blood result.

- Interpret the platelet trend in relation to the chronology of drug exposure, procedures and transfusion.
- Repeat an unexpected result, review the blood film and assess for competing causes.
- The urgency of correction depends on the bleeding phenotype and the planned intervention.
- Check the treatment response and revisit the diagnosis if the expected increment or haemostatic improvement does not occur.

## Self-marking checklist

- Urgency/source and specialist coordination
- Infection, marrow failure and relevant drug toxicity
- TLS/organ and mass effects assessed selectively
- Product modifications by actual indication
- Distinguishes CVC/major surgery/neuraxial thresholds
- Appropriate airway/access/perfusion precautions
- Postoperative organ, infection, bleeding/VTE and treatment plan

items.title: 31. Describe the haematological emergencies that may alter the immediate…
items.q: Describe the haematological emergencies that may alter the immediate anaesthetic plan in a patient with leukaemia, lymphoma or myeloma.
items.a:
### Recognise time-critical disease beyond a low blood count

- Assess clinical urgency, disease/treatment status, infection, organ reserve, bleeding/thrombosis, airway/mediastinal compression and the reason for surgery.
- Call haematology early.
- FBC/film, clotting/fibrinogen, blood gas, renal/electrolytes, calcium/phosphate, urate and LDH are directed by the suspected emergency.
- Treat sepsis, shock, hypoxaemia and major bleeding concurrently; avoid a generic anaesthetic plan before identifying the dominant risk.

| Emergency | Immediate implications |
|---|---|
| Suspected APL with coagulopathy | Bleeding and thrombosis can be catastrophic. Haematology-led **ATRA should begin on suspicion**, without waiting for molecular confirmation; support platelets/fibrinogen/plasma and avoid nonessential invasive procedures. Do not use routine TXA/heparin or leukapheresis as generic treatment |
| Hyperleukocytosis/leukostasis | Respiratory/neurological dysfunction can be an emergency even without a universal WCC cutoff. Urgent cytoreduction and careful fluid/metabolic support; RBC transfusion may worsen viscosity, so coordinate essential transfusion rather than chasing a normal Hb |
| Tumour lysis | Hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, secondary hypocalcaemia, hyperuricaemia and AKI can precede or follow treatment. Monitor ECG/serial biochemistry and urine; treat dangerous hyperkalaemia, use specialist urate-lowering therapy and renal support when indicated |
| Hyperviscosity/paraproteinaemia | Visual/neurological symptoms and mucosal bleeding require specialist assessment, sometimes urgent plasma exchange; coordinate transfusion and volume strategy rather than increasing viscosity indiscriminately |
| Neutropenic sepsis | Immediate antibiotics/source control with appropriate haemodynamic support; an apparently mild fever may be serious |

### Distinguish treatment hazards and prepare safely

- For tumour-lysis prevention/treatment, prescribe fluids to actual cardiac/renal tolerance with close reassessment.
- Rasburicase lowers existing urate; allopurinol prevents new urate formation.
- Check G6PD before rasburicase and avoid it in deficiency.
- Routine urine alkalinisation is not recommended.
- Isolated asymptomatic hypocalcaemia in severe hyperphosphataemia is managed differently from symptomatic arrhythmia/seizure: involve renal/haematology rather than automatic repeated calcium replacement.

- Myeloma also raises concerns about renal injury, hypercalcaemia, infection and fragile bones.
- Daratumumab can interfere with indirect antiglobulin compatibility testing; inform the blood bank early, retrieve pretreatment phenotype/genotype where available and let the laboratory use validated methods.
- DTT can obscure Kell antigens, changing product selection.
- This is not necessarily a new alloantibody or active haemolysis.

Coordinate haemostatic targets, invasive access, ICU and rescue resources; defer nonessential procedures until the immediate emergency is treated. Detailed malignancy therapy and mediastinal-mass anaesthesia remain in their specialist sets; this answer tests the haematological problems that change today's plan.

### Worked treatment-related deterioration: CAR-T

- Ask about recent CAR-T therapy and contact the treating centre immediately when fever, hypoxia, hypotension or neurological change develops.
- **Cytokine-release syndrome (CRS)** can produce vasodilatory shock and respiratory failure; infection, tumour lysis and other causes may coexist.
- Provide cultures and prompt indicated antimicrobials, cautious fluid reassessment, oxygen/ventilation and vasopressors as needed.
- Treat CRS under the current centre grading/pathway, commonly with IL-6 receptor blockade (tocilizumab), with steroids or additional immunomodulation when indicated; do not withhold necessary rescue solely from fear of impairing cancer therapy.

- **ICANS** may present with inattention, aphasia, altered handwriting, confusion, seizures or reduced consciousness, with or without simultaneous CRS.
- Record a baseline/serial ICE assessment, check glucose/electrolytes and exclude haemorrhage, infection and nonconvulsive seizures; obtain urgent neurological/ICU input, EEG and imaging as indicated.
- Corticosteroids are central to significant ICANS treatment.
- Tocilizumab is used for associated CRS, **not as the sole treatment of isolated ICANS**.
- Secure the airway and manage seizures/cerebral oedema when necessary.
- Cytopenias, hypogammaglobulinaemia and later infections also matter after CAR-T.
- Immune-effector-cell-associated HLH-like deterioration needs the specialist team's separate assessment; not every high ferritin after CAR-T is interchangeable with CRS.

## Self-marking checklist

- Identifies the dominant haematological emergency before induction
- APL: urgent specialist ATRA and haemostatic support
- Leukostasis/viscosity and cautious necessary RBC transfusion
- Recognises and manages tumour-lysis metabolic/renal risk
- Rasburicase/G6PD and no routine alkalinisation
- Recognises sepsis, paraprotein and myeloma organ risks
- Communicates anti-CD38 compatibility interference and procedure timing
- Recognises CAR-T CRS/ICANS, treats possible sepsis concurrently and uses the treating centre pathway
- Does not use tocilizumab alone for isolated ICANS; monitors neurological deterioration and cytopenias

items.title: 32. A patient with haemophilia receiving non-factor prophylaxis is booked for major…
items.q: A patient with haemophilia receiving non-factor prophylaxis is booked for major surgery. The APTT is normal. Compare the implications of emicizumab, antithrombin-lowering treatment and anti-TFPI therapy for assessment, haemostatic cover and laboratory monitoring.
items.a:
### Identify the treatment before interpreting the test

- Obtain the haemophilia-centre plan, diagnosis (A or B), baseline severity, inhibitor status, exact agent, last dose, prior bleeding/thrombosis and the proposed operation.
- Non-factor prophylaxis changes haemostasis without necessarily replacing FVIII/FIX.
- A normal APTT does **not** prove normal factor activity or adequate major-surgery cover.
- Do not interrupt an unfamiliar long-acting drug or add high-dose factor/bypassing agents empirically: coordinate the specialist perioperative and rescue plans well ahead of elective surgery.

### Compare the mechanisms

| Treatment family | Mechanism and implications |
|---|---|
| **Emicizumab** | Bispecific antibody that bridges FIXa/FX and mimics part of FVIIIa cofactor activity in haemophilia A; it does not treat haemophilia B or eradicate a FVIII inhibitor |
| **Fitusiran** | Antithrombin-directed siRNA lowers antithrombin synthesis and increases thrombin generation; a rebalancing strategy for haemophilia A/B, with or without inhibitors in its US approval |
| **Anti-TFPI agents** (for example concizumab/marstacimab) | Reduce tissue-factor-pathway-inhibitor activity to rebalance coagulation; exact approved population, breakthrough-bleed treatment and monitoring are product-specific |

Availability and approval differ by country; a US label is evidence of a therapy and its safety requirements, not a claim that it is funded or stocked locally. These are prophylactic strategies, not universal acute surgical reversal products.

### Laboratory interpretation and major-surgery cover

- Emicizumab markedly shortens APTT and invalidates many APTT-based FVIII/inhibitor measurements.
- Use an appropriately validated **bovine-reagent chromogenic FVIII assay** and inhibitor testing when indicated, with the laboratory aware of the drug.
- One-stage FVIII results must not be used to declare major surgery protected.
- Major surgery usually still requires factor or bypassing cover, selected by inhibitor status and the written centre plan.
- In an emicizumab-treated inhibitor patient, **rFVIIa is generally preferred to aPCC**, because aPCC exposure can cause TMA/thrombosis; the drug-specific rescue policy remains essential.

- For antithrombin-lowering and anti-TFPI agents, conventional clotting tests are not a general validated perioperative target.
- Fitusiran uses scheduled antithrombin-activity monitoring under its label and requires special breakthrough-bleed/surgery guidance; over-treatment with conventional factor/bypassing regimens can cause thrombosis.
- Its 2025 US approval carries major warnings for thrombotic events and gallbladder disease, with hepatic monitoring.
- Do not copy a historical fixed trial dose or extrapolate an emicizumab assay/rescue rule to every rebalancing drug.

### Integrate the anaesthetic plan and follow-up

- Use an experienced centre and confirm access to the chosen haemostatic products, assays and rescue team before incision.
- Plan atraumatic airway/vascular techniques, conservative regional decisions, surgical haemostasis, appropriate TXA where suitable, normothermia and postoperative analgesia/rehabilitation.
- A normal APTT is not clearance for a neuraxial catheter.
- Monitor actual bleeding, Hb and appropriate specialist assays, as well as thrombotic/TMA features, renal dysfunction and drug-specific adverse effects.
- Document which tests are unreliable and who controls rescue dosing at every transfer.
- Treatment innovation improves prophylaxis but does not remove the need for an individual major-surgery haemostatic plan.

## Self-marking checklist

- Establishes A/B phenotype, inhibitor status, exact drug and centre plan
- Distinguishes factor mimicry from antithrombin/TFPI rebalancing
- Explains why a normal APTT does not prove major-surgery protection
- Uses validated bovine chromogenic/inhibitor assays with emicizumab
- Plans factor/bypassing cover and emicizumab/aPCC risk appropriately
- Recognises fitusiran drug-specific monitoring and thrombotic/gallbladder/hepatic risks
- Does not assume foreign licensing equals local availability
- Provides safe technique, postoperative monitoring and clear rescue/assay handover

items.title: 2025.2 Q5: Point-of-care testing in acute haemorrhage
items.q: Evaluate point-of-care testing modalities used in the management of acute intraoperative haemorrhage.
items.model:
### Why point-of-care testing (POCT)

Conventional PT/APTT/fibrinogen testing assesses selected plasma pathways; platelet count is a separate cellular test. Laboratory turnaround varies and may lag rapid bleeding. Early VEM amplitudes and blood gases are often available within minutes, supporting targeted decisions; a complete VEM/lysis assessment takes longer.

### Modalities

**Viscoelastic tests (TEG, ROTEM, Sonoclot, ClotPro)**

- *Basis*: whole-blood clot formation measured over time (clotting time, clot kinetics, maximum clot firmness, lysis).
- *Advantages*: assess selected components of **whole-blood clot initiation, strength and lysis under low shear**, without reproducing the whole in-vivo haemostatic system (factors, fibrinogen, platelets, fibrinolysis)
  - Rapid early amplitude values (A5/A10) guide therapy
  - Can reduce component use when integrated into validated bleeding algorithms, with evidence differing by setting
  - Detect **hyperfibrinolysis** (and so guide tranexamic acid).
- *Limitations*: do not assess **platelet function** well (without platelet mapping), von Willebrand disease or the effect of antiplatelet drugs
  - Insensitive to some **anticoagulants** (some DOACs) and typically run at 37°C, so may conceal the patient's hypothermic impairment
  - Do not assume a normal trace excludes physiological or unmeasured defects
  - Variability between machines and reagents
  - Sample handling and operator error
  - Good evidence in cardiac and liver surgery but **weaker in trauma and obstetrics**
  - Need training and quality control.

**Platelet function tests (multiplate, VerifyNow, TEG platelet mapping):** assess antiplatelet drug effect and platelet contribution; limited by thrombocytopenia, haematocrit and by being a snapshot; uncertain correlation with bleeding.

**Activated clotting time (ACT):** heparin monitoring for bypass and vascular surgery; **non-specific**, affected by hypothermia, haemodilution and platelet count.

**Point-of-care INR/PT/aPTT:** selected coagulation endpoints measured by platform-specific methods; many devices use whole blood but report a plasma-pathway result. Accuracy and validation may be limited outside their intended anticoagulant-monitoring use, particularly in shock, low haematocrit and extreme results.

**Blood gas analysers:** **haemoglobin, ionised calcium, lactate, pH and potassium** guide transfusion and calcium therapy; no coagulation information alone.

**Fibrinogen assays (functional fibrinogen from viscoelastic tests):** key because fibrinogen is the first factor to fall; the Clauss method lab result is slow.

### Evaluation

- Viscoelastic-guided algorithms reduce blood product use and probably bleeding in cardiac surgery, but mortality benefit is unproven and **trials in trauma (ITACTIC) were inconclusive**.
- POCT works best with a **local algorithm**, regular quality assurance, and clinical judgement; no single test addresses all components, so combine viscoelastic testing, platelet testing as indicated, blood gas and clinical findings.
rubric: Rationale: speed and goal-directed therapy compared with laboratory tests
Viscoelastic tests: basis, advantages and limitations
Platelet function and ACT testing described
Blood gas parameters (haemoglobin, calcium, lactate) as POCT
Specific limitations (platelets, DOACs, hypothermia, sample handling)
Combines tests within a local algorithm

items.title: 2025.1 Q5: Major transfusion reactions under general anaesthesia
items.q: Outline the diagnosis and management of major transfusion reactions during general anaesthesia.
items.model:
### Context

Under anaesthesia, the usual warning symptoms (fever, rigors, pain, dyspnoea) are masked. Diagnosis rests on **unexplained cardiovascular or respiratory change, bleeding, haemoglobinuria, or rash** during or soon after a transfusion.

### Types and diagnosis

- **Acute haemolytic reaction (ABO incompatibility):** hypotension, tachycardia, **diffuse oozing (DIC)**, haemoglobinuria (red or brown urine), raised temperature, bronchospasm. Check the bag against the patient; send blood for repeat crossmatch, direct antiglobulin test, free haemoglobin, bilirubin, LDH, coagulation, and urine.
- **Anaphylaxis (multiple mechanisms; anti-IgA in selected patients):** hypotension, bronchospasm, urticaria, angioedema; tryptase.
- **TRALI:** acute hypoxaemia and **bilateral pulmonary infiltrates** within 6 hours, permeability oedema without hydrostatic overload as the main explanation. Coexisting cardiac disease and mixed TRALI/TACO are possible; filling pressure/BNP alone does not decide.
- **TACO:** hypertension, raised JVP, pulmonary oedema, positive fluid balance; high BNP; improves with diuresis.
- **Bacterial contamination/sepsis** (platelets especially): fever, hypotension, rigors, positive cultures.
- **Febrile non-haemolytic reaction** (mild), **hyperkalaemia**, **hypocalcaemia** with rapid transfusion, hypothermia.
- Differentials: drug anaphylaxis, sepsis, surgical haemorrhage, embolism.

### Management

- **1.** **Stop the transfusion**, keep the bag and giving set; **maintain IV access with a fresh set/line and 0.9% saline**; do not flush the implicated blood into the patient or restart a unit implicated in a major reaction.
- **2.** Call for help, 100% oxygen, secure airway, and **resuscitate by ABC**.
- **3.** **Check identity** (patient, bag, compatibility) and call the **blood bank/transfusion service** to investigate and quarantine blood.
- **4.** **Supportive therapy:** fluids, vasopressors (adrenaline for anaphylaxis), restore renal perfusion and monitor urine/electrolytes; avoid indiscriminate fluid loading or forced mannitol/diuresis as a substitute for treating shock (diuretics only for a justified indication after assessment), treat DIC with products guided by viscoelastic tests, treat hyperkalaemia, ventilate (TRALI: lung-protective), diuretics for TACO.
- **5.** **Antibiotics** (broad-spectrum) for suspected bacterial contamination, cultures of patient and product.
- **6.** **Monitor in ICU/HDU**, renal function, and complete incident reporting/haemovigilance and **disclosure**.

- Keep the implicated bag and giving set for transfusion service investigation.
- Maintain emergency resuscitation through fresh tubing or alternate access.
- If the patient still needs urgent components, agree on the safest replacement with transfusion medicine.
- Once stabilised, document the sequence of products, symptoms and treatments and communicate the suspected reaction to the patient and future treating teams.

items.title: 2024.2 Q10: Intraoperative cell salvage: circuit, indications and drawbacks
items.q: Outline the functional elements of an intraoperative cell salvage system. (30%) Discuss the indications, advantages and disadvantages of intraoperative cell salvage. (70%)
items.model:
### Collection, processing and administration

- Use trained staff, a separate salvage suction circuit and a clearly identified patient.
- Anticoagulant (heparinised IV-grade saline or citrate at the manufacturer's specified concentration/rate) mixes with shed blood; low suction, commonly −100 to −150 mmHg, and aspiration from a pool limit haemolysis.
- The collection reservoir filters gross debris.
- Swab washing may recover cells using IV-grade isotonic saline; avoid hypotonic irrigation fluid.

- A centrifuge separates cells by density.
- Discard supernatant and wash the red cells with IV-grade 0.9% saline according to the device programme, removing most anticoagulant, free Hb, plasma and contaminants.
- Return a labelled **washed RBC suspension**, commonly haematocrit around 50–70%, through an appropriate administration filter.
- This supplies essentially **no platelets or clotting factors**.
- Follow the device/local expiry; the BJAEd review recommends reinfusion within **6 h of first collection**, rather than applying the allogeneic 4-hour rule to every salvage system.
- Do not pressurise the salvage bag or force blood through a leucocyte-depletion filter: air embolism, bag rupture and hypotension are risks.

### Indications and benefits

- Consider collection when anticipated loss exceeds **500 mL or 10% blood volume**, with processing governed by yield and economics: major vascular/cardiac, revision orthopaedic/spinal, trauma and selected obstetric/oncological operations.
- Particularly useful with rare antibodies or accepted alternatives to donor blood.
- Reduced allogeneic exposure conserves stock and avoids some donor-related hazards.
- Cells retain oxygen-carrying function without a donor storage period; this does not guarantee better survival or eliminate every transfusion risk.
- Initial set-up does not mean processed blood is immediately available in exsanguination.

### Limitations and contamination decisions

Equipment, disposables, staff training, quality assurance and sufficient case volume determine value. Haemolysis, identification error, hypothermia, air embolism, residual contamination, and reinfusion hypotension—especially with some leucocyte filters—can occur. Large-volume RBC-only salvage still requires haemostatic component and calcium monitoring.

- Divert suction away from faeces, urine, gross pus, chlorhexidine/iodine, topical haemostatic agents and unset bone cement.
- **Sepsis and malignancy are not absolute contraindications:** use individual risk assessment, careful collection/washing and selected filtration; filters do not guarantee sterility or removal of all malignant cells.
- Routine irradiation of salvaged cancer blood is not a universal requirement.
- Obstetric use requires a specific protocol; leucocyte-depletion filters are not universally mandatory and can impede rapid flow/cause hypotension.
- RhD-negative unsensitised mothers with RhD-positive infants need assessment for fetomaternal haemorrhage and anti-D under local policy.
- Sickle disease/trait and thalassaemia require specialist consideration of sickling/fragility.
- Obtain individual consent, including whether a continuous circuit or swab washing is accepted.
