items.title: 2022.2 Q5: Haemophilia A for total knee replacement
items.q: A 56-year-old male with haemophilia A is scheduled to undergo a total knee replacement. Describe the pathogenesis of haemophilia A and its complications. (50%) Discuss how the presence of haemophilia A influences your perioperative management of this patient. (50%)
items.model:
### Pathogenesis and complications (50%)

- **Haemophilia A** is an **X-linked recessive deficiency (or dysfunction) of factor VIII**, causing failure of the intrinsic tenase complex (FIXa, FVIIIa) and impaired thrombin generation, so clots are unstable and slow.
- It affects males, with female carriers variably affected.
- **Severity by factor VIII level:** severe (under 1%), moderate (1 to 5%), mild (5 to 40%).
- Coagulation tests: typically **prolonged aPTT, normal PT and platelets**, but mild disease can have a normal aPTT.
- Factor assays establish activity; emicizumab can normalise aPTT despite severe endogenous FVIII deficiency.
- **Complications**

- **Haemarthrosis** (knee, elbow, ankle) leading to **haemophilic arthropathy**, synovitis and joint destruction (the reason for the knee replacement).
- Muscle haematoma, **intracranial haemorrhage**, airway and retroperitoneal bleeding.
- **Inhibitors** (alloantibodies to FVIII, 20 to 30% in severe disease), **blood-borne viruses** (hepatitis C and HIV from older plasma products), and renal and chronic pain problems.

### Perioperative management (50%)

- **Major centre** with a haemophilia team; **multidisciplinary plan with haematology** well in advance.
- **Preoperative:** FVIII level and **inhibitor screen**, FBC and group and screen, viral status, liver function; plan recombinant factor VIII (or extended half-life product, or emicizumab with adjunct as directed); optimise Hb.
- **Factor replacement:** raise FVIII to **80 to 100% before surgery**, then maintain a specialist-defined peak/trough plan (WFH higher-dose **peak** examples: **60–80% days 1–3, 40–60% days 4–6, 30–50% days 7–14**) including rehabilitation; give by **bolus or continuous infusion**, **measure levels** (pre, post, daily).
  - If inhibitors exist, select specialist factor/bypassing treatment.
  - In an emicizumab-treated inhibitor patient, **rFVIIa is preferred over aPCC/FEIBA** because of TMA/thrombosis risk; use validated bovine-reagent chromogenic FVIII/inhibitor assays.
  - Emicizumab alone is not adequate cover for major surgery.
- **Adjuncts:** **tranexamic acid** (IV, with caution in renal bleeding), desmopressin in mild disease, and meticulous surgical haemostasis; **avoid IM injections** and NSAIDs.
- **Anaesthesia:** GA is usual; **neuraxial/regional blocks are risky** unless factor levels are normal and the haematologist agrees; use ultrasound and fine needles for peripheral blocks; **avoid nasal intubation**, gentle laryngoscopy, and take care with positioning and tourniquet.
- **Blood management:** assess physiological tolerance of anaemia, use appropriate transfusion thresholds, consider salvage only with appropriate selection, and use tranexamic acid, and anticipate **postoperative bleeding**.
- **Postoperative:** HDU, continued factor cover, multimodal analgesia (no NSAIDs), thromboprophylaxis (mechanical, individualised), and rehabilitation planning.
rubric: Factor VIII deficiency, X-linked, severity classification
Surgery in a major centre with haematology input
Factor VIII replacement with targets, timing and level monitoring
Tranexamic acid and avoidance of NSAIDs and IM injections

items.title: 2021.1 Q14: Warfarin for atrial fibrillation: perioperative anticoagulation
items.q: Discuss the options for anticoagulation management in the perioperative period for a patient taking warfarin for atrial fibrillation who requires a laparotomy for ischaemic bowel.
items.model:
### Overview

This is **emergency surgery**, so there is no time for the usual 5-day interruption. The priority is **rapid reversal of warfarin** while weighing the **embolic risk** (the likely cause of the ischaemia) against **surgical bleeding**.

### Preoperative

- **Assess urgency** (resuscitate, antibiotics, and proceed within hours), the last INR, last dose, and the indication: **AF with prior embolism** is high risk; CHA2DS2-VASc score.
- **Reversal:**
  - **Prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC)** 25 to 50 units/kg (INR-based) **plus vitamin K 5 to 10 mg IV** (slow). PCC acts within minutes, IV vitamin K begins sustained correction over several hours but maintains the effect.
  - FFP is slower and large-volume (volume overload); use only if PCC is unavailable.
  - Aim for INR **below 1.5** (neuraxial placement needs normalised INR under the relevant guideline and is inappropriate during this unstable urgent scenario).
- Weigh vitamin K dose: high doses can make later re-anticoagulation difficult, but at this stage safety comes first.

### Intraoperative

- **Plan for bleeding:** arterial line, large-bore access, blood available, viscoelastic testing, TXA only for an appropriate bleeding indication rather than automatically in ischaemic bowel, selected cell salvage, and normothermia.
- Avoid regional/neuraxial block unless INR is normal; use **TAP/rectus sheath** only with caution.

### Postoperative

- **Restart anticoagulation early** once haemostasis is secure (timing individualised to haemostasis, bowel/vascular findings and ongoing embolic risk; therapeutic treatment after major surgery may need ≥48–72 h or longer), after evaluating the actual embolic cause/risk; if a true ongoing high-risk embolic indication requires therapeutic treatment while nil by mouth, titratable IV UFH may be selected once bleeding allows.
  - Do not automatically bridge AF or prescribe a fixed UFH-to-LMWH sequence.
  - Restart warfarin and any overlap only under the agreed specialist plan; give ordinary VTE prophylaxis separately when safe.
- ICU monitoring for bleeding, re-ischaemia, and renal function; involve haematology/surgeons.

- Establish the indication, last dose, measured INR, recent thrombosis or stroke and surgical timing in parallel with resuscitation.
- Recheck INR after reversal and follow its trajectory after the short-lived replacement factors.
- The decision to restart depends on durable haemostasis and the independent risk of interruption.
- Distinguish prophylactic anticoagulation from returning to full-dose therapy and document a named review time.
rubric: Balance of embolic risk versus bleeding
Reversal with PCC and vitamin K (doses and INR target)
Individualises postoperative anticoagulation, route and timing; no automatic therapeutic bridge

items.title: 2019.2 Q11: Rivaroxaban in a patient on a transplant waiting list
items.q: A patient on an organ transplantation waiting list is taking rivaroxaban for recurrent pulmonary emboli. Discuss your perioperative anticoagulation plan.
items.model:
### Key issues

- **High thrombotic risk** (recurrent PE) with **unpredictable timing** of a **high-bleeding-risk** operation (organ transplantation), so the transplant is effectively elective until the call, then urgent.
- **Rivaroxaban:** direct factor Xa inhibitor, peak 2 to 4 hours, **half-life 5 to 9 hours (up to 11 to 13 hours in the elderly)**, about **one-third renally cleared**; **no routine INR-based monitoring**; normal PT/APTT cannot exclude relevant activity.
  - A drug-calibrated anti-Xa assay is preferred when quantification will change an urgent decision.

### Planning (in consultation)

Multidisciplinary plan with **transplant team, haematology and anaesthesia** well before the call.

**At listing (stable phase)**

- Consider a transplant-specific **alternative maintenance strategy:** selected LMWH with renal adjustment, or warfarin because INR is measurable and rapid reversal is available; warfarin is not short-acting.
  - IV UFH is a short-acting, titratable inpatient option when justified, not routine chronic outpatient therapy.
  - The organ, anticipated call interval, renal function and thrombotic risk determine the plan with haematology.
- If rivaroxaban continues, maintain a written call-in plan and a reliable last-dose record; ask and verify the time rather than assuming it is unknown.

**At the call (urgent surgery)**

- **Ask the time of the last dose**, renal function, weight, and perform an anti-Xa level if available.
- If surgery cannot wait (usually transplant ischaemic times are limited), **delay induction where feasible** towards a drug/renal-function-specific low residual level (routine high-bleeding-risk interruption is usually longer than 12–24 h; organ ischaemic time may preclude waiting) or use **reversal:** specialist-directed **4-factor PCC (often 25–50 IU/kg under protocol)** if clinically indicated.
  - Do not present andexanet as routine preoperative reversal: indications/availability are restricted, thrombosis is a major concern, and it can cause heparin unresponsiveness if CPB is required.
  - US sales ended in December 2025 after an FDA safety review; this does not establish NZ availability.
  - Activated charcoal is an early-ingestion option with airway protection, usually within about 2 h; later use is drug-specific specialist advice.
- Plan for **bleeding:** viscoelastic testing, blood products, tranexamic acid, cell salvage; avoid neuraxial block.

**Postoperative**

- Restart anticoagulation early at therapeutic dose once bleeding allows (usually ≥48–72 h after high-bleeding-risk surgery, and only when haemostasis permits); use **UFH or LMWH** initially because of renal graft function, drug interactions (calcineurin inhibitors) and the flexibility needed.
rubric: Recognises high thrombotic risk and high bleeding risk surgery
Considers a transplant-specific alternative maintenance/call-up strategy; no routine DOAC bridge
Time of last dose and urgent options at the call
Indication-specific PCC/reversal decisions, andexanet safety/access limits and early charcoal caveats
Bleeding plan and avoidance of neuraxial block
Postoperative restart with renal and drug interaction awareness

items.title: 2019.1 Q13: Family history of von Willebrand disease
items.q: Outline your approach to the perioperative management of a patient who gives a strong family history of von Willebrand disease.
items.model:
### Overview

- Von Willebrand disease (VWD) is the **commonest inherited bleeding disorder** (laboratory low-VWF phenotypes are more prevalent than clinically significant diagnosed disease), autosomal, due to deficiency or dysfunction of **von Willebrand factor (VWF)**, which mediates platelet adhesion and carries factor VIII.
- Presentation: mucocutaneous bleeding (epistaxis, menorrhagia, easy bruising, postpartum haemorrhage), and surgical bleeding.

### Confirm the diagnosis

- **History:** personal bleeding (dental extraction, surgery, menstrual, postpartum), drugs (aspirin, NSAIDs, anticoagulants), and a structured bleeding score.
- **Tests:** FBC, **aPTT** (may be prolonged), PT; **VWF antigen, VWF activity (ristocetin cofactor/GPIbM), factor VIII**, VWF multimers, blood group (group O has lower VWF); repeat testing, because levels vary with stress, pregnancy, exercise and oestrogen.
- **Types:** **Type 1** (partial quantitative deficiency; most common, mild), **Type 2** (qualitative: 2A, 2B, 2M, 2N), **Type 3** (virtually absent VWF, severe).
- **Refer to haematology** well before elective surgery.

### Management

- **Responders (mostly type 1):** **desmopressin (DDAVP) 0.3 micrograms/kg IV** over 30 minutes, an hour before surgery (VWF and FVIII rise 2- to 5-fold), after a **test dose** with levels.
  - Limit to 24 to 48 hours (**tachyphylaxis**); **fluid restriction and sodium monitoring** (hyponatraemia, seizures); caution in the elderly, ischaemic heart disease, and children under 2 years.
- **Non-responders, severe/type 3 disease, most type 2 disease, or major surgery** (selected type 2 responders require specialist testing; DDAVP must not be sole major-surgery cover): **VWF/FVIII concentrate** (e.g. Biostate, Wilate), aiming for **VWF activity and FVIII above 50 to 100%** before surgery and both **VWF activity and FVIII ≥0.50 IU/mL for at least 3 days** after major surgery, extended according to procedure/bleeding risk and serial trough levels.
  - **Type 2B:** desmopressin is contraindicated (thrombocytopenia).
  - Platelets in Type 3 with alloantibodies.
- **Adjuncts:** **tranexamic acid** (also as mouthwash), local haemostasis, avoid NSAIDs/aspirin, and for menorrhagia hormonal therapy.
- **Anaesthesia:** neuraxial/deep blocks require an individualised haemostasis plan, adequate VWF **and FVIII**, no additional coagulopathy and a safe catheter-removal/maintenance plan with haematology; one value above 50% is not a universal clearance; avoid nasal intubation, IM injections; take care with laryngoscopy.
- **Postoperative:** monitor for bleeding for several days, continue prophylaxis, and plan follow-up.
rubric: History, family history and bleeding scores
Regional anaesthesia criteria and postoperative monitoring

items.title: 2019.1 Q10: Microcytic anaemia before revision hip replacement
items.q: These are the blood results of a 65-year-old man scheduled for a revision total hip replacement. Hb 120 g/L (130-165), MCV 78 fL (80-100), WCC 5.5, Plt 250, Na 136, K 4.0, Urea 5.5, Cr 100. Iron 8 µmol/L (5-30), transferrin 3.2 g/L (2.0-3.2), transferrin saturation 12% (10-45), ferritin 40 µg/L (25-300), C-reactive protein 8.0 mg/L (0-5). Interpret these results. (30%) How would you manage this patient preoperatively? (70%)
items.model:
### Interpretation (30%)

- **Mild microcytic anaemia** (Hb 120, MCV 78) in a man.
- **Iron studies:** low-normal iron and **transferrin saturation 12% (low for assessment of iron availability)**, **ferritin 40, not reassuring in this inflammatory/microcytic context**.
  - With **CRP mildly raised**, ferritin (an acute-phase protein) is falsely elevated, so **iron deficiency cannot be excluded:** a ferritin under 100 µg/L with TSAT under 20% in inflammation is consistent with **absolute or functional iron deficiency** (mixed with anaemia of chronic inflammation from the arthritic/failed joint).
- Normal white cells and platelets, and no major biochemical renal abnormality evident, but creatinine 100 alone does not establish normal CrCl/eGFR in a 65-year-old.
- **Differential for microcytosis:** iron deficiency (including **occult gastrointestinal blood loss**, especially in a 65-year-old man), anaemia of chronic disease, thalassaemia trait, sideroblastic anaemia.

### Preoperative management (70%)

- **1.** **Investigate the cause:** history (melaena, weight loss, NSAIDs, diet), examination, appropriate referral for **GI investigation (endoscopy/colonoscopy)**
  - A negative stool-blood test must not be used to exclude the source or delay indicated investigation since a man of this age with iron deficiency needs a source
  - Consider B12/folate, reticulocytes, haemoglobin electrophoresis if indicated.
- **2.** **Treat the anaemia** (patient blood management): **IV iron** (a locally available formulation dosed to calculated deficit, body weight and product limits) is preferred if oral iron is ineffective, not tolerated, or surgery is within 4 to 6 weeks (oral iron about 40–60 mg elemental daily or 80–100 mg on alternate days, according to formulation/tolerance)
  - Recheck Hb in 2 to 4 weeks
  - Erythropoietin only in selected cases.
- **3.** **Timing:** revision hip surgery has high blood loss (often 1 to 2 litres), so discuss deferring elective surgery for investigation/optimisation; **130 g/L is an optimisation aim, not a universal cancellation or transfusion target**.
- **4.** **Blood loss minimisation:** tranexamic acid, cell salvage, normothermia, restrictive transfusion triggers, group and screen with crossmatch, and review of antiplatelets and anticoagulants.
- **5.** **Other optimisation:** cardiovascular assessment, and stop NSAIDs where possible.

> **Current evidence:** PREVENTT did not show lower transfusion/death with preoperative IV iron in its anaemic major-abdominal-surgery population. Treat demonstrated deficiency, investigate its cause and monitor response without promising a universal transfusion or survival benefit. IV iron risks include hypersensitivity, extravasation staining and formulation-related hypophosphataemia.

- Use the indices together.
- Low transferrin saturation signals limited available iron and inflammation can elevate ferritin.
- Look for menstrual or gastrointestinal blood loss as appropriate, and investigate the underlying cause in parallel with replacement.
- Document a repeat haemoglobin and a date to reconsider surgery.
- Where delay itself has consequences, agree on the plan with the treating team and patient.
rubric: Interprets Hb, MCV and iron studies in the context of raised CRP
Identifies likely iron deficiency or mixed anaemia
Investigates the cause (occult GI loss) in a man of 65
Iron therapy (oral versus IV) and recheck

items.title: 2017.2 Q13: Coagulopathy in the multitrauma patient
items.q: Discuss your strategy for the management of coagulopathy in the multitrauma patient.
items.model:
### Mechanisms

**Trauma-induced coagulopathy** is present on arrival in about 25% of severe trauma. It combines **tissue injury and shock** (endothelial/glycocalyx injury, variable fibrinolytic phenotypes, platelet dysfunction and early fibrinogen depletion) with **resuscitation-related** dilution, **hypothermia, acidosis, hypocalcaemia**, consumption (DIC), and pre-existing anticoagulants.

### Diagnosis and monitoring

- Early **clinical recognition** (shock, mechanism, bleeding, oozing).
- **Viscoelastic testing** (ROTEM/TEG) to guide products: fibrinogen deficiency (low A5/MCF), fibrinolysis (lysis index), platelet and factor deficiency.
  - Conventional tests (INR, aPTT, platelet count, **Clauss fibrinogen**) are slower but used in parallel; **ionised calcium**, lactate, base excess, haemoglobin and temperature repeatedly (every 30 minutes).

### Strategy

- **1.** **Control the source** quickly (damage control surgery, interventional radiology, pelvic binder, tourniquet).
- **2.** **Minimise crystalloid**; permissive hypotension (SBP 80 to 90 mmHg; MAP 50 to 60) until bleeding is controlled, but not in head or spinal cord injury.
- **3.** **Massive transfusion protocol:** balanced initial components under the local MHP.
  - If using **RBC:FFP:platelet donor-equivalent ratios 1:1:1 or 2:1:1**, specify that an adult platelet dose contains multiple donor-equivalent units; this is not one adult platelet bag per RBC, then goal-directed by viscoelastic tests.
  - PROPPR did not demonstrate a significant overall mortality difference; haemostasis and early exsanguination outcomes favoured 1:1:1.
  - State ratio order and adult platelet-dose equivalence.
- **4.** **Tranexamic acid** 1 g over 10 minutes then 1 g over 8 hours, started within **3 hours** (CRASH-2); do not wait for, withhold or stop the indicated early regimen solely because standard VEM shows no hyperfibrinolysis.
- **5.** **Fibrinogen replacement:** cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate to maintain fibrinogen **above 1.5 to 2 g/L**.
- **6.** **Calcium:** replace to ionised calcium above **1.1 mmol/L** using serial results and clinical physiology; 0.9 mmol/L is not a desired resuscitation target.
- **7.** **PCC** for a specific justified indication, particularly urgent VKA reversal; do not give empirically to all trauma patients (PROCOAG found no transfusion benefit and increased thromboembolism); consider desmopressin for platelet dysfunction.
- **8.** **Prevent the lethal triad:** warm fluids and room, forced-air warmer, correct acidosis by perfusion; target temperature above 36 degrees.
- **9.** **Platelets** above 50 x 10^9/L (100 in head injury); **haemoglobin** 70 to 90 g/L.
- **10.** **Agents of uncertain value:** recombinant factor VIIa (not recommended routinely), whole blood (in use in some military and civilian trauma systems).
- **11.** **Thromboprophylaxis** once bleeding is controlled (trauma is a hypercoagulable state later).
rubric: Diagnosis and repeated monitoring (viscoelastic tests, calcium)

items.title: 2016.1 Q15: Preoperative anaemia (Hb 80) before hysterectomy
items.q: A 40-year-old patient who is scheduled for elective total abdominal hysterectomy has a haemoglobin level of 80 g/l. Describe your preoperative assessment and optimisation of this patient's anaemia.
items.model:
### Overview

An Hb of 80 g/L (moderate–severe) before elective surgery should be **investigated and treated**, because preoperative anaemia increases transfusion, complications, and mortality. In a premenopausal woman scheduled for hysterectomy, the likely cause is **iron deficiency from menorrhagia** (fibroids, adenomyosis), but I must exclude others.

### Assessment

- **History:** menstrual history and quantity, other blood loss (GI), diet, pregnancy, symptoms (fatigue, breathlessness, angina), medications (NSAIDs, anticoagulants), family history (thalassaemia, haemoglobinopathy), and chronic disease.
- **Examination:** pallor, haemodynamics, signs of heart failure, spleen/lymph nodes.
- **Investigations:** FBC with **MCV**, reticulocytes, blood film, **ferritin, transferrin saturation, iron**, CRP, B12, folate, renal and liver function, thyroid tests, haemoglobin electrophoresis if indicated, and a group and screen. Consider bowel investigation if the pattern is not explained.
- **Differential:** iron deficiency (microcytic), B12/folate deficiency (macrocytic), chronic disease/inflammation, haemoglobinopathy, haemolysis, bone marrow disease.

### Optimisation

- **1.** **Timely approach:** **postpone** elective surgery until Hb is corrected, unless malignancy or serious bleeding; liaise with the gynaecologist.
- **2.** **Iron replacement:** **IV iron** (a product-specific calculated IV iron dose within its weight/maximum infusion limits) is preferred for Hb 80 with time pressure, intolerance or poor oral absorption; oral iron (ferrous sulphate or fumarate about 40–60 mg elemental iron daily or 80–100 mg on alternate days, with vitamin C) if time allows.
  - Expect an increase of **10 to 20 g/L over 2 to 4 weeks**.
- **3.** **Treat menorrhagia** medically (tranexamic acid, progestogens, levonorgestrel IUS) to stop ongoing loss while waiting.
- **4.** **Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents** in selected cases only, with iron; **B12/folate** if deficient.
- **5.** **Transfusion** is reserved for symptomatic patients, those with cardiovascular compromise, or urgent surgery (restrictive trigger of 70 g/L), after discussion about risks.
- **6.** **Intraoperative blood-sparing** measures: tranexamic acid, cell salvage, and meticulous haemostasis.

> **Current evidence:** PREVENTT did not show lower transfusion/death with preoperative IV iron in its anaemic major-abdominal-surgery population. Treat demonstrated deficiency, investigate its cause and monitor response without promising a universal transfusion or survival benefit. IV iron risks include hypersensitivity, extravasation staining and formulation-related hypophosphataemia.

- Use the indices together.
- Low transferrin saturation signals limited available iron and inflammation can elevate ferritin.
- Look for menstrual or gastrointestinal blood loss as appropriate, and investigate the underlying cause in parallel with replacement.
- Document a repeat haemoglobin and a date to reconsider surgery.
- Where delay itself has consequences, agree on the plan with the treating team and patient.

Check for symptoms at rest and on exertion as well as the trajectory of blood loss.
